antq_gootenberg_bible.title: Gutenberg Bible
sents: lead
The Gutenberg Bible, also known as the 42-line Bible, the Mazarin Bible or the B42, is the earliest major book printed in Europe using mass-produced metal movable type.
lead
It marked the start of the "Gutenberg Revolution" and the age of printed books in the West.
lead
The book is valued and revered for its high aesthetic and artistic qualities and its historical significance.
lead
The Gutenberg Bible is an edition of the Latin Vulgate printed in the 1450s by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz (Holy Roman Empire), in present-day Germany.
lead

Out of either 158 or 180 copies that were originally printed, 49 survive in at least substantial portion, 21 of them in entirety; of these, the copy with the earliest visible print date is marked as 15 August 1456.
lead
They are thought to be among the world's most valuable books, although no complete copy has been sold since 1978.
lead
In March 1455, the future Pope Pius II wrote that he had seen pages from the Gutenberg Bible, displayed in Frankfurt to promote the edition.
lead
The 36-line Bible, said to be the second printed Bible, is also sometimes referred to as a Gutenberg Bible, but may be the work of another printer.
Printing history
Preparation of the Bible probably began soon after 1450, and the first finished copies were available in 1454 or 1455.
Printing history
The first precisely datable printing is Gutenberg's 31-line Indulgence which certainly existed by 22 October 1454.
Printing history
Some time later, after more sheets had been printed, the number of lines per page was increased from 40 to 42, presumably to save paper.
Printing history
Therefore, pages 1 to 9 and pages 256 to 265, presumably the first ones printed, have 40 lines each.
Printing history
Page 10 has 41, and from there on the 42 lines appear.
Printing history
Consequently, there are two distinct settings in folios 1–32 and 129–158 of volume I and folios 1–16 and 162 of volume II.
Printing history
The most reliable information about the Bible's date comes from a letter.
Printing history
In March 1455, the future Pope Pius II wrote that he had seen pages from the Gutenberg Bible, being displayed to promote the edition, in Frankfurt.
Printing history
It is not known how many copies were printed, with the 1455 letter citing sources for both 158 and 180 copies.
Printing history
Scholars today think that examination of surviving copies suggests that somewhere between 160 and 185 copies were printed, with about three-quarters on paper and the others on vellum.
The production process: ''Das Werk der Bücher''
Many book-lovers have commented on the high standards achieved in the production of the Gutenberg Bible, some describing it as one of the most beautiful books ever printed.
Pages
The 42-line Bible was printed on the size of paper known as 'Royal'.
Pages
A full sheet of Royal paper measures 42 x and a single untrimmed folio leaf measures 42 x.
Pages
There have been attempts to claim that the book was printed on larger paper measuring 44.5 x, but this assertion is contradicted by the dimensions of existing copies.
Pages
For example, the leaves of the copy in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, measure 40 ×.
Pages
Most fifteenth-century printing papers have a width-to-height ratio of 1:1.4 (e.g.
Pages
30:42 cm) which, mathematically, is a ratio of 1 to the square root of 2 or, simply,.
Pages
Many suggest that this ratio was chosen to match the so-called Golden Ratio,, of 1:1.6; in fact the ratios are, plainly, not at all similar (equating to a difference of about 12 per cent).
Pages
The ratio of 1:1.4 was a long established one for medieval paper sizes.
Type
Each unique character requires a piece of master type in order to be replicated.
Rubrication, illumination and binding
The place of decoration can be known or inferred for about 30 of the surviving copies.
Rubrication, illumination and binding

There has been speculation that the "Master of the Playing Cards", an unidentified engraver who has been called "the first personality in the history of engraving," was partly responsible for the illumination of the copy held by the Princeton University library.
Rubrication, illumination and binding
Most of these copies were bound in either Mainz or Erfurt.
Rubrication, illumination and binding
Most copies were divided into two volumes, the first volume ending with The Book of Psalms.
Early owners
At least some copies are known to have sold for 30 florins (equivalent to about 100 g of gold), which was about three years' wages for a clerk.
Early owners
Although this made them significantly cheaper than manuscript Bibles, most students, priests or other people of moderate income would not have been able to afford them.
Early owners
At present only one copy is known to have been privately owned in the fifteenth century.
Influence on later Bibles
It provided the model for several later editions, including the 36 Line Bible, Mentelin's Latin Bible, and the first and third Eggestein Bibles.
Forgeries

Joseph Martini, a New York book dealer, found that the Gutenberg Bible held by the library of the General Theological Seminary in New York had a forged leaf, carrying part of Chapter 14, all of Chapter 15, and part of Chapter 16 of the Book of Ezekiel.
Forgeries
This made it "the first imperfect Gutenberg Bible ever restored to completeness." In 1978, this copy was sold for US$2.2 million to the Württembergische Landesbibliothek in Stuttgart, Germany.
Surviving copies
, 49 Gutenberg Bibles are known to exist, but of these only 25 are complete.
Fragments
Several fragments and single leaves sold at Christie's Auction House or Sotheby's in the 21st century.
Recent history
Few copies remain in religious institutions, with most now owned by university libraries and other major scholarly institutions.
Recent history
After centuries in which all copies seem to have remained in Europe, the first Gutenberg Bible reached North America in 1847.
Recent history
During the 20th century several long-lost copies were discovered, considerably improving the understanding of how the Bible was produced and distributed.
Recent history
In 1921, a New York rare book dealer, Gabriel Wells, bought a damaged copy, dismantled the book and sold sections and individual leaves to book collectors and libraries.
Recent history
In 1953 Charles Scribner's Sons, also book dealers in New York, dismembered a damaged paper copy of volume II.
Recent history
The largest portion of this, the New Testament, is now owned by Indiana University.
Recent history

The leaf carrying part of Chapter 14, all of Chapter 15, and part of Chapter 16 of the Book of Ezekiel was donated to the General Theological Seminary to repair their copy of the bible (now located at the Württembergische Landesbibliothek).
Recent history
The matching first volume of this copy was subsequently discovered in Mons, Belgium, having been bequeathed by Edmond Puissant to the city in 1934.
Recent history
The only copy held outside Europe and North America is the first volume of a Gutenberg Bible (Hubay 45) at Keio University in Tokyo.
Recent history
The Humanities Media Interface Project (HUMI) at Keio University is known for its high-quality digital images of Gutenberg Bibles and other rare books.
Recent history

Under the direction of Professor Toshiyuki Takamiya, the HUMI team has made digital reproductions of 11 sets of the bible in nine institutions, including both full-text facsimiles held in the collection of the British Library.
Recent history
The last sale of a complete Gutenberg Bible took place in 1978, which sold for $2.4 million (equivalent to $ million in ).
Recent history
The price of a complete copy today is estimated at $25−35 million.
Recent history
A two-volume paper edition of the Gutenberg Bible was stolen from Moscow State University in 2009 and subsequently recovered in an FSB sting operation in 2013.

General bibliography
New York: The Library of The General Theological Seminary, 1953..

antq_shakespear_first_folio.title: First Folio

name: Mr. William Shakespeare's Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies
caption: Title page of the first impression (1623)
author: William Shakespeare
publisher: Edward Blount and William and Isaac Jaggard

sents: lead

William Shakespeare's Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies is a collection of plays by William Shakespeare, commonly referred to by modern scholars as the First Folio, published in 1623, about seven years after Shakespeare's death.
lead
It is considered one of the most influential books ever published.
lead
Printed in folio format and containing 36 of Shakespeare's plays, it was prepared by Shakespeare's colleagues John Heminges and Henry Condell.
lead
It was dedicated to the "incomparable pair of brethren" William Herbert, 3rd Earl of Pembroke, and his brother Philip Herbert, Earl of Montgomery (later 4th Earl of Pembroke).
lead

Although 19 of Shakespeare's plays had been published in quarto before 1623, the First Folio is arguably the only reliable text for about 20 of the plays, and a valuable source text for many of those previously published.
lead
Eighteen of the plays in the First Folio, including The Tempest, Twelfth Night, Macbeth, Julius Caesar and Measure for Measure among others, are not known to have been previously printed.
lead

The Folio includes all of the plays generally accepted to be Shakespeare's, except the following plays which are believed likely to have been written, at least partly, by Shakespeare: Pericles, Prince of Tyre; The Two Noble Kinsmen; Edward III; and the two lost plays, Cardenio and Love's Labour's Won.
lead
Some believe the last of these is an alternative title for a known published Shakespeare play.
Background

After a long career as an actor, dramatist, and sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men (later the King's Men) from until, William Shakespeare died in Stratford-upon-Avon, on 23 April 1616, and was buried in the chancel of the Church of the Holy Trinity two days later.
Background

Shakespeare's works—both poetic and dramatic—had a rich history in print before the publication of the First Folio: from the first publications of Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594), 78 individual printed editions of his works are known.
Background
Of these, 23 consist of his poetry and the remaining 55 his plays.
Background
Counting by number of editions published before 1623, the best-selling works were Venus and Adonis (12 editions), The Rape of Lucrece (six editions), and Henry IV, Part 1 (six editions).
Background
Of the 23 editions of the poems, 16 were published in octavo; the rest, and almost all of the editions of the plays, were printed in quarto.
Background
The average quarto measured 7 by and was typically made up of nine sheets, giving 72 total pages.
Background
Octavos—made by folding a sheet of the same size three times, forming eight leaves with 16 pages—were about half as large as a quarto.
Background

Since the cost of paper represented about 50-75% of a book's total production costs, octavos were generally cheaper to manufacture than quartos, and a common way to reduce publishing costs was to reduce the number of pages needed by compressing (using two columns or a smaller typeface) or abbreviating the text.
Background
Editions of individual plays were typically published in quarto and could be bought for 6d without a binding.
Background
From (Venus and Adonis) and 1598 (The Rape of Lucrece), Shakespeare's narrative poems were published in octavo.
Background
In The Cambridge Companion to Shakespeare's First Folio, Tara L.
Background

Ultimately, however, the choice was a financial one: Venus and Adonis in octavo needed four sheets of paper, versus seven in quarto, and the octavo The Rape of Lucrece needed five sheets, versus 12 in quarto.
Printing

The contents of the First Folio were compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell; the members of the Stationers Company who published the book were the booksellers Edward Blount and the father/son team of William and Isaac Jaggard.
Printing

William Jaggard has seemed an odd choice by the King's Men because he had published the questionable collection The Passionate Pilgrim as Shakespeare's, and in 1619 had printed new editions of 10 Shakespearean quartos to which he did not have clear rights, some with false dates and title pages (the False Folio affair).
Printing
William Jaggard was old, infirm and blind by 1623, and died a month before the book went on sale; most of the work in the project must have been done by his son Isaac.
Printing

The First Folio's publishing syndicate also included two stationers who owned the rights to some of the individual plays that had been previously printed: William Aspley (Much Ado About Nothing and Henry IV, Part 2) and John Smethwick (Love's Labour's Lost, Romeo and Juliet, and Hamlet).
Printing
The printing of the Folio was probably done between February 1622 and early November 1623, and the book was entered into the Stationers' Register on 8 November 1623 (Julian calendar).
Contents
The 36 plays of the First Folio occur in the order given below.
Contents

Troilus and Cressida was originally intended to follow Romeo and Juliet, but the typesetting was stopped, probably due to a conflict over the rights to the play; it was later inserted as the first of the tragedies, when the rights question was resolved.
Compositors
As far as modern scholarship has been able to determine, the First Folio texts were set into type by five compositors, with different spelling habits, peculiarities, and levels of competence.
Compositors
Researchers have labelled them A through E, A being the most accurate, and E an apprentice who had significant difficulties in dealing with manuscript copy.
Compositors
Compositor "E" was most likely one John Leason, whose apprenticeship contract dated only from 4 November 1622.
Compositors
One of the other four might have been a John Shakespeare, of Warwickshire, who apprenticed with Jaggard in 1610 to 1617.
The First Folio and variants
Greg has argued that Edward Knight, the "book-keeper" or "book-holder" (prompter) of the King's Men, did the actual proofreading of the manuscript sources for the First Folio.
The First Folio and variants
Some pages of the First Folio—134 out of the total of 900—were proofread and corrected while the job of printing the book was ongoing.
The First Folio and variants
There were about 500 corrections made to the Folio in this way.
The First Folio and variants

These corrections by the typesetters, however, consisted only of simple typos, clear mistakes in their own work; the evidence suggests that they almost never referred back to their manuscript sources, let alone tried to resolve any problems in those sources.
The First Folio and variants
The well-known cruxes in the First Folio texts were beyond the typesetters' capacity to correct.
The First Folio and variants
The Folio was typeset and bound in "sixes"—three sheets of paper, taken together, were folded into a booklet-like quire or gathering of six leaves, 12 pages.
The First Folio and variants

The sheets were printed in two-page formes, meaning that pages 1 and 12 of the first quire were printed simultaneously on one side of one sheet of paper (which became the "outer" side); then pages 2 and 11 were printed on the other side of the same sheet (the "inner" side).
The First Folio and variants
The same was done with pages 3 and 10, and 4 and 9, on the second sheet, and pages 5 and 8, and 6 and 7, on the third.
The First Folio and variants
Then the first quire could be assembled with its pages in the correct order.
The First Folio and variants
The next quire was printed by the same method: pages 13 and 24 on one side of one sheet, etc.
The First Folio and variants
The First Folio was reprinted three times in the 17th century, each time by different groups of stationers; these editions are referred to as the Second Folio, Third Folio, and Fourth Folio.
Holdings, sales and valuations

Jean-Christophe Mayer, in The Cambridge Companion to Shakespeare's First Folio (2016), estimates the original retail price of the First Folio to be about 15s for an unbound copy, and up to £1 for one bound in calfskin.
Holdings, sales and valuations
It is believed that around 750 copies of the First Folio were printed, of which there are 235 known surviving copies.
Holdings

The world's largest collection is in the possession of the Folger Shakespeare Library (82 copies) in Washington, D.C., followed by Meisei University (12) in Tokyo, the New York Public Library (six) in New York City, and the British Library (five) in London.
Holdings
Together, the nine largest First Folio collections comprise more than half of all known extant copies.
Holdings
Thirty-one American colleges and universities own a total of 38 copies of the First Folio, while seven British universities own 14 copies.
Holdings
In Canada, the University of Toronto's Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library owns a copy and the University of British Columbia another.
Holdings
Ireland's only copy resides in the Old Library at Trinity College Dublin.
Sales and valuations
The First Folio is one of the most valuable printed books in the world: a copy sold at Christie's in New York in October 2001 made $6.16 million hammer price (then £3.73m).
Sales and valuations
In October 2020, a copy sold by Mills College at Christie's fetched a price of $10 million, making it the most expensive work of literature ever auctioned.
Sales and valuations
Oriel College, Oxford, raised a conjectured £3.5 million from the sale of its First Folio to Sir Paul Getty in 2003.
Sales and valuations

To commemorate the 400th anniversary of Shakespeare's death in 2016, the Folger Shakespeare Library toured some of its 82 First Folios for display in all 50 U.S. states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
In 2003, Anthony West identified a book previously thought to be a Second Folio in the collection of Craven Museum in Skipton, North Yorkshire, as a First Folio.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
On 13 July 2006, a complete copy of the First Folio owned by Dr Williams's Library was auctioned at Sotheby's auction house.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
The book, which was in its original 17th-century binding, sold for £2,808,000, less than Sotheby's top estimate of £3.5 million.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
This copy is one of only about 40 remaining complete copies (most of the existing copies are incomplete); only one other copy of the book remains in private ownership.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
On 11 July 2008, it was reported that a copy stolen from Durham University, in 1998 had been recovered after being submitted for valuation at the Folger Shakespeare Library.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios

News reports estimated the folio's value at anywhere from £250,000 in total for the First Folio and all the other books and manuscripts stolen (BBC News, 1998), up to $30 million (The New York Times, 2008).
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
The folio was returned to public display on 19 June 2010 after its 12-year absence.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
Fifty-three-year-old Raymond Scott received an eight-year prison sentence for handling stolen goods, but was acquitted of the theft itself.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
A July 2010 BBC programme about the affair, Stealing Shakespeare, portrayed Scott as a fantasist and petty thief.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
In November 2014, a previously unknown First Folio was found in a public library in Saint-Omer, Pas-de-Calais, France, where it had lain for 200 years.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios

The name "Neville", written on the first surviving page, may indicate that it once belonged to Edward Scarisbrick, who fled England due to anti-Catholic repression, attended the Jesuit Saint-Omer College, and was known to use that alias.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
In March 2016, Christie's announced that a previously unrecorded copy once owned by 19th-century collector Sir George Shuckburgh-Evelyn would be auctioned on 25 May 2016.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
According to the Antiques Trade Gazette, an American collector paid £1,600,000 for it; the buyer also successfully bid on copies of the second, third and fourth folios.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
In April 2016, another new discovery was announced: a First Folio found in Mount Stuart House on the Isle of Bute, Scotland, that originally belonged to Isaac Reed.
Discoveries of previously unknown Folios
Smith has cautioned about overstating the importance of the First Folio.

antq_the_burds_of_america.title: The Birds of America

name: The Birds of America
original_title: The Birds of America; from original drawings by John James Audubon
caption: The cover shows a Louisiana heron
Egretta tricolor (now called tricolored heron)
author: John James Audubon
subject: Birds – North America; Birds – pictorial works

sents: lead
The Birds of America is a book by naturalist and painter John James Audubon, containing illustrations of a wide variety of birds of the United States.
lead
It was first published as a series in sections between 1827 and 1838, in Edinburgh and London.
lead

Not all of the specimens illustrated in the work were collected by Audubon himself; some were sent to him by John Kirk Townsend, who had collected them on Nathaniel Jarvis Wyeth's 1834 expedition with Thomas Nuttall.
lead
The work consists of 435 hand-coloured, life-size prints, made from engraved plates, measuring around 39 by.
lead

It includes images of five extinct birds and three more possibly extinct birds: Carolina parakeet, passenger pigeon, Labrador duck, great auk, heath hen, and, possibly, the Eskimo curlew, ivory-billed woodpecker, and Bachman's warbler.
lead

Also, there are five more images of 'mystery birds' that are not identified with any extant species: Townsend's finch (identified in a later edition as Townsend's bunting), Cuvier's kinglet, carbonated swamp warbler, small-headed flycatcher, and Blue Mountain warbler.
lead
Art historians describe Audubon's work as being of high quality and printed with "artistic finesse".
lead
The plant life backgrounds of some 50 of the bird studies were painted by Audubon's assistant Joseph Mason, but he is not credited for his work in the book.
Early publication history
About 1820, around the age of 35, Audubon declared his intention to paint every bird in North America.
Early publication history
As early as 1807, he developed a method of using wires and threads to hold dead birds in lifelike poses while he drew them.
Early publication history
In 1823, Audubon went to Philadelphia and New York, looking for financial support using subscriptions to enable him to publish his artwork.
Early publication history
The prints were produced from 1827 to 1838 that cost each subscriber around $1,000.
Early publication history
Each set consists of 435 individual plates that are based upon the original paintings.
Early publication history
While William Lizars, of Edinburgh, engraved the first ten plates, Havell actually finished some of those.
Early publication history

As a result, in 1826, he set sail for the United Kingdom with 250 of his original illustrations, looking for the financial support of subscribers and the technical abilities of engravers and printers.
Early publication history
Lizars engraved up to ten of the first plates but was unable to continue the project when his colourists went on strike.
Early publication history
In 1827, Audubon engaged the noted London animal engraver Robert Havell Jr., and his father, Robert Havell Sr.
Early publication history
Havell Jr. oversaw the project through to its completion in 1838.
Early publication history

The original edition of The Birds of America (sometimes called the Havell Edition after its printer, and sometimes called the "Double Elephant Folio", because of its size) was printed on handmade paper 39.5 inches tall by 28.5 inches wide.
Early publication history
From 1826 to 1829, he travelled around the UK and to Paris, lecturing on ornithology and frontier American life in an effort to entice wealthy patrons to subscribe to the series of prints.
Early publication history
Subscribers included: King Charles X of France; Queen Adelaide of the United Kingdom; the 2nd Earl Spencer; and, later, the Americans Daniel Webster and Henry Clay.
Early publication history

An accompanying text, issued separately, was written by Audubon and the Scottish naturalist and ornithologist William MacGillivray and published in five volumes in Edinburgh between 1831 and 1839, under the title Ornithological Biography, or, An account of the habits of the birds of the United States of America.
Early publication history
The additional cost of the five volumes of text brought the total cost of plates and text to about $1000.
Early publication history

Audubon had personally visited Columbia in 1833 and displayed his drawings to the college's president, William Alexander Duer, after which the college raised $800 for its subscription, which was completed in 1838.
Early publication history
Bowen and his team created a smaller Royal Octavo edition, which was issued to subscribers in seven volumes and completed in 1844.
Early publication history
The octavo edition used the text of the Ornithological biography but increased the number of plates to 500, separating some birds which had originally appeared together.
Early publication history
Some new drawings were included, mostly by Audubon's youngest son John Woodhouse Audubon, though Audubon and members of Bowen's team also contributed.
Early publication history
The Bien Edition (after chromolithography pioneer Julius Bien), was a full-sized reissue published in 1858 by Roe Lockwood in New York under the supervision of John Woodhouse Audubon.
Early publication history
Due in part to the Civil War, the edition was never finished; only 15 parts of the 44 part series were completed.
Early publication history
Fewer than 100 subscriptions were sold, making this edition rarer than other early editions.
Public exhibitions
A full 8-volume, double-elephant folio version is on public display in the Audubon Room at the Harlan Hatcher Graduate Library at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.
Public exhibitions
This, the first book purchased by the university, was bought in 1839 for $970 (equivalent to $ in ), at the time an amazing sum.
Public exhibitions
The entire volume of 435 plates is also available for viewing online at the websites of the University of Michigan and the Public Library of Cincinnati and Hamilton County.
Public exhibitions
Since 1992, the Louisiana State University Libraries have hosted "Audubon Day," a semi-annual public showing of all four volumes of LSU's copy of the Birds of America.
Public exhibitions
The set formerly belonged to one of the original subscribers, the Duke of Northumberland, and was purchased with a grant from the Crown Zellerbach Corporation in 1964.
Public exhibitions
In recent years, the event has drawn more than 200 visitors.
Public exhibitions

In 2003, the University of Pittsburgh, which owns a complete collection of Birds of America that had been recently restored and preserved by the Etherington Conservation Center, mounted a major exhibition of 62 selected plates and other materials in its University Art Gallery.
Public exhibitions

In 2007, the university undertook a project to digitize every plate from Birds of America, as well as Audubon's Ornithological Biography, and, for the first time, presented the complete set for public viewing through one site on the internet.
Public exhibitions
This event, called "Audubon day" was first conducted in 2011.
Public exhibitions
In 2004, there was an attempted heist of the Transylvania University's four double-sized folios of Birds of America by four college students.
Public exhibitions

From September 25, 2005 - March 26, 2006, the National Gallery of Art exhibited 50 hand-colored prints from its early edition of The Birds of America, “…one of only 2 known sets of prints preserved in their original unbound state” in Audubon's Dream Realized.
Public exhibitions
In 2007, the book was the subject of an exhibition by the Teylers Museum in Haarlem, which owns a copy it ordered from the original subscription.
Public exhibitions

To commemorate the book's record-breaking sale, the museum decided to display its copy (for which the museum eventually paid 2200 guilders—a fortune at the time—during the years 1827–1838) until January 2011.
Public exhibitions
The Buffalo & Erie County Public Library's Rare Book Room has a complete Birds of America, which is often on display.
Public exhibitions
Only this copy and that owned by the Stark Museum of Art contain 13 additional plates, added late in the project to correct earlier mistakes by compositing new plates onto previous prints.
Public exhibitions
The Field Museum produced and displayed an exhibit based around their copy of Birds of America in 2019–2020.
Public exhibitions
In 2010, the North Carolina Museum of Art began a five-year exhibition of its restored four-volume set purchased for the state by Governor William Alexander Graham in 1846.
Public exhibitions

In 2022, the National Museum of Scotland hosted a major Audubon exhibition, exhibiting a copy of the book, along with prints from their archive and emphasizing the book's historical ties with Edinburgh.
Public exhibitions
Two copies are on permanent display on the mezzanine level of the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library at Yale University.
Public exhibitions
The Rubenstein Rare Book & Manuscript Library at Duke University maintains a four-volume set.
Public exhibitions

Audubon scholars Waldemar Fries and Susanne Low have each attested to the high quality of Trinity’s copy, Fries proclaiming it “probably the finest extant” example of Audubon’s work and Low stating that it “has perhaps the most subtle and true-to-life colors” of the surviving copies.
Collections and archives
Though individual prints are commonly available, only 120 complete sets are known to exist.
Collections and archives

Dartmouth College in New Hampshire owns a partial set that originally belonged to Daniel Webster, along with an even more rare copy of Audubon's original prospectus shared with publishers, of which there are only 16 extant copies.
Collections and archives
It was donated to the college in 1900 by Gurdon Wadsworth Russell, an 1834 graduate of Trinity.
Collections and archives
Union College in Schenectady, NY, possesses a complete copy that was purchased by its president Eliphalet Nott in 1844.
Collections and archives

Toronto Public Library also holds a copy; originally a four-volume set, it was unbound to preserve the individual plates which have been digitized in the library's Digital Archive and stored in custom-made boxes in the Toronto Reference Library.
Collections and archives
Another complete copy of the prints, bound in 17 volumes, belongs to the Library of Parliament in Ottawa, Canada.
Collections and archives
In Australia, the Melbourne Public Library (now State Library Victoria) purchased a four-volume complete copy in 1871 from William Stallard, a school principal in Geelong.
Collections and archives
The library's president, Sir Redmond Barry, negotiated to purchase the copy for £100, half what had been asked, and the library spent a further £16 on restoring the bindings on three of the volumes.
Recent sales
In March 2000, Sheikh Saud Al-Thani of Qatar purchased a copy of The Birds of America at a Christie's auction for $8.8 million, a record for any book at auction.
Recent sales
In December 2010, The Economist magazine estimated that, adjusted for inflation, five of the ten highest prices ever paid for printed books were paid for copies of The Birds of America.
Recent sales
Of the 120 copies known to survive, only thirteen are held in private collections.
Recent sales
In March 2000, the Fox-Bute copy sold at Christie's, New York, for $8,802,500.
Recent sales
In December 2005, an unbound copy, the Providence Athenaeum Set, sold, again at Christie's, New York, for $5.6 million.
Recent sales

On 6 December 2010, a complete copy of the first edition was sold in London at Sotheby's for £7,321,250 during the sale of Magnificent Books, Manuscripts and Drawings from the collection of the 2nd Baron Hesketh.
Recent sales
The winning bid was a record auction price for a printed book and was placed by London-based art dealer Michael Tollemache, who outbid three others during the auction.
Recent sales

According to the provenance details reported by the auction house, the copy's original owner was Henry Witham of Durham, listed as subscriber 11 in Audubon's Ornithological Biography; the first volume of the set bears a presentation inscription from Witham's wife, dated 24 June 1831.
Recent sales
Lord Hesketh had bought the copy from a descendant of Witham at a Christie's auction on 3 July 1951, paying £7,000.
Recent sales
On 20 January 2012, a complete copy of the first edition was sold by the heirs of the 4th Duke of Portland at Christie's, New York, for $7.9 million.
Recent sales

The buyer was identified only as "an American collector who bid by phone." The sale brought the number of copies known to have survived to 120 – 107 in institution collections and 13 in private hands.
Recent sales
On 18 December 2019, a complete copy of the first edition was sold by Sotheby's, New York, for $6.6 million.
Textiles
In 1830s, immediately after the publication, several plates were used as a basis for the design of a series of roller-printed furnishing fabric, produced in Lancashire, United Kingdom.

antq_bay_palm_book.title: Bay Psalm Book
sents: lead
The Whole Booke of Psalmes Faithfully Translated into English Metre, commonly called the Bay Psalm Book, is a metrical psalter first printed in 1640 in Cambridge, Colony of Massachusetts Bay.
lead
It was the first book printed in British North America.
lead
The psalms in it are metrical translations into English.
lead
The translations are not particularly polished, and none have remained in use, although some of the tunes to which they were sung have survived.
lead
Its production, however, just 20 years after the Pilgrims' arrival at Plymouth, Massachusetts, represents a considerable achievement.
lead
It went through several editions and remained in use for well over a century.
lead
In November 2013, one of eleven known surviving copies of the first edition sold at auction for $14.2 million, a record for a printed book.
17th century

The early residents of the Massachusetts Bay Colony brought with them several books of psalms: the Ainsworth Psalter (1612), compiled by Henry Ainsworth for use by Puritan "separatists" in Holland; the Ravenscroft Psalter (1621); and the Sternhold and Hopkins Psalter (1562), of which there were several editions.
17th century
The first printing was the third product of the printing press in Cambridge, the first and only press in the colonies, which was owned by Elizabeth Glover and managed by Stephen Daye.
17th century

The book consisted of a 148 small quarto leaves, including a 12-page preface, "The Psalmes in Metre", "An Admonition to the Reader", and an extensive list of errata headed "Faults escaped in printing".
17th century

Subsequent editions were explicitly printed for sale in Boston by the first bookseller in British America, Hezekiah Usher, and it is hypothesized that Usher may have also intended to sell this first edition from his shop in Cambridge.
17th century
An estimated 1,700 copies of the first edition were printed.
17th century
The third edition (1651) was extensively revised by Henry Dunster and Richard Lyon.
17th century

The ninth edition (1698), the first to contain notated music (rather than simply identifying tunes by name), included 13 tunes from John Playford's A Breefe Introduction to the Skill of Musick (London, 1654).
18th century
In the early part of the 18th century, several updated psalms, notably those written by Tate and Brady and by Isaac Watts, were published.
18th century
In 1718, Cotton Mather undertook the revision of the original Bay Psalm Book which he had studied since youth.
18th century
Two subsequent revisions were published in 1752, by John Barnard of Marblehead and in 1758 by Thomas Prince.
Extant copies and auction records
Eleven copies of the first edition of the Bay Psalm Book are still known to exist, of which only five copies are complete.
Extant copies and auction records
Only one of the eleven copies is currently held outside the United States.

antq_principia_mathematicka.title: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica

name: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
caption: Title page of Principia, first edition (1687)
author: Isaac Newton
wikisource: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy

sents: lead
(English: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), often called simply the , is a book by Sir Isaac Newton that expounds Newton's laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation.
lead
The Principia is written in Latin and comprises three volumes, and was authorized (imprimatur) by Samuel Pepys, then-president of the Royal Society on 5 July 1686 and first published in 1687.
lead

After annotating and correcting his personal copy of the first edition, Newton published two further editions, one of 1713 with errors in the 1687 version corrected, and another, improved one of 1726.
lead
The Principia forms a mathematical foundation for the theory of classical mechanics, and is generally considered to be one of the most important works in the history of science.
lead
It has been referred to as "the greatest scientific work in history" and "the supreme expression in human thought of the mind's ability to hold the universe fixed as an object of contemplation".
lead

Recent research has challenged the long-held view that the Principia had only a limited initial readership, suggesting that its early influence on Enlightenment science was substantially greater than previously recognized.
lead

In formulating his physical laws, Newton developed and used mathematical methods now included in the field of calculus, expressing them in the form of geometric propositions about "vanishingly small" shapes.
lead
In a revised conclusion to the Principia, Newton emphasized the empirical nature of the work with the expression Hypotheses non fingo ("I frame/feign no hypotheses").
Expressed aim and topics covered
The opening sections of the Principia contain, in revised and extended form, nearly all of the content of Newton's 1684 tract De motu corporum in gyrum.
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''
Book 1, subtitled De motu corporum (On the motion of bodies) concerns motion in the absence of any resisting medium.
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''
It opens with a collection of mathematical lemmas on "the method of first and last ratios", a geometrical form of infinitesimal calculus.
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''

Propositions 11–31 establish properties of motion in paths of eccentric conic-section form including ellipses, and their relationship with inverse-square central forces directed to a focus and include Newton's theorem about ovals (lemma 28).
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''

Propositions 43–45 are demonstration that in an eccentric orbit under centripetal force where the apse may move, a steady non-moving orientation of the line of apses is an indicator of an inverse-square law of force.
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''
Book 1 contains some proofs with little connection to real-world dynamics.
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''
Propositions 57–69 deal with the "motion of bodies drawn to one another by centripetal forces".
Book 1, ''De motu corporum''
Propositions 70–84 deal with the attractive forces of spherical bodies.
Book 2, part 2 of ''De motu corporum''
Part of the contents originally planned for the first book was divided out into a second book, which largely concerns motion through resisting mediums.
Book 2, part 2 of ''De motu corporum''
Through Book II, Newton was an important pioneer of fluid mechanics, and a later analysis showed that of its 53 propositions almost all are correct, with only two or three open to question.
Book 2, part 2 of ''De motu corporum''
Book 2 discusses (in Section 5) hydrostatics and the properties of compressible fluids; he also derives Boyle's law (incorrectly; for an ideal gas is not like an elastic fluid).
Book 2, part 2 of ''De motu corporum''
In Section 8, he derives rules to determine the speed of waves in fluids and relates them to the density and condensation (Proposition 48; this would become very important in acoustics).
Book 2, part 2 of ''De motu corporum''

Less of Book 2 has stood the test of time than of Books 1 and 3, and it has been said that Book 2 was largely written to refute a theory of Descartes which had some wide acceptance before Newton's work (and for some time after).
Book 2, part 2 of ''De motu corporum''
Newton concluded Book 2 by commenting that the hypothesis of vortices was completely at odds with the astronomical phenomena, and served not so much to explain as to confuse them.
Book 3, ''De mundi systemate''
Book 3, subtitled De mundi systemate (On the system of the world), is an exposition of many consequences of universal gravitation, especially its consequences for astronomy.
Book 3, ''De mundi systemate''
Here (introduced by Proposition 22, and continuing in Propositions 25–35) are developed several of the features and irregularities of the orbital motion of the Moon, especially the variation.
Book 3, ''De mundi systemate''
Book 3 also considers the harmonic oscillator in three dimensions, and motion in arbitrary force laws.
Book 3, ''De mundi systemate''

In Book 3 Newton also made clear his heliocentric view of the Solar System, modified in a somewhat modern way, since already in the mid-1680s he recognised the "deviation of the Sun" from the centre of gravity of the Solar System.
Book 3, ''De mundi systemate''

Newton estimated the mass ratios Sun:Jupiter and Sun:Saturn, and pointed out that these put the centre of the Sun usually a little way off the common center of gravity, but only a little, the distance at most "would scarcely amount to one diameter of the Sun".
Commentary on the ''Principia''

Newton's defence has been adopted since by many famous physicists—he pointed out that the mathematical form of the theory had to be correct since it explained the data, and he refused to speculate further on the basic nature of gravity.
Rules of Reason
Perhaps to reduce the risk of public misunderstanding, Newton included at the beginning of Book 3 (in the second (1713) and third (1726) editions) a section titled "Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy".
Rules of Reason
In the four rules, as they came finally to stand in the 1726 edition, Newton effectively offers a methodology for handling unknown phenomena in nature and reaching towards explanations for them.
Rules of Reason
In the third (1726) edition of the Principia, Newton explains each rule in an alternative way and/or gives an example to back up what the rule is claiming.
Rules of Reason
The first rule is explained as a philosophers' principle of economy.
General Scholium
The General Scholium is a concluding essay added to the second edition, 1713 (and amended in the third edition, 1726).
General Scholium
Here Newton used the expression hypotheses non fingo, "I formulate no hypotheses", in response to criticisms of the first edition of the Principia.
Halley and Newton's initial stimulus
In January 1684, Edmond Halley, Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke had a conversation in which Hooke claimed to not only have derived the inverse-square law but also all the laws of planetary motion.
Halley and Newton's initial stimulus
Halley was at that time a Fellow and Council member of the Royal Society in London (positions that in 1686 he resigned to become the Society's paid Clerk).
Halley and Newton's initial stimulus
Halley's visit to Newton in Cambridge in 1684 probably occurred in August.
Halley and Newton's initial stimulus
The first of the three constituent books was sent to Halley for the printer in spring 1686, and the other two books somewhat later.
Preliminary version
The first volume was to be titled De motu corporum, Liber primus, with contents that later appeared in extended form as Book 1 of the Principia.
Preliminary version
The result was numbered Book 3 of the Principia rather than Book 2 because in the meantime, drafts of Liber primus had expanded and Newton had divided it into two books.
Preliminary version

After Newton's death in 1727, the relatively accessible character of its writing encouraged the publication of an English translation in 1728 (by persons still unknown, not authorised by Newton's heirs).
Preliminary version

The System of the World was sufficiently popular to stimulate two revisions (with similar changes as in the Latin printing), a second edition (1731), and a "corrected" reprint of the second edition (1740).
Halley's role as publisher
The text of the first of the three books of the Principia was presented to the Royal Society at the close of April 1686.
Halley's role as publisher
Samuel Pepys, as president, gave his imprimatur on 30 June 1686, licensing the book for publication.
Halley's role as publisher
After Halley had personally financed the publication of Principia, he was informed that the society could no longer afford to provide him the promised annual salary of £50.
Beginnings of the Scientific Revolution

Descartes' book of 1644 Principia philosophiae (Principles of philosophy) stated that bodies can act on each other only through contact: a principle that induced people, among them himself, to hypothesize a universal medium as the carrier of interactions such as light and gravity—the aether.
Newton's role
During this period (1664–1666) he created the basis of calculus and performed the first experiments in the optics of colour.
Newton's early work on motion
After his 1679–1680 correspondence with Hooke, described below, Newton adopted the language of inward or centripetal force.
Newton's early work on motion
Newton also clearly expressed the concept of linear inertia in the 1660s: for this Newton was indebted to Descartes' work published 1644.
Controversy with Hooke
Hooke published his ideas about gravitation in the 1660s and again in 1674.
Controversy with Hooke

Newton's reply offered "a fansy of my own" about a terrestrial experiment (not a proposal about celestial motions) which might detect the Earth's motion, by the use of a body first suspended in air and then dropped to let it fall.
Controversy with Hooke

In 1686, when the first book of Newton's Principia was presented to the Royal Society, Hooke claimed that Newton had obtained from him the "notion" of "the rule of the decrease of Gravity, being reciprocally as the squares of the distances from the Center".
Controversy with Hooke
Newton acknowledged Wren, Hooke and Halley in this connection in the Scholium to Proposition 4 in Book 1.
Location of early edition copies

It has been estimated that as many as 750 copies of the first edition were printed by the Royal Society, and "it is quite remarkable that so many copies of this small first edition are still in existence... but it may be because the original Latin text was more revered than read".
Location of early edition copies

A survey published in 1953 located 189 surviving copies with nearly 200 further copies located by the most recent survey published in 2020, suggesting that the initial print run was larger than previously thought.
Location of early edition copies
Cambridge University Library has Newton's own copy of the first edition, with handwritten notes for the second edition.
Location of early edition copies
The Čaplovič Library in Dolný Kubín holds a first edition copy, legacy of collector Vavrinec Čaplovič (1778-1853).
Location of early edition copies
The Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William & Mary has a first edition copy of the Principia.
Location of early edition copies
Brasch Collection of Newton and Newtoniana in Stanford University also has a first edition of the Principia.
Location of early edition copies
A first edition forms part of the Crawford Collection, housed at the Royal Observatory, Edinburgh.
Location of early edition copies
The Uppsala University Library owns a first edition copy, which was stolen in the 1960s and returned to the library in 2009.
Location of early edition copies
The Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington, D.C. owns a first edition, as well as a 1713 second edition.
Location of early edition copies
The Iron Library in Switzerland holds a first edition copy that was formerly in the library of the physicist Ernst Mach.
Location of early edition copies
The University of St Andrews Library holds both variants of the first edition, as well as copies of the 1713 and 1726 editions.
Location of early edition copies
The Fisher Library in the University of Sydney has a first-edition copy, annotated by a mathematician of uncertain identity and corresponding notes from Newton himself.
Location of early edition copies
The Linda Hall Library holds the first edition, as well as a copy of the 1713 and 1726 editions.
Location of early edition copies
The Teleki-Bolyai Library of Târgu-Mureș holds a 2-line imprint first edition.
Location of early edition copies
The University of Toronto has a copy in the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Collection.
Location of early edition copies
In 2016, a first edition sold for $3.7 million.
Location of early edition copies
The second edition (1713) were printed in 750 copies, and the third edition (1726) were printed in 1,250 copies.
Location of early edition copies
A facsimile edition (based on the 3rd edition of 1726 but with variant readings from earlier editions and important annotations) was published in 1972 by Alexandre Koyré and I.
Second edition, 1713

Two later editions were published by Newton: Newton had been urged to make a new edition of the Principia since the early 1690s, partly because copies of the first edition had already become very rare and expensive within a few years after 1687.
Second edition, 1713

Newton also maintained annotated copies of the first edition specially bound up with interleaves on which he could note his revisions; two of these copies still survive, but he had not completed the revisions by 1708.
Second edition, 1713

Richard Bentley, master of Trinity College, persuaded Newton to allow him to undertake a second edition, and in June 1708 Bentley wrote to Newton with a specimen print of the first sheet, at the same time expressing the (unfulfilled) hope that Newton had made progress towards finishing the revisions.
Second edition, 1713

The correspondence of 1709–1713 shows Cotes reporting to two masters, Bentley and Newton, and managing (and often correcting) a large and important set of revisions to which Newton sometimes could not give his full attention.
Second edition, 1713
Under the weight of Cotes' efforts, but impeded by priority disputes between Newton and Leibniz, and by troubles at the Mint, Cotes was able to announce publication to Newton on 30 June 1713.
Second edition, 1713
Bentley sent Newton only six presentation copies; Cotes was unpaid; Newton omitted any acknowledgement to Cotes.
Second edition, 1713
The Second Edition was the basis of the first edition to be printed abroad, which appeared in Amsterdam in 1714.
Third edition, 1726

After his serious illness in 1722 and after the appearance of a reprint of the second edition in Amsterdam in 1723, the 80-year-old Newton began to revise once again the Principia in the autumn of 1723.
Third edition, 1726

The third edition was published 25 March 1726, under the stewardship of Henry Pemberton, M.D., a man of the greatest skill in these matters...; Pemberton later said that this recognition was worth more to him than the two hundred guinea award from Newton.
Third edition, 1726
In 1739–1742, two French priests, Pères Thomas LeSeur and François Jacquier (of the Minim order, but sometimes erroneously identified as Jesuits), produced with the assistance of J.-L.
Third edition, 1726
Calandrini an extensively annotated version of the Principia in the 3rd edition of 1726.
Third edition, 1726
Du Châtelet's translation is the only complete one to have been done in French and hers remains the standard French translation to this day.
Translations
Four full English translations of Newton's Principia have appeared, all based on Newton's 3rd edition of 1726.
Translations
The first, from 1729, by Andrew Motte, was described by Newton scholar I.
Translations

The 1729 version was the basis for several republications, often incorporating revisions, among them a widely used modernised English version of 1934, which appeared under the editorial name of Florian Cajori (though completed and published only some years after his death).
Translations
The third such translation is due to Ian Bruce, and appears, with many other translations of mathematical works of the 17th and 18th centuries, on his website.
Legacy
The French mathematical physicist Alexis Clairaut described the Principia in 1747: "The famous book of Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy marked the epoch of a great revolution in physics.
Legacy
A 2020 study established a new census of owners of the first edition of the Principia, identifying 387 copies, significantly more than the long-held estimate of about 250.
Varia

In 1977, the spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2 left earth for the interstellar space carrying a picture of a page from Newton's Principia Mathematica, as part of the Golden Record, a collection of messages from humanity to extraterrestrials.
Varia
Tim Peake's Principia launched on 15 December 2015 aboard Soyuz TMA-19M.
Latin versions
