antq_de_revolutionibus_orbium_celes.title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
sents: lead
De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres) is the seminal work on the heliocentric theory of the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543 CE).
lead
The book, first printed in 1543 CE in Nuremberg, Holy Roman Empire, offered an alternative model of the universe to Ptolemy's geocentric system, which had been widely accepted since ancient times.
History
A physician's library list dating to 1514 includes a manuscript whose description matches the Commentariolus, so Copernicus must have begun work on his new system by that time.
History
Most historians believe that he wrote the Commentariolus after his return from Italy, possibly only after 1510.
History

Among other techniques, the heliocentric Copernican model made use of the Urdi Lemma developed in the 13th century by the Arab astronomer Mu'ayyad al-Din al-'Urdi, the first of the Maragha astronomers to develop a geocentric but non-Ptolemaic model of planetary motion.
History

Observations of Mercury by Bernhard Walther (1430–1504) of Nuremberg, a pupil of Regiomontanus, were made available to Copernicus by Johannes Schöner, 45 observations in total, 14 of them with longitude and latitude.
History
Copernicus used three of them in De revolutionibus, giving only longitudes, and erroneously attributing them to Schöner.
History
Copernicus' values differed slightly from the ones published by Schöner in 1544 in Observationes XXX annorum a I.
History
After his death, it was given to his pupil, Rheticus, who for publication had only been given a copy without annotations.
History
Via Heidelberg, it ended up in Prague, where it was rediscovered and studied in the 19th century.
History
Apparently Copernicus began by making a few astronomical observations to provide new data to perfect his models.
History
By the 1530s a substantial part of the book was complete, but Copernicus hesitated to publish.
History
In 1536, Cardinal Nikolaus von Schönberg wrote to Copernicus and urged him to publish his manuscript.
History
In 1539, Georg Joachim Rheticus, a young mathematician from Wittenberg, arrived in Frauenburg (Frombork) to study with him.
History
Rheticus' friend and mentor Achilles Gasser published a second edition of the Narratio in Basel in 1541.
History

Due to its friendly reception, Copernicus finally agreed to publication of more of his main work—in 1542, a treatise on trigonometry, which was taken from the second book of the still unpublished De revolutionibus.
History

Under strong pressure from Rheticus, and having seen that the first general reception of his work had not been unfavorable, Copernicus finally agreed to give the book to his close friend, Bishop Tiedemann Giese, to be delivered to Rheticus in Wittenberg for printing by Johannes Petreius at Nürnberg (Nuremberg).
History
The plan failed but the copy was found during the 18th century and was published later.
History
It is kept at the Jagiellonian University Library in Kraków, where it remains bearing the library number BJ 10 000.
Contents

From the first edition, Copernicus' book was prefixed with an anonymous preface which argues that the following is a calculus consistent with the observations, and cannot resolve philosophical truths.
Contents
Only later was this revealed to be the unauthorized interjection by Lutheran preacher Andreas Osiander, who lived in Nuremberg when the first edition was printed there.
Contents
Book I chapters 1–11 are a general vision of the heliocentric theory, and a summarized exposition of his cosmology.
Contents
Chapters 12–14 give theorems for chord geometry as well as a table of chords.
''Ad lectorem''
Only the handful of "Philosophical purists like the Averroists... demanded physical consistency and thus sought for realist models."
''Ad lectorem''
In 1609, Johannes Kepler modified Copernicus' theory by stating that the planets orbit the Sun not in circles, but ellipses.
''Ad lectorem''
Only after Kepler's refinement of Copernicus' theory was the need for deferents and epicycles abolished.
''Ad lectorem''
Rather than having Pico's focus on human effort, Osiander followed Cusa's idea that understanding the Universe and its Creator only came from divine inspiration rather than intellectual organization.
''Ad lectorem''
Schreiber, who died in 1547, left in his copy of the book a note about Osiander's authorship.
''Ad lectorem''
The most knowledgeable astronomers of the time had realized that the foreword was Osiander's doing.
''Ad lectorem''

Johannes Praetorius (1537–1616), who learned of Osiander's authorship from Rheticus during a visit to him in Kraków, wrote Osiander's name in the margin of the foreword in his copy of De revolutionibus.
Reception
This fool wishes to reverse the entire science of astronomy; but sacred Scripture tells us [Joshua 10:13] that Joshua commanded the sun to stand still, and not the earth.
Reception
When the book was finally published, demand was low, with an initial print run of 400 failing to sell out.
Reception
Copernicus had made the book extremely technical, unreadable to all but the most advanced astronomers of the day, allowing it to disseminate into their ranks before stirring great controversy.
Reception
Erasmus Reinhold hailed the work in 1542 and by 1551 had developed the Prutenic Tables ("Prussian Tables";; ) using Copernicus' methods.
Reception
The Prutenic Tables, published in 1551, were used as a basis for the calendar reform instituted in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII.
Reception
In Spain, rules published in 1561 for the curriculum of the University of Salamanca gave students the choice between studying Ptolemy or Copernicus.
Reception
One of those students, Diego de Zúñiga, published an acceptance of Copernican theory in 1584.
Reception

In 1549, Melanchthon, Luther's principal lieutenant, wrote against Copernicus, pointing to the theory's apparent conflict with Scripture and advocating that "severe measures" be taken to restrain the impiety of Copernicans.
Reception
De revolutionibus was not formally banned but merely withdrawn from circulation, pending "corrections" that would clarify the theory's status as hypothesis.
Reception
After these corrections were prepared and formally approved in 1620 the reading of the book was permitted.
Reception
But the book was never reprinted with the changes and was available in Catholic jurisdictions only to suitably qualified scholars, by special request.
Reception
It remained on the Index until 1758, when Pope Benedict XIV (1740–58) removed the uncorrected book from his revised Index.
Census of copies

Owen Gingerich, an eminent astronomer and historian of science who has written on both Nicolaus Copernicus and Johannes Kepler, disproved this after a 35-year project to examine every surviving copy of the first two editions.
Census of copies
Gingerich's efforts and conclusions are recounted in The Book Nobody Read, published in 2004 by Walker & Co.
Census of copies
His census included 276 copies of the first edition (by comparison, there are 228 extant copies of Shakespeare's First Folio) and 325 copies of the second.
Census of copies
The research behind this book earned its author the Polish government's Order of Merit in 1981.
Census of copies
Due largely to Gingerich's scholarship, De revolutionibus has been researched and catalogued better than any other first-edition historic text except for the original Gutenberg Bible.
Census of copies
In January 2017, a second-edition copy was stolen as part of a heist of rare books from Heathrow Airport and remains unrecovered.
Editions
Another 1543 copy is present in the Special Collections of Leiden University Libraries.
Editions
1854, Warsaw, with Polish translation and the authentic preface by Copernicus.
Editions
1873, Thorn; German translation sponsored by the local Coppernicus Society, with all of Copernicus' textual corrections given as footnotes.
Latin texts available online
1543, Nuremberg, by Johannes Petreius; online from Harvard University.
English texts available online
Copernicus, Nicolaus (1543) De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium; online from Source Library.
Translations
Duncan, Newton Abbot, David & Charles,; New York: Barnes and Noble, 1976,.
Translations
On the Revolutions; translation and commentary by Edward Rosen, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1992,.

antq_hypnero_tomaccia_poliphilly.title: Hypnerotomachia Poliphili

name: The Strife of Love in a Dream
original_title: Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, ubi humana omnia non nisi somnium esse docet. Atque obiter plurima scitu sane quam digna commemorat.
caption: First edition
author: Francesco Colonna

sents: lead
Hypnerotomachia Poliphili , called in English Poliphilo's Strife of Love in a Dream or The Dream of Poliphilus, is a book attributed to the 15th-century Italian monk Francesco Colonna.
lead
Hypnerotomachia Poliphili presents a mysterious arcane allegory in which the main protagonist, Poliphilo, pursues his love, Polia, through a dreamlike landscape.
lead
In the end, he is reconciled with her by the "Fountain of Venus".
lead
It is a famous example of an incunable (a work of early printing).
lead
The work was first published in 1499 in Venice by Aldus Manutius as a sort of graphic novel.
lead
This first edition has an elegant page layout, with refined woodcut illustrations in an Early Renaissance style.
lead
The Aldine Press issued a second edition after the death of Aldus.
History
The Hypnerotomachia Poliphili was printed by Aldus Manutius in Venice in December 1499.
History
An acrostic formed by the first, elaborately decorated letter in each chapter reads "POLIAM FRATER FRANCISCVS COLVMNA PERAMAVIT" 'Brother Francesco Colonna has dearly loved Polia'.
History
Most of them have been drawn from a late antique text of dubious origin called Hieroglyphica.
History
The book has long been sought after as one of the most beautiful incunabula ever printed.
History
The typography is famous for its quality and clarity.
History
Its roman typeface, cut by Francesco Griffo, is a revised version of a type which Aldus had first used in 1496 for the De Aetna of Pietro Bembo.
History
The type is thought to be one of the first examples of the roman typeface, and in incunabula, it is unique to the Aldine Press.
History
The type was revived by the Monotype Corporation in 1923 as "Poliphilus".
History
In 1929, Stanley Morison directed another revival of the earlier version of Griffo's type.
History
The Hypnerotomachia Poliphili is illustrated with 168 woodcuts showing the scenery, architectural settings, and some of the characters Poliphilo encounters in his dreams.
Translations
A French translation or rather adaptation appeared in the 1540s.
Translations
In 1999, a first complete English translation by musicologist Joscelyn Godwin was published.
Translations
Since the 500th anniversary in 1999, several other modern translations have been published.
Translations
A complete Russian translation by the art historian Boris Sokolov is now in progress, of which the "Cythera Island" part was published in 2005 and is available online.
Translations
Ten of the monuments described in the Hypnerotomachia were reconstructed with computer graphics and were first published by Esteban A.
Plot summary
Venus blesses their love, and Poliphilo and Polia are united at last.
In other works
Liane Lefaivre and other scholars regard the 16th century Gardens of Bomarzo to be illustrations of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili.
In other works

The German composer Alexander Moosbrugger took the text of his 2021 opera Wind, staging the search of Poliphilo for Polia, from the Hypnerotomachia's German translation by Thomas Reiser and the English one by Joscelyn Godwin.
In other works
In the novel The Rule of Four by Ian Caldwell and Dustin Thomason the protagonists decode hidden meanings in the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili.
The 1592 English edition
Contains the 1592 edition, and a summary of the rest of the book, with all the illustrations from the original, notes and glossary; available in various formats or can be read online.
The French editions
1600 Edition created by Béroalde de Verville at e-rara.ch, Swiss digital library's C.G.

antq_de_humani_corporis_fabricka.title: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem

name: De Humani Corporis Fabrica
caption: Title page. Andreae Vesalii Bruxellensis, scholae medicorum Patauinae professoris, de Humani corporis fabrica Libri septem (Andreas Vesalius of Brussels, professor at the school of medicine at Padua, On the Fabric of the Human Body in Seven Books).
author: Andreas Vesalius
subject: Anatomy

sents: lead
De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem (Latin, "On the Fabric of the Human Body in Seven Books") is a set of books on human anatomy written by Andreas Vesalius.
lead
The collection of books is based on his Paduan lectures, during which he deviated from common practice by dissecting a corpse to illustrate what he was discussing.
lead
Dissections had previously been performed by a barber surgeon under the direction of a doctor of medicine, who was not expected to perform manual labour.
lead
Vesalius's and the complete structure of the human body.
lead

This would not have been possible without the many advances that had been made during the Renaissance, including artistic developments in literal visual representation and the technical development of printing with refined woodcuts.
lead
Because of these developments and his careful, immediate involvement, Vesalius was able to produce illustrations superior to any produced previously.
Book 1: The Bones and Cartilages
The first book constitutes about a quarter of the entire collection.
Books 3 and 4: The Veins and Arteries; The Nerves
In Books 3 and 4, Vesalius describes the veins, arteries, and nerves as vessels, but notes their differing physical structure: veins and arteries contains a hollow channel, but nerves do not.
Book 5: The Organs of Nutrition and Generation
In the first half of the book, Vesalius describes the peritoneum, the esophagus, the stomach, the omentum, the intestines and the mesentery.
Galen's errors

Some older historical accounts claimed that Vesalius' findings led to a decline in his favor with the Church because they allegedly contradicted a biblical interpretation of human anatomy, particularly regarding the "rib of Adam" (the belief that men had one fewer rib than women, based on Genesis 2:21–22).
Galen's errors
Overall, Vesalius's use of human corpses allowed him to rectify approximately 300 of Galen's errors.
1543 edition
Vesalius had the work published at the age of 28, taking great pains to ensure its quality, and dedicated it to Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor.
1543 edition

The more than 250 illustrations are of great artistic merit and are generally attributed by modern scholars to the "studio of Titian" rather than Johannes Stephanus of Calcar, who provided drawings for Vesalius' earlier tracts.
1543 edition
The woodcuts were greatly superior to the illustrations in anatomical atlases of the day, which were never made by anatomy professors themselves.
1555 edition
Annotations in a copy of that edition preserved in KU Leuven Libraries have been identified as Vesalius's own, showing that he was contemplating a third edition, never achieved.
Reception
To accompany the Fabrica, Vesalius published a condensed and less expensive Epitome: at the time of publication in 1543, it cost 10 batzen.
Human remains
During the 16th century, the dissection of human bodies was strictly prohibited by the Church.
Human remains
For example in 1828 the case of Burke and Hare, whereby the bodies were delivered to anatomists for dissection, were murdered specifically for financial gain.
Surviving copies
More than 700 copies survive from the 1543 and 1555 editions.
Surviving copies
Of those, by 2018 some 29 copies were in London, 20 in Paris, 14 in Boston, 13 in New York, 12 in Cambridge (England), one in Puebla's Biblioteca Palafoxiana (Mexico), and 11 each in Oxford and Rome.
Surviving copies
In February 2024, a second-edition copy was sold at a Christie's online auction for $2,228,000, making it one of the most expensive scientific documents ever to be sold at auction.
Surviving copies
The copy, which had last been sold in 2007 for €13,200, was found to have been Vesalius' personal copy.
Legacy
De Humani Corporis Fabrica, a 2022 documentary film about the human body by Lucien Castaing-Taylor and Véréna Paravel, was named after the book series.
Translations
An Annotated Translation of the 1543 and 1555 Editions, edited by D.H.
Translations
La Fabrique du corps humain (1543), livre I dans La fabrique de Vésale et autres textes.

antq_nurembird_chronicle.title: Nuremberg Chronicle
sents: lead
The Nuremberg Chronicle is an illustrated encyclopedia consisting of world historical accounts, as well as accounts told through biblical paraphrase.
lead
Subjects include human history in relation to the Bible, illustrated mythological creatures, and the histories of important Christian and secular cities from antiquity.
lead
Finished in 1493, it was originally written in Latin by Hartmann Schedel, and a German version was translated by Georg Alt.
lead
It is one of the best-documented early printed books—an incunabulum—and one of the first to successfully integrate illustrations and text.
lead
Latin scholars refer to it as the Liber Chronicarum ('Book of Chronicles') as this phrase appears in the index introduction of the Latin edition.
lead
English-speakers have long referred to it as the Nuremberg Chronicle after the city in which it was published.
lead
German-speakers refer to it as Schedelsche Weltchronik ('Schedel's chronicle of the world') in honour of its author.
Production
Two Nuremberg merchants, Sebald Schreyer (1446–1503) and his son-in-law, Sebastian Kammermeister (1446–1520), commissioned the Latin version of the chronicle on 29 December 1491.
Production
They also commissioned Georg Alt (1450–1510), a scribe at the Nuremberg treasury, to translate the work into German.
Production
The first contract, from December 1491, established the relationship between the illustrators and the patrons.
Production
The patrons agreed to advance 1,000 gulden for paper, printing costs, and the distribution and sale of the book.
Production
A second contract between the patrons and the printer was executed in March 1492.
Production
According to an inventory done in 1498, Schedel's personal library contained 370 manuscripts and 670 printed books.
Production
It has been estimated that about 90% of the text is pieced together from works on humanities, science, philosophy, and theology, while about 10% of the chronicle is Schedel's original composition.
Production
Nuremberg was one of the largest cities in the Holy Roman Empire in the 1490s, with a population of between 45,000 and 50,000.
Production
Anton Koberger, printer of the Nuremberg Chronicle, printed the first humanist book in Nuremberg in 1472.
Publication
The Chronicle was first published in Latin on 12 July 1493, in the city of Nuremberg.
Publication
This was quickly followed by a German translation on 23 December 1493.
Publication
An estimated 1,400 to 1,500 Latin and 700 to 1,000 German copies were published.
Publication
A document from 1509 records that 539 Latin versions and 60 German versions had not been sold.
Publication

Unusually many copies survive: Paul Needham's census documents 1,287 copies of the Latin edition and 343 of the German, making the Chronicle one of the best-preserved major printed books of the fifteenth century.
Publication
The publisher and printer was Anton Koberger, the godfather of Albrecht Dürer, who, in the year of Dürer's birth in 1471, ceased goldsmithing to become a printer and publisher.
Publication
He quickly became the most successful publisher in Germany, eventually owning 24 printing presses and having many offices in Germany and abroad, from Lyon to Buda.
Illustrations
The large workshop of Michael Wolgemut, Nuremberg's leading artist in various media, provided the unprecedented 1,809 woodcut illustrations (before duplications are eliminated; see below).
Illustrations
Sebastian Kammermeister and Sebald Schreyer financed the printing in a contract dated March 16, 1492, although preparations had been well under way for several years.
Illustrations

Wolgemut and his stepson Wilhelm Pleydenwurff were first commissioned to provide the illustrations in 1487–1488, and a further contract of December 29, 1491, commissioned manuscript layouts of the text and illustrations.
Illustrations

Albrecht Dürer was an apprentice with Wolgemut from 1486 to 1489, so may well have participated in designing some of the illustrations for the specialist craftsmen (called "formschneiders") who cut the blocks, onto which the design had been drawn, or a drawing glued.
Illustrations
From 1490 to 1494 Dürer was travelling.
Illustrations
A drawing by Wolgemut for the elaborate frontispiece, dated 1490, is in the British Museum.
Illustrations
Illustrations depicted many never-before-illustrated major cities in Europe and the Near East.
Illustrations
Only the city of Nuremberg is given a double-page illustration with no text measuring about 342 by.
Illustrations
The illustration for the city of Venice is adapted from a much larger woodcut of 1486 by Erhard Reuwich in the first illustrated printed travel book, the Sanctae Perigrinationes of 1486.
Unauthorized editions

Due to the success and prestige of the Nuremberg Chronicle, which had one of the largest print-runs of an edition during the incunabula (also known as the incunable period of book production –1500), one of the first large-scale pirated editions of the Chronicle appeared on the market.
Unauthorized editions

The culprit was Johann Schönsperger (–1521), a printer working out of Augsburg who produced smaller editions of the Chronicle in 1496, 1497, and 1500 in German, Latin, and a second edition also in German.
Unauthorized editions
Despite the pirating of a successful book, Schönsperger went bankrupt in 1507.

antq_don_quicksote.title: Don Quixote

name: Don Quixote
original_title: El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha
image: Title page first edition Don Quijote.jpg
caption: Don Quijote de la Mancha, first edition, 1605, printed by Juan de la Cuesta
author: Miguel de Cervantes

sents: lead
Don Quixote is a novel by Miguel de Cervantes, written in Early Modern Spanish and published in two parts in 1605 and 1615.
lead
It is considered a founding work of Western literature and the first modern novel.
lead
Don Quixote is one of the most-translated books in the world and one of the best-selling books in history.
lead

The plot revolves around the adventures of a member of the lowest nobility, a hidalgo from La Mancha named Alonso Quijano, who reads so many chivalric romances that he decides to become a knight-errant (caballero andante) to revive chivalry and serve his nation, under the name Don Quixote de la Mancha.
lead
He recruits as his squire a simple farm labourer, Sancho Panza, who brings an earthy wit to Don Quixote's lofty rhetoric.
lead
In the first part of the book, Don Quixote does not see the world for what it is and prefers to imagine that he is living out a knightly story meant for the annals of all time.
lead

As Salvador de Madariaga pointed out in his Guía del lector del Quijote (1972 ), opposing Quixotization with Sanchification, "Sancho's spirit ascends from reality to illusion" while Don Quixote's does the opposite.
lead

The book had a major influence on the literary community, being directly referenced in works of 19thcentury French literature such as Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers (1844) and Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac (1897).
Summary
For Cervantes and the readers of his day, Don Quixote was a one-volume book published in 1605, divided internally into four parts, not the first part of a two-part set.
Summary

The mention in the 1605 book of further adventures yet to be told was totally conventional, did not indicate any authorial plans for a continuation, and was not taken seriously by the book's first readers.
The first sally

Cervantes, in a metafictional narrative, writes that the first few chapters were taken from "the archives of La Mancha", and the rest were translated from an Arabic text by the Moorish historian Cide Hamete Benengeli.
The first sally
Alonso Quixano is an hidalgo nearing 50 years of age who lives in a deliberately unspecified region of La Mancha with his niece and housekeeper.
The first sally

While Quixote lies unconscious in his bed, his niece, the housekeeper, the parish curate, and the local barber decide to burn most of his chivalric and other books, seeing them as the root of his madness.
The second sally
Inspired by Cardenio, Quixote decides to imitate what he has read in his chivalric romances and live like a hermit in a display of devotion to Dulcinea.
Part 2
In an early example of metafiction, Part Two includes characters who have read the first part of the novel and are thus familiar with the history and peculiarities of the two protagonists.
The third sally
Since Quixote only sees the peasant girls, Sancho goes on to pretend that an enchantment of some sort is at work.
The third sally
As part of one prank, Quixote and Sancho are led to believe that the only way to release Dulcinea from her spell is for Sancho to give himself three thousand three hundred lashes.
The third sally
Sancho tries to restore his faith and his interest in Dulcinea, but Quixano only renounces his previous ambition and apologizes for the harm he has caused.
''The Ill-Advised Curiosity'' summary
Fearing that Anselmo will kill her, the maid says she will tell Anselmo a secret the next day.
Use of language

In Don Quixote, there are basically two different types of Castilian: Old Castilian is spoken only by Don Quixote, while the rest of the roles speak a contemporary (late 16th century) version of Spanish.
Use of language
In Old Castilian, the letter x represented the sound written sh in modern English, so the name was originally pronounced.
Use of language

In Australian English, the preferred pronunciation amongst members of the educated classes was until well into the 1970s, as part of a tendency for the upper class to "anglicise its borrowing ruthlessly".
Meaning
Harold Bloom says Don Quixote is the first modern novel, and that the protagonist is at war with Freud's reality principle, which accepts the necessity of dying.
Meaning
You are never certain that you truly got it.
Themes

Although burlesque on the surface, the novel, especially in its second half, has served as an important thematic source not only in literature but also in much of art and music, inspiring works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss.
Spurious ''Second Part'' by Avellaneda

Some modern scholars suggest that Don Quixote's fictional encounter with Avellaneda's book in Chapter 59 of Part II should not be taken as the date that Cervantes encountered it, which may have been much earlier.
Spurious ''Second Part'' by Avellaneda
In his introduction to The Portable Cervantes, Samuel Putnam, a noted translator of Cervantes' novel, calls Avellaneda's version "one of the most disgraceful performances in history".
Location

In 2004, a team of academics from Complutense University, led by Francisco Parra Luna, Manuel Fernández Nieto, and Santiago Petschen Verdaguer, deduced that the village was that of Villanueva de los Infantes.
Location

Translators of Don Quixote, such as John Ormsby, have commented that the region of La Mancha is one of the most desertlike, unremarkable regions of Spain, the least romantic and fanciful place that one would imagine as the home of a courageous knight.
Legacy
In 2002 the Norwegian Nobel Institute conducted a study among writers from 55 countries, the majority voted Don Quixote "the greatest work of fiction ever written".
In science
Dulcibella camanchaca, a deep-sea amphipod species, was named after the character Dulcinea in the novel, following the tradition of naming amphipods after literary figures.
In science
Lohuecotitan pandafilandi and Qunkasaura pintiquiniestra are dinosaurs named after minor characters in the novel.
In science
The family, genus, and gastropod species Quijotidae, Quijote, and Quijote cervantesi are named after the novel and its author.
Publication
In July 1604, Cervantes sold the rights of El ingenioso hidalgo don Quixote de la Mancha (known as Don Quixote, Part I) to the publisher-bookseller Francisco de Robles for an unknown sum.
Publication
License to publish was granted in September, the printing was finished in December, and the book came out on 16 January 1605.
Publication
Most of the 400 copies of the first edition were sent to the New World, with the publisher hoping to get a better price in the Americas.
Publication
Although most of them disappeared in a shipwreck near La Havana, approximately 70 copies reached Lima, from where they were sent to Cuzco, in the heart of the defunct Inca Empire.
Publication
In 1614 a fake second part was published by a mysterious author under the pen name Avellaneda.
Publication
By August 1605, there were two Madrid editions, two published in Lisbon, and one in Valencia.
Publication
Robles, the Madrid publisher, found it necessary to meet demand with a third edition, a seventh publication in all, in 1608.
Publication
Popularity of the book in Italy was such that a Milan bookseller issued an Italian edition in 1610.
Publication
Since then, numerous editions have been released and in total, the novel is believed to have sold more than 500 million copies worldwide.
Publication
The work has been produced in numerous editions and languages, the Cervantes Collection, at the State Library of New South Wales includes over 1,100 editions.
Publication
In 1613, Cervantes published the Novelas ejemplares, dedicated to the Maecenas of the day, the Conde de Lemos.
Publication
Eight and a half years after Part One had appeared came the first hint of a forthcoming Segunda Parte (Part Two).
Publication

"You shall see shortly", Cervantes says, "the further exploits of Don Quixote and humours of Sancho Panza." Don Quixote, Part Two, published by the same press as its predecessor, appeared late in 1615, and was quickly reprinted in Brussels and Valencia (1616) and Lisbon (1617).
Publication
Parts One and Two were published as one edition in Barcelona in 1617.
Publication

In 1632, Cardinal Zapata ordered that the sentence "and remember, Sancho, that works of charity done in a lukewarm and half-hearted way are without merit and of no avail", should be removed from future editions.
English editions in translation

Seven years after the Parte Primera appeared, Don Quixote had been translated into French, German, Italian, and English, with the first French translation of 'Part II' appearing in 1618, and the first English translation in 1620.
English editions in translation
One abridged adaptation, authored by Agustín Sánchez, runs slightly over 150 pages, cutting away about 750 pages.
English editions in translation
Thomas Shelton's English translation of the First Part appeared in 1612 while Cervantes was still alive, although there is no evidence that Shelton had met the author.
English editions in translation
Shelton's translation of the novel's Second Part appeared in 1620.
English editions in translation
Near the end of the 17th century, John Phillips, a nephew of poet John Milton, published what Putnam considered the worst English translation.
English editions in translation
In Smollett's translation of 1755 he notes that the original text reads literally "you will see when the eggs are fried", meaning "time will tell".
English editions in translation
A translation by Captain John Stevens, which revised Thomas Shelton's version, also appeared in 1700, but its publication was overshadowed by the simultaneous release of Motteux's translation.
English editions in translation
In 1742, the Charles Jervas translation appeared, posthumously.
English editions in translation
Through a printer's error, it came to be known, and is still known, as "the Jarvis translation".
English editions in translation
Nevertheless, it became the most frequently reprinted translation of the novel until about 1885.
English editions in translation
Another 18th-century translation into English was that of Tobias Smollett, himself a novelist, first published in 1755.
English editions in translation
A translation by Alexander James Duffield appeared in 1881 and another by Henry Edward Watts in 1888.
English editions in translation
Most modern translators take as their model the 1885 translation by John Ormsby.
English editions in translation
An expurgated children's version, under the title The Story of Don Quixote, was published in 1922 (available on Project Gutenberg).
English editions in translation
The most widely read English-language translations of the mid-20th century are by Samuel Putnam (1949), J.
English editions in translation
Cohen (1950; Penguin Classics), and Walter Starkie (1957).
English editions in translation
The last English translation of the novel in the 20th century was by Burton Raffel, published in 1996.
English editions in translation
The 21st century has already seen five new translations of the novel into English.
English editions in translation

Reviewing the novel in The New York Times, Carlos Fuentes called Grossman's translation a "major literary achievement" and another called it the "most transparent and least impeded among more than a dozen English translations going back to the 17th century."
English editions in translation
In 2005, the year of the novel's 400th anniversary, Tom Lathrop published a new English translation of the novel, based on a lifetime of specialized study of the novel and its history.
English editions in translation
The fourth translation of the 21st century was released in 2006 by former university librarian James H.
English editions in translation
Montgomery, 26 years after he had begun it, in an attempt to "recreate the sense of the original as closely as possible, though not at the expense of Cervantes' literary style."
English editions in translation
The latest and the sixth translation of the 21st century is Diana de Armas Wilson's 2020 revision of Burton Raffel's translation.
In public domain

John Ormsby (1885) – the original version available free on the Internet Archive, is to be preferred to the Wikisource and similar versions that do not include Ormsby's careful notes and with his Introduction much abbreviated.
In copyright
Joseph Ramon Jones and Kenneth Douglas (1981) (revision of Ormsby).
In copyright

Reviewing 27 out of the current 30 English translations as a whole in 2008, Daniel Eisenberg stated that there is no one translation ideal for every purpose but expressed a preference for those of Putnam and the revision of Ormsby's translation by Douglas and Jones.

antq_euclyd_s_elements.title: Euclid's Elements

name: Elements
author: Euclid
image: P.Penn. Museum inv. E02748 Euclid's Elements 2.5.jpg
caption: Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 29, a fragment of Euclid's Elements dated to .
Found at Oxyrhynchus, the diagram accompanies Book II, Proposition 5.
subject: Euclidean geometry, number theory, incommensurability

sents: lead
The Elements ( Stoikheîa) is a mathematical treatise written by the Ancient Greek mathematician Euclid.
lead
The Elements is the oldest extant large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics.
lead

These include the Pythagorean theorem, Thales' theorem, the Euclidean algorithm for greatest common divisors, Euclid's theorem that there are infinitely many prime numbers, and the construction of regular polygons and polyhedra.
lead
Often referred to as the most successful textbook ever written, the Elements has continued to be used for introductory geometry.
lead

It was translated into Arabic and Latin in the medieval period, where it exerted a great deal of influence on mathematics in the medieval Islamic world and in Western Europe, and has proven instrumental in the development of logic and modern science, where its logical rigor was not surpassed until the 19th century.
Background
Euclid's Elements is the oldest extant large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics.
Background
The Elements version available today also includes "post-Euclidean" mathematics, probably added later by later editors such as the mathematician Theon of Alexandria in the 4th century.
Contents
Using Aristotle's terminology, these may be generally separated into two categories: "first principles" and "second principles".
Contents
The first group includes statements labeled as a "definition" ( or ὁρισμός), "postulate" (αἴτημα), or a "common notion" (κοινὴ ἔννοια).
Contents
The postulates (that is, axioms) and common notions occur only in book I.
Book I
Euclid then presents 10 assumptions (see table, right), grouped into five postulates and five common notions.
Book I
While the first four postulates are relatively straightforward, the fifth is not.
Book I

Book I also includes 48 propositions, which can be loosely divided into: basic theorems and constructions of plane geometry and triangle congruence (1–26), parallel lines (27–34), the area of triangles and parallelograms (35–45), and the Pythagorean theorem and its converse (46–48).
Book I

Proposition 5, that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, became known in the Middle Ages as the pons asinorum, or bridge of asses, separating the mathematicians who could prove it from the fools who could not.
Book I
Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 29, a 3rd-century AD papyrus, contains fragments of propositions 8–11 and 14–25.
Book I
The last two propositions of Book I comprise the earliest surviving proof of the Pythagorean theorem, described by Sialaros as "remarkably delicate".
Book II

In the late 19th and 20th centuries, Book II was interpreted by some mathematical historians to establish a "geometric algebra", an expression of algebraic manipulation of linear and quadratic equations in terms of geometric concepts of length and area, centered on the quadratic case of the binomial theorem.
Book II
Proposition 11 of Book II subdivides a given line segment into extreme and mean proportions, now called the golden ratio.
Book III
Book III begins with a list of 11 definitions, and follows with 37 propositions that deal with circles and their properties.
Book III
Propositions 2 through 15 concern chords, and intersecting and tangent circles.
Book III
Tangent lines to circles are the subjects of propositions 16 through 19.
Book III

Next are propositions on inscribed angles (20 through 22), and on chords, arcs, and angles (23 through 30), including the inscribed angle theorem relating inscribed to central angles as proposition 20.
Book III
Propositions 31 through 34 concern angles in circles, including Thales's theorem that an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (part of proposition 31).
Book III
The remaining propositions, 35 through 37, concern intersecting chords and tangents; proposition 35 is the intersecting chords theorem, and proposition 36 is the tangent–secant theorem.
Book IV
These problems are solved in sequence for triangles and then for constructible regular polygons (i.e., those that have a straightedge and compass construction) with 4, 5, 6, and 15 sides.
Book V

Heath and other translators have formulated its first six propositions in symbolic algebra, as forms of the distributive law of multiplication over division and the associative law for multiplication.
Book V

Much of Book V was probably ascertained from earlier mathematicians, perhaps Eudoxus, although certain propositions, such as V.16, dealing with "alternation" (if a: b:: c: d, then a: c:: b: d) likely predate Eudoxus.
Book VI
Proposition 25 constructs, from any two polygons, a third polygon similar to the first and with the same area as the second.
Book VI

The famous ancient Greek problem of doubling the cube, now known impossible with compass and straightedge, is a special case of the analogous 3d problem of constructing a figure with a specified shape and volume.
Book VI
The book ends as it begins, by connecting two types of ratios: ratios of angles, and ratios of circular arc lengths, in proposition 33.
Books VII to X: Number theory
Book VII begins with a set of 22 definitions for parity (whether a number is even or odd), prime numbers, and other arithmetic-related concepts.
Book VIII

The first part of Book VIII (propositions 1 through 10) deals with the construction and existence of geometric progressions of integers in general, and the divisibility of members of a geometric progression by each other.
Book VIII

Propositions 11 to 27 deal with square numbers and cube numbers in geometric progressions, and the relation between these special progressions and the elements two or three steps apart in an arbitrary geometric progression.
Book IX
Alhazen conjectured, and in the 18th century Leonhard Euler proved, that this construction generates all even perfect numbers.
Book X
Of the Elements, book X is by far the largest and most complex, dealing with (in modern terms) irrational numbers in the context of magnitudes.
Book X
Proposition 9 (as restated in modern terms) proves the irrationality of the square roots of all non-square integers such as, the square root of 2.
Book X
A lemma to Proposition 29 gives Euclid's formula for producing all fundamental Pythagorean triples.
Books XI to XIII: Solid geometry
By introducing a list of 37 definitions, Book XI contextualizes the next two.
Book XI
The three sections of Book XI include content on: solid geometry (1–19), solid angles (20–23), and parallelepipeds (24–37).
Apocryphal books
The practice of adding to the works of famous authors, exemplified by these books, was not unusual in ancient Greek mathematics.
Euclid's method and style of presentation
For example, he proves the Pythagorean theorem by first inscribing a square on the sides of a right triangle, but only after constructing a square on a given line one proposition earlier.
Euclid's method and style of presentation
For proofs involving case analysis, the Elements often includes details only of the most difficult case; some of these case analyses have been filled out by later editors such as Theon.
Euclid's method and style of presentation
Euclid's presentation was limited by the mathematical ideas and notations in common currency in his era, and this causes the treatment to seem awkward to the modern reader in some places.
Euclid's method and style of presentation

For example, there was no notion of an angle greater than two right angles, the number 1 was sometimes treated separately from other positive integers, and, as multiplication was treated geometrically, as the area of a rectangle with given side lengths, he did not use the product of more than 3 different numbers.
Reception
Euclid's Elements has been referred to as the most successful textbook ever written.
Reception
The Elements is often considered after the Bible as the most frequently translated, published, and studied book in history.
Reception
With Aristotle's Metaphysics, the Elements is perhaps the most successful ancient Greek text, and was the dominant mathematical textbook in the Medieval Islamic world and Western Europe.
Reception

It was one of the very earliest mathematical works to be printed after the invention of the printing press and has been estimated to be second only to the Bible in the number of editions published since the first printing in 1482, the number reaching well over one thousand.
Classical antiquity

The oldest extant evidence for Euclid's Elements are a set of six ostraca (clay fragments with writing scratched onto them) found among the Elephantine papyri and ostraca, from the 3rd century BC, that deal with propositions XIII.10 and XIII.16, on the construction of a dodecahedron.
Classical antiquity
The earliest extant papyrus containing the actual text of the Elements is Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 29, a fragment containing the text of Book II, Proposition 5 and an accompanying diagram, dated to.
Classical antiquity

In the 4th century AD, Theon of Alexandria produced an edition of Euclid which was so widely used that it became the only surviving Greek-language source (in multiple manuscripts) until François Peyrard's 1808 discovery at the Vatican of a manuscript not derived from Theon's.
Classical antiquity
Vat.gr.190, was transcribed in the 10th century.
Classical antiquity

Revisiting this issue, Wilbur Knorr sides with Klamroth in suggesting that the Arabic sources were closer to the original, but concludes that "We have never had a 'genuine' text of Euclid, and we never will have one."
Classical antiquity
Although Euclid was known to Cicero, for instance, no record exists of the text having been translated into Latin prior to Boethius in the fifth or sixth century.
Medieval era
The Islamic world received the Elements from the Byzantine Empire around 760.
Medieval era
Another Arabic translation was made later in the 9th century by Ishaq ibn Hunayn and revised by Thābit ibn Qurra.
Medieval era

The Byzantine scholar Arethas commissioned the copying of one of the Greek manuscripts of Euclid in the late ninth century; it and another Byzantine manuscript are the two oldest surviving copies of the Greek text.
Medieval era
Although known in Byzantium, the Elements was lost to Western Europe until about 1120, except through fragments of a translation into Latin by Boethius , quoted in other works.
Medieval era
In about 1120, the English monk Adelard of Bath translated the Elements into Latin from an Arabic translation.
Medieval era
A relatively recent discovery was made of a Greek-to-Latin translation from the 12th century at Palermo, Sicily.
Medieval era

Campanus of Novara relied heavily on these Arabic translations to create his edition (sometime before 1260) which ultimately came to dominate Latin editions until the availability of Greek manuscripts in the 16th century.
Medieval era
There are more than 100 pre-1482 Campanus manuscripts still available today.
Medieval era

After its availability in Europe, the first books of the Elements became standard in medieval universities as part of the quadrivium, the second stage of instruction after the trivium of grammar, logic, and rhetoric.
Renaissance and early modern period

The first printed edition of the Elements was published by Erhard Ratdolt in 1482, based on Campanus's version, and since then it has been translated into many languages and published in over a thousand different editions.
Renaissance and early modern period
A manuscript descended from Theon's Greek version was recovered and a Latin translation was published in Venice in 1505 by Bartolomeo Zamberti.
Renaissance and early modern period
The first to translate the Elements into a modern European language was Nicolo Tartaglia, who published an Italian edition in 1543.
Renaissance and early modern period
In 1570, John Dee provided a widely respected "Mathematical Preface", along with copious notes and supplementary material, to the first English edition by Henry Billingsley.
Renaissance and early modern period
In 1607, The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci and the Chinese mathematician Xu Guangqi published the first Chinese edition of Euclid's Elements.
Renaissance and early modern period
Pacioli lectured in Venice on Euclid, and his commentary was included in a 1509 edition of the Elements.
Renaissance and early modern period

Although this period also saw an explosion in newly published textbooks, teachers often stuck to the classics: a list of recommended readings by 16th century Dutch humanist Joachim Sterck van Ringelbergh, for instance, lists the Elements as its only mathematics book.
Modern mathematics
Charles Dodgson (better known as Lewis Carroll), in particular, railed against this replacement of Euclid in his book Euclid and His Modern Rivals (1879).
Non-Euclidean geometry
One of the most notable influences of Euclid on modern mathematics and, beyond mathematics, modern physics and the discovery of general relativity, is the discussion of the parallel postulate.
Non-Euclidean geometry
Many attempts were made to prove the fifth postulate based on the other four, but they never succeeded.
Non-Euclidean geometry
Eventually in 1829, mathematician Nikolai Lobachevsky published a description of acute geometry (or hyperbolic geometry), a geometry which assumed a different form of the parallel postulate.
Axiomatics
Hilbert's hopes were dashed in the foundational crisis of the early 20th century, in which Kurt Gödel and others discovered that any sound axiom system for set theory must necessarily be incomplete.
Axiomatics
In the 21st century, a new standard for rigor arose, computer-assisted proofs, and the propositions of the Elements (with some updates to their proofs) have withstood computer checking.
Axiomatics

For example, in the first construction of Book 1, of an equilateral triangle, Euclid used a premise that was neither postulated nor proved: that two circles sharing the same line segment as a radius will cross each other in two points, rather than somehow not crossing.
Axiomatics
In 2017, Michael Beeson et al. used computer proof assistants to create and check a set of axioms similar to Euclid's.
Axiomatics
Beeson et al. chose Tarski's system as their starting point, instead of Hilbert's, because it is closer to Euclid's, and uses only points as the variables in its formulas.
Selected editions
The editio princeps (in Latin), based on the 13th century translation and commentary of Campanus.
Selected editions
First full-text Latin translation directly from the Greek.
Selected editions

The confusion in the title between Euclid of Alexandria, the author of the Elements, and Euclid of Megara, a philosopher from almost a century earlier, was a common mistake in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.
Selected editions
The first edition published in France.
Selected editions

Selected editions
Tartaglia's translation of the Elements into Italian was the first into any modern European language, and was based on both Campanus and Zamberti.
Selected editions
"The reference edition for the scholarly community up until the early nineteenth century"; Italian translation published in 1575 by Commandino's son-in-law, Valerio Spaccioli.
Selected editions

Based on multiple sources, but most closely related to the version of Magnien and Gracilis.

Despite the title this includes only the first six books, with parallel columns of Greek from Grynaeus 1533 and Latin corrected from Commandino 1572.

Euclid's Elements: Completing Oliver Byrne's work, a modern redrawing extended to the rest of the Elements, was published by Kronecker Wallis, 2019.

antq_paradise_mislaid.title: Paradise Lost

name: Paradise Lost
caption: Title page of the first edition (1667)
author: John Milton

sents: lead
Paradise Lost is an epic poem in blank verse by the English poet John Milton (1608–1674).
lead
The poem concerns the biblical story of the fall of man: the temptation of Adam and Eve by the fallen angel Satan and their expulsion from the Garden of Eden.
lead
The first version, published in 1667, consists of ten books with over ten thousand lines of verse.
lead
A second edition followed in 1674, arranged into twelve books (in the manner of Virgil's Aeneid) with minor revisions throughout.
lead
It is considered to be Milton's masterpiece, and it helped solidify his reputation as one of the greatest English poets.
Synopsis
At the end of the debate, Satan volunteers to corrupt the newly created Earth and God's new and most favoured creation, Mankind.
Synopsis
After eating the fruit, Adam and Eve experience lust for the first time, which renders their next sexual encounter with one another more passionate.
Synopsis
At first, Adam is convinced that Eve was right in thinking that eating the fruit would be beneficial.
Composition
John Aubrey (1626–1697), Milton's contemporary and biographer, says that it was written between 1658 and 1663.
Composition
Having gone blind in 1652, Milton wrote Paradise Lost entirely through dictation with the help of amanuenses and friends.
Composition
Milton scholar John Leonard notes that Milton "did not at first plan to write a biblical epic".
Composition

Since epics were typically written about heroic kings and queens (and with pagan gods), Milton originally envisioned his epic to be based on a legendary Saxon or British king like the legend of King Arthur.
Publication
The 1667 version of Paradise Lost divided the poem into ten books.
Publication
Starting in 1668, some printings inserted "Arguments" (brief summaries) at the beginning of each book.
Publication
Mary was increasingly relying on her son Samuel to help her manage the business and the first book that Samuel Simmons registered for publication in his name was Paradise Lost in 1667.
Biblical epic
Rather than invoking the classical muses, however, Milton addresses the Christian God as his "Heav'nly Muse" (1.1).
Blank verse
Although Milton was not the first to use blank verse, his use of it was very influential and he became known for the style.
Blank verse
Blank verse was not much used in the non-dramatic poetry of the 17th century until Paradise Lost.
Blank verse
Milton also wrote Paradise Regained (1671) and parts of Samson Agonistes (1671) in blank verse.
Acrostics

Milton used at least two acrostics in the poem, perhaps mimicking the acrostics found in Dante's Divine Comedy, although these acrostics were not remarked in the scholarly literature until the 20th century.
Acrostics
Later, five lines describing the serpent's sidelong approach towards Eve spell out "SATAN" (9.510–514), with perhaps another truncated "FAL" just above at 9.503–505.
Double syntax
For example, in book 9 Milton writes of Adam awaiting Eve's return "Great joy he promised to his thoughts, and new/ Solace in her return..." (9.843-844).
Satan
Satan, formerly called Lucifer, is the first major character introduced in the poem.
Satan
The rebellion stems from Satan's pride and envy, derived from God's proclamation that the Son of God was "anointed" as the saviour (5.660-664ff).
Satan

Some scholars have noted that Milton's use of heroic language, demonstrated in Satan's depiction of having a "fixt mind", "unconquerable Will" and "courage never to submit or yield", contributes to the human-like complexity of his character (1.97, 106, 108).
Satan
For Satan declares in Book 1 that "in [his] choyce", he would rather have leadership in Hell than Heaven, emphasising that his defying God was personal agency (261).
Satan
Despite Blake thinking that Milton intended for Satan to have a heroic role in the poem, Blake himself described Satan as the "state of error," and as beyond salvation.
Adam
Adam is the first human created by God.
Adam
Raphael advises him to "take heed lest Passion sway / Thy Judgment" (5.635–636).
Eve
When she first meets Adam, she turns away, being more interested in returning to the watery reflection, Milton's allusion to the myth of Narcissus.
Eve
Recounting this to Adam she confesses that she found him less enticing than her reflection (4.477–480).
Eve
Book four, lines 440-491 is the first instance in the poem of Eve speaking.
Eve
Later in book four, Milton depicts Satan whispering into Eve's ear as she sleeps, and her resulting dream reinforces her earlier admiration for her own reflection (4.800-809).
Eve
In Book 9, Milton stages a domestic debate between Adam and Eve about whether they should separate for a time to work in different parts of the Garden.
The Son of God
The Son of God is the spirit who will become incarnate as Jesus Christ, though he is never named explicitly because he has not yet entered human form.
The Son of God
Milton believed in a subordinationist doctrine of Christology that regarded the Son as secondary to the Father and as God's "great Vice-regent" (5.609).
The Son of God
Milton's God in Paradise Lost refers to the Son as "My word, my wisdom, and effectual might" (3.170).
The Son of God
The Father then asks whether there "Dwels in all Heaven charitie so deare?" (3.216) and the Son volunteers himself.
Raphael
The first pair are "regal with ornament" (5.280).
Raphael
The next pair are "dipped in colors of Heaven" (5.283) The third pair then "shadowed either heel with feathered mail" (5.284).
Raphael
When Raphael finally reaches the bower, where Adam and Eve dwell, his conversation with Adam and Eve extends all the way from Book 5 to Book 8.
Raphael
In Book 5, the discussion between Adam and Raphael pertains to the nature of the angels in Heaven, including the fact that angels eat food.
Raphael
In Book 6, Raphael tells a heroic tale about the War in Heaven.
Raphael
In Book 7, Adam asks Raphael about the creation of the cosmos, to which Raphael "responds mild" and proceeds to tell Adam about each day of creation (7.110).
Raphael
In Book 8, Adam asks about the planets and the stars, wondering why the Sun, which is much larger, appears to orbit the smaller Earth.
Raphael
Raphael responds telling Adam that his role is not to question the secrets of the cosmos but "Rather admire" (8.75).
Raphael
Raphael seems to blush at this statement "with a smile that glowed / Celestial rosy red" and confirms that angels have their own ways of loving and being intimate (8.618-619).
Michael
He leads in battle and uses a sword which was "giv'n him temperd so, that neither keen / Nor solid might resist that edge" (6.322–323).
Abdiel
Abdiel first appears in the host of angels listening to Satan's speech, in which Satan calls for rebellion against God.
Abdiel
He is characterized by his "zeal" in obeying the "divine commands" (5.805-806), and serves as the lone angel in Satan's audience to argue with Satan, and refuse to take part in the rebellion.
Sin
Sin is the first female character presented in the epic and is introduced in Book 2.
Sin
She is Satan's daughter and lover, born in Heaven through parthenogenesis (2.757-760).
Sin
After the angels fall from Heaven, God charges Sin with the responsibility of guarding the gates of Hell (2.850-853).
Sin

Tatlock attributes James 1:15 as the foundation for Milton's allegory of Sin and her son Death: "Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death." Robert B.
Sin
Joseph Addison published his critiques in his magazine The Spectator in the early 18th century.
Death
Readers are first introduced to Death in Book 2 when Satan encounters Death at the gates of Hell.
Death
In Book 10, Satan returns towards of Hell and encounters Sin and Death who are going down to earth, which Satan has effectively conquered by successfully tempting Adam and Eve.
Death
In Book 10, Death again is described as merely a "shadow" (10.264).
Death
Beelzebub, in Paradise Lost, is Satan's second-in-command and the fallen angel who plays a central role in organising the demons after their expulsion from Heaven (1.79).
Death
He is depicted as cunning, persuasive, and politically strategic, often acting as the voice that articulates Satan's broader plans to the infernal council (2.378-380).
Death
Throughout the epic, Beelzebub's speeches help shape the demons' course of action, positioning him as one of Hell's leaders (2.299-301).
Hell
Paradise Lost takes place in many different settings, the first of which is Hell.
Hell
Pandæmonium is a city erected in Hell under the leadership of Mammon, one of Satan's followers, whom Milton calls "the least erected spirit that fell from Heav'n (1.679).
Hell
The fallen angels dig up metal and "ribs of gold" (1.690) and use a smelting technique to grow a grand palace up out of the ground in a parody of organic creation.
Hell

Lewis in A Preface to Paradise Lost writes that Mammon "believes that Hell can be made into a substitute for Heaven" and that Mammon's tragedy is that he "never understood the difference between Hell and Heaven at all.
Marriage
A year after Mary Powell left him weeks after their marriage in 1642, Milton published The Divorce Tracts, detailing his opinions on marriage and divorce.
Idolatry
Milton's 17th-century contemporaries by and large criticised his ideas and considered him a radical, mostly because of his republican political views and heterodox theological opinions.
Idolatry
One of Milton's most controversial arguments centred on his concept of what is idolatrous, a subject which is deeply embedded in Paradise Lost.
Idolatry
Milton's first criticism of idolatry focused on the constructing of temples and other buildings to serve as places of worship.
Idolatry
By linking Saint Peter's Basilica and the Pantheon to Pandemonium—an ideally false structure—the two famous buildings take on a false meaning.
Criticism of monarchy
Satan raises "impious war in Heav'n" (i 43) by leading a third of the angels in revolt against God.
Criticism of monarchy
In his poem, however, he takes the side of "Heav'n's awful Monarch" (iv 960).
Moral ambiguity

From there, Empson gives fake praise that is really an attack, saying that "Milton deserves credit for making God wicked, since the God of Christianity is 'a wicked God'." John Leonard states that "Empson never denies that Satan's plan is wicked.
Moral ambiguity
Not only will the Son sacrifice himself pre-emptively in Book 3 for the not-yet-occurred Fall of Man, but Man himself will have a role in his own salvation.
Moral ambiguity

Lewis wrote: "The first qualification for judging any piece of workmanship from a corkscrew to a cathedral is to know what it is - what it was intended to do and how it is meant to be used." Lewis said the poem was a genuine Christian morality tale.
Free will
One of the major themes seen throughout Milton's Paradise Lost is free will, used as a way to "justify the ways of God to men" (PL 1.
Christian epic
Tobias Gregory wrote that Milton was "the most theologically learned among early modern epic poets.
Iconography
By 1730, the same images had been re-engraved on a smaller scale by Paul Fourdrinier.
Iconography
Some of the most notable illustrators of Paradise Lost included William Blake, Gustave Doré, and Henry Fuseli.
Iconography
Outside of book illustrations, the epic has also inspired other visual works by well-known painters like Salvador Dalí who executed a set of ten colour engravings in 1974.
Iconography
Milton's achievement in writing Paradise Lost while blind (he dictated to helpers) inspired loosely biographical paintings by both Fuseli and Eugène Delacroix.
Tamil
Book 1 of Paradise Lost was translated into Tamil under the title Swarga Neekam MutharKandam (1895) by V.
Other information
John Milton's Paradise Lost: 2008-09 exhibition at the Morgan Library & Museum.

name: A Dictionary of the English Language
caption: Title page from the second edition of the Dictionary
author: Samuel Johnson
subject: Dictionary

precededby: The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
author: Samuel Johnson

sents: lead
A Dictionary of the English Language, sometimes published as Johnson's Dictionary, was published on 15 April 1755 and written by Samuel Johnson.
lead
It is among the most influential dictionaries in the history of the English language.
lead

There was dissatisfaction with the dictionaries of the period, so in June 1746 a group of London booksellers contracted Johnson to write a dictionary for the sum of 1,500 guineas (£1,575), equivalent to about £ in.
lead
Johnson took seven years to complete the work, although he had claimed he could finish it in three.
lead
He did so single-handedly, with only clerical assistance to copy the illustrative quotations that he had marked in books.
lead
Johnson produced several revised editions during his life.
lead
Until the completion of the Oxford English Dictionary 173 years later, Johnson's was viewed as the pre-eminent English dictionary.
lead

According to Walter Jackson Bate, the Dictionary "easily ranks as one of the greatest single achievements of scholarship, and probably the greatest ever performed by one individual who labored under anything like the disadvantages in a comparable length of time".
Background

The rise of literacy among the general public, combined with the technical advances in the mechanics of printing and bookbinding, meant that for the first time, books, texts, maps, pamphlets and newspapers were widely available to the general public at a reasonable cost.
Background

In 1746, a consortium of London's most successful printers, including Robert Dodsley and Thomas Longman – none could afford to undertake it alone – set out to satisfy and capitalise on this need by the ever-increasing reading and writing public.
Background
Johnson's dictionary was not the first English dictionary, nor even among the first dozen.
Background
Over the previous 150 years more than twenty dictionaries had been published in England, the oldest of these being a Latin-English "wordbook" by Sir Thomas Elyot published in 1538.
Background
The next to appear was by Richard Mulcaster, a headmaster, in 1583.
Background
Though it contained only 2,449 words, and no word beginning with the letters W, X, or Y, this was the first monolingual English dictionary.
Background
Benjamin Martin's Lingua Britannica Reformata (1749) and Ainsworth's Thesaurus Linguae Latinae (1737) are both significant, in that they define entries in separate senses, or aspects, of the word.
Background

In English (among others), John Cowell's Interpreter, a law dictionary, was published in 1607, Edward Phillips' The new world of English words came out in 1658 and a dictionary of 40,000 words had been prepared in 1721 by Nathan Bailey, though none was as comprehensive in breadth or style as Johnson's.
Background
Johnson's dictionary was the first to comprehensively document the English lexicon.
Background
Johnson's dictionary was prepared at 17 Gough Square, London, an eclectic household, between the years of 1746 and 1755.
Background
By 1747 Johnson had written his Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language, which spelled out his intentions and proposed methodology for preparing his document.
Background
Johnson's Plan received the patronage of Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield but not to Johnson's pleasure.
Background
Seven years after first meeting Johnson to discuss the work, Chesterfield wrote two anonymous essays in The World that recommended the Dictionary.
The text
It was printed as a folio, measuring 16 × 9 inches (422 × 251 mm).
The text
The paper was of the finest quality available, the cost of which ran to nearly £1,600, more than Johnson had been paid to write the book.
The text
The preface and headings were set in 4.6 mm "English" type, the text—double columned—was set in a typeface like Caslon.
The text
This first edition of the dictionary contained a 42,773-word list, to which only a few more were added in subsequent editions.
The text
One of Johnson's important innovations was to illustrate the meanings of his words by literary quotation, of which there are around 114,000, from around 500 authors.
The text
The authors most frequently cited by Johnson include Shakespeare, Milton and Dryden.
The text
Unlike most modern lexicographers, Johnson introduced humour or prejudice into quite a number of his definitions.
The text
Subsequent printings ran to four volumes; even these formed a stack 10 in tall, and weighed in at nearly 21 lb.
The text
In addition to the sheer physical heft of Johnson's dictionary, came the equally hefty price: £4/10/– (equivalent to approximately £ in ).
The text

So discouraging was the price that by 1784, thirty years after the first edition was published, when the dictionary had by then run through five editions, only about 6,000 copies were in circulation—an average sale of 200 books a year for thirty years.
Initial reception
Yet, just as Johnson was plunging into another trough of despondency, the reputation of the Dictionary at last brought reward.
Initial reception
In July 1762 Johnson was granted a state pension of £300 a year by the twenty-four-year-old monarch, George III.
Criticism

Johnson's general rule, therefore, can only take place where custom has not plainly decided.' Nevertheless, Walker scrupulously followed Johnson's explanations of words, as did many contemporary dictionaries.
Influence in Britain
In the end the OED reproduced around 1,700 of Johnson's definitions, marking them simply 'J.'."
Influence in Britain
In 2005, the Royal Mint issued a commemorative fifty pence coin celebrating the 250th anniversary of the dictionary's publication.
Influence in America
In 1846 he completed his Universal and Critical Dictionary of the English Language.
Influence in America
Legislators are much occupied with ascertaining 'first meanings', with trying to secure the literal sense of their predecessors' legislation...
Folio and abridged editions
The first was the 1755 Folio edition, which came in two large volumes on 4 April.
Folio and abridged editions
The third edition was published in 1765, but it was the fourth, which came out in 1773 which included significant revisions by Johnson of the original work.
Folio and abridged editions
The Abridged edition came out in 1756 in two octavo volumes with entries, "abstracted from the folio edition by the author", laid out as two columns per page.
Replica editions

The entire first Folio editions of 1755 1st edition and 1773 4th edition are available on Johnson's Dictionary Online, a project funded by the National Endowment for the Humanities and created by a team of scholars at the University of Central Florida.
In popular culture
At the end of Chapter 1 of Vanity Fair by William Makepeace Thackeray, Becky Sharp disdainfully throws a copy of Johnson's Dictionary out the window.
In popular culture
Johnson's Great Dictionary" appears as a plot device in the 1944 Sherlock Holmes film The Pearl of Death, starring Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce.
In popular culture
Johnson had given his only manuscript to the Prince of Wales and it was presumably destroyed by Blackadder's apprentice dogsbody Baldrick.
In popular culture
The manuscript is later found intact, only for Johnson to discover he had forgotten to include the word "sausage".

Micrographia: or Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses.
lead
With Observations and Inquiries Thereupon is a historically significant book by Robert Hooke about his observations through various lenses.
lead
It was the first book to include illustrations of insects and plants as seen through microscopes.
lead
Published in January 1665, the first major publication of the Royal Society, it became the first scientific best-seller, inspiring a wide public interest in the new science of microscopy.
lead
The book originated the biological term "cell".
Observations
Hooke most famously describes a fly's eye and a plant cell (where he coined that term because plant cells, which are walled, reminded him of the cells of a monastery).
Reception
Micrographia illustrations of the miniature world captured the public's imagination in a radically new way; Samuel Pepys called it "the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life".

name: Robinson Crusoe
original_title: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, of York, Mariner: Who lived Eight and Twenty Years, all alone in an un-inhabited Island on the Coast of America, near the Mouth of the Great River of Oroonoque; Having been cast on Shore by Shipwreck, wherein all the Men perished but himself. With An Account how he was at last as strangely deliver'd by Pyrates. Written by Himself.
caption: Title page from the first edition
author: Daniel Defoe

followedby: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
author: Daniel Defoe

sents: lead
Robinson Crusoe is an English adventure novel by Daniel Defoe, first published on 25 April 1719.
lead
It is often credited as marking the beginning of realistic fiction as a literary genre in the English language, and has been described as the first novel in English – although this label is disputed.
lead

The story has been thought to be based on the life of Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish castaway who lived for four years on a Pacific island called "Más a Tierra" (now part of Chile) which was renamed Robinson Crusoe Island in 1966.
lead
Pedro Serrano is another real-life castaway whose story might have inspired the novel.
lead
The first edition credited the work's protagonist Robinson Crusoe as its author, leading many readers to believe he was a real person and that the book was a non-fiction travelogue.
lead
Despite its simple narrative style, Robinson Crusoe was well received in the literary world.
lead

Before the end of 1719, the book had already run through four editions, and it has gone on to become one of the most widely published books in history, spawning so many imitations, not only in literature but also in film, television, and radio, that its name is used to define a genre, the Robinsonade.
Plot summary

Robinson Crusoe (the family name coming from the German name "Kreutznaer") sets sail from Kingston upon Hull, England, on a sea voyage in August 1651, against the wishes of his parents, who wanted him to pursue a career in law.
Plot summary

Years later, Crusoe joins an expedition to purchase slaves from Africa but the ship gets blown off course in a storm about forty miles out to sea and runs aground on the sandbar of an island off the Venezuelan coast (which he calls the Island of Despair) near the mouth of the Orinoco River on 30 September 1659.
Plot summary
After more cannibals arrive to partake in a feast, Crusoe and Friday kill most of them and save two prisoners.
Plot summary
Crusoe leaves the island on 19 December 1686 and arrives in England on 11 June 1687.
Plot summary
Friday accompanies him and, en route, they endure one last adventure together as they fight off famished wolves while crossing the Pyrenees.
Reception and sequels
The book was published on 25 April 1719.
Reception and sequels
Before the end of the year, this first volume had run through four editions.
Reception and sequels
Defoe went on to write a lesser-known sequel, The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719).
Reception and sequels

It was intended to be the last part of his stories, according to the original title page of the sequel's first edition, but a third book was published (1720), Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprising Adventures of Robinson Crusoe: With his Vision of the Angelick World.
Interpretations of the novel

The idealized master-servant relationship Defoe depicts between Crusoe and Friday can also be seen in terms of cultural assimilation, with Crusoe representing the "enlightened" European while Friday is the "savage" who can only be redeemed from his cultural manners through assimilation into Crusoe's culture.
Interpretations of the novel
The book tells the story of how Robinson becomes closer to God, not through listening to sermons in a church but through spending time alone amongst nature with only a Bible to read.
Interpretations of the novel
Defoe was a Puritan moralist and normally worked in the guide tradition, writing books on how to be a good Puritan Christian, such as The New Family Instructor (1727) and Religious Courtship (1722).
Interpretations of the novel

"Crusoe" may have been taken from Timothy Cruso, a classmate of Defoe's who had written guide books, including God the Guide of Youth (1695), before dying at an early age – just eight years before Defoe wrote Robinson Crusoe.
Interpretations of the novel
The denouement culminates not only in Crusoe's deliverance from the island, but his spiritual deliverance, his acceptance of Christian doctrine, and in his intuition of his own salvation.
Economics and civilization

Early critics, such as Robert Louis Stevenson, admired it, saying that the footprint scene in Crusoe was one of the four greatest in English literature and most unforgettable; more prosaically, Wesley Vernon has seen the origins of forensic podiatry in this episode.
Economics and civilization
