Publication history
Written after the publication of Pride and Prejudice, Austen submitted Emma to the London publisher John Murray II in the autumn of 1815.
Publication history
Murray offered her £450 for the rights to Emma and the copyrights to Mansfield Park and Sense and Sensibility.
Publication history
She rejected his offer and instead published 2000 copies of the novel at her own expense, retaining the copyright and paying Murray a 10% commission.
Publication history
The publication in December 1815 (dated 1816) consisted of a three-volume set in duodecimo at the selling price of £1.1s (one guinea) per set.
Publication history
In the United States, copies of the first publication were sold in 1818 for $4 each , as well as an American edition published by Mathew Carey of Philadelphia in 1816.
Publication history
A later American edition was published in 1833 and again in 1838 by Carey, Lea, and Blanchard.
Publication history
A French version was published in 1816 by Arthus Bertrand, publisher for Madame Isabelle De Montolieu.
Publication history

Publication history

Publication history
Emma has remained in continuous publication in English throughout the remainder of the nineteenth century and into the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.

One important review, requested by John Murray prior to publication and written by Sir Walter Scott, appeared anonymously in March 1816 in the Quarterly Review, although the date of the journal was October 1815.
Reception

The subjects are not often elegant, and certainly never grand: but they are finished up to nature, and with a precision which delights the reader.Two other unsigned reviews appeared in 1816, one in The Champion, also in March, and another in September of the same year in Gentleman's Magazine.
Reception
Emma herself is the most interesting to me of all her heroines.
Reception
Although Austen's Pride and Prejudice is the most popular of her novels, Robert McCrum suggests that Emma "is her masterpiece, mixing the sparkle of her early books with a deep sensibility".
Highbury as a character
Irvine points out the adjective "charming" appears to the narrator speaking, but notes the sentence goes on to associate "perfect" with "usual", which he pointed out was an incongruity.
Highbury as a character

Irvine suggested the next sentence "would always be called ten" is in fact the voice of the community of Highbury, which wants the fiancée of Mr Elton to be "perfect", whom the narrator sarcastically calls the "usual" sort of community gossip is about a new arrival in Highbury, whom everyone thinks is "charming".
Highbury as a character

Wiltshire noted that Austen put the population of Highbury as 352 people, and said that although clearly most of these people do not appear as characters - or at best as minor characters - Austen created the impression of Highbury as a "social commonwealth".

Fortune I do not want; employment I do not want; consequence I do not want." However, political power still resides with men in the patriarchal society of Regency England, as the book notes that Mr Knightley is not only a member of the gentry, but also serves as the magistrate of Highbury.
Highbury as a character
Mrs Elton is only a first generation gentry, as her father bought the land that she grew up on with money he had raised in trade.
Highbury as a character

Likewise, Jane Fairfax, who is too poor to live off her wealth and must work as a governess, which excludes her from the female social elite of Highbury, does marry well after all, which makes her story the only one of real feminine worth triumphing over the lack of wealth in Emma.
Nationhood and the "Irish Question"

In 1801, the Act of Union had brought Ireland into the United Kingdom, but there was a major debate about what was Ireland's precise status in the United Kingdom; another kingdom, province, or a colony?
Female empowerment
Looser states that if you define feminism broadly as a movement relating to how women are limited and devalued within a culture then Austen's work applies to this concept of feminism.
Wealth
Emma is a wealthy young woman, having a personal fortune amounting to £30,000.
Parenting
In fact, most of the time it seems that Emma is parenting her father, taking on the role of both daughter and mother.
Class
Brown wrote that Austen had a strong appreciation of the land as not only a source of aesthetic pleasure, but also a source of money, an aspect of pre-industrial England that many now miss.
Food
For the most part, the poor in Emma are overlooked by the characters in the novel due to their socioeconomic status.
Food
"These gifts are not without motive, and food—as it pertains to Emma Woodhouse—only becomes interesting when it pertains to love...[R]omance is a far more interesting subject than food.
Food
Emma quickly reduces the topic of eating to a run of the mill 'any thing,' an arbitrary and empty screen that only becomes interesting when projected on by those in love".
Masculinity
Mr Knightley is Jane Austen's perfect gentleman figure in Emma.

name: Crime and Punishment
caption: 1956 Random House printing of Crime and Punishment, translated by Constance Garnett
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

sents: lead
Crime and Punishment is a novel by the Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky.
lead
It was first published in the literary journal The Russian Messenger in twelve monthly installments during 1866.
lead
It was later published in a single volume.
lead
It is the second of Dostoevsky's full-length novels following his return from ten years of exile in Siberia.
lead
Crime and Punishment is considered the first great novel of his mature period of writing and is often cited as one of the greatest works of world literature.
lead

Crime and Punishment follows the mental anguish and moral dilemmas of Rodion Raskolnikov, an impoverished former law student in Saint Petersburg who plans to kill an unscrupulous pawnbroker, an old woman who stores money and valuable objects in her flat.
lead

He theorises that with the money he could liberate himself from poverty and go on to perform great deeds, and seeks to convince himself that certain crimes are justifiable if they are committed in order to remove obstacles to the higher goals of "extraordinary" men.
lead
Once the deed is done, however, he finds himself wracked with confusion, paranoia, and disgust.
Background
At the time, Dostoevsky owed large sums of money to creditors and was trying to help the family of his brother Mikhail, who had died in early 1864.
Background
After appeals elsewhere failed, Dostoevsky turned as a last resort to the publisher Mikhail Katkov and sought an advance on a proposed contribution.
Background
Dostoevsky, having been engaged in polemical debates with Katkov in the early 1860s, had never published anything in its pages before.
Background
In a letter to Katkov written in September 1865, Dostoevsky explained to him that the work was to be about a young man who yields to "certain strange, 'unfinished' ideas, yet floating in the air".
Background
In letters written in November 1865, an important conceptual change occurred: the "story" had become a "novel".
Background

These have been distinguished as the Wiesbaden edition, the Petersburg edition, and the final plan, involving the shift from a first-person narrator to Dostoevsky's innovative use of third-person narrative to achieve first-person narrative perspectives.
Background

Dostoevsky initially considered four first-person plans: a memoir written by Raskolnikov, his confession recorded eight days after the murder, his diary begun five days after the murder, and a mixed form in which the first half was in the form of a memoir, and the second half in the form of a diary.
Background
According to Joseph Frank, "one possibility is that his protagonist began to develop beyond the boundaries in which he had first been conceived".
Background
The final version of Crime and Punishment came into being only when, in November 1865, Dostoevsky decided to recast his novel in the third person.
Background
The first part of Crime and Punishment appeared in the January 1866 issue of The Russian Messenger, and the last one was published in December 1866.
Part 1
In 1866, Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov, a former law student, lives in extreme poverty in a tiny rented room in Saint Petersburg.
Part 1
Shaken by his actions, he steals only a handful of items and a small purse, leaving much of the pawnbroker's wealth untouched.
Part 2
In a feverish and semi-delirious state, Raskolnikov conceals the stolen items and falls asleep exhausted.
Part 2
Fearing a search, he hides the stolen items under a large rock in an empty yard, noticing in humiliation that he has not even checked how much money is in the purse.
Part 2
Raskolnikov gives his last twenty-five rubles (from money sent to him by his mother) to Marmeladov's consumptive widow, Katerina Ivanovna, saying it is the repayment of a debt to his friend.
Part 3
Timidly, she explains that he left his address with them last night, and that she has come to invite him to attend her father's funeral.
Part 3
Raskolnikov tries to find out what he wants, but the artisan says only one word – "murderer", and walks off.
Part 4
Svidrigailov also mentions that his wife, who defended Dunya at the time of the unpleasantness but died shortly afterwards, has left her 3000 rubles in her will.
Part 4
The meeting with Luzhin that evening begins with talk of Svidrigailov—his depraved character, his presence in Petersburg, the unexpected death of his wife and the 3000 rubles left to Dunya.
Part 4
Dunya tells him to leave and never come back.
Part 4

Now free and with significant capital, they excitedly begin to discuss plans for the future, but Raskolnikov suddenly gets up and leaves, telling them, to their great consternation, that it might be the last time he sees them.
Part 4
Raskolnikov begins to realize that Sonya is sustained only by her faith in God.
Part 5
Outraged, Katerina Ivanovna abuses Luzhin and sets about emptying Sonya's pockets to prove her innocence, but a folded 100-ruble note does indeed fly out of one of the pockets.
Part 5
But it is only a prelude to his confession that he is the murderer of the old woman and Lizaveta.
Part 6
When Raskolnikov finally turns home, Dunya, who has been watching them, approaches Svidrigailov and demands to know what he meant in his letter about her brother's "secret".
Epilogue

Due to the fullness of his confession at a time when another man had already confessed, and his state of mind at the time of the murders, Raskolnikov is sentenced to only eight years of penal servitude.
Epilogue
Sonya follows Raskolnikov to Siberia, but he is initially hostile towards her as he is still struggling to acknowledge moral culpability for his crime, feeling himself to be guilty only of weakness.
Major characters
Raskolnikov discerns in her the same feelings of shame and alienation that he experiences, and she becomes the first person to whom he confesses his crime.
Major characters
When Dunya tells him she could never love him (after attempting to shoot him) he lets her go.
Other characters
Ilya Petrovich (Илья Петрович) – A police official and Nikodim Fomich's assistant, nicknamed "Gunpowder" for his very bad temper.
Other characters

Raskolnikov had been engaged to her daughter, a sickly girl who had died, and Praskovya Pavlovna had granted him extensive credit on the basis of this engagement and a promissory note for 115 roubles.
Nihilism, rationalism and utilitarianism

In the novel, Dostoevsky pinpointed the dangers of both utilitarianism and rationalism, the main ideas of which inspired the radicals, continuing a fierce criticism he had already started with his Notes from Underground.
Nihilism, rationalism and utilitarianism
The radicals refused to recognize themselves in the novel's pages, since Dostoevsky pursued nihilistic ideas to their most extreme consequences.
Nihilism, rationalism and utilitarianism
Dostoevsky believed that such ideas limited man to a product of physics, chemistry and biology, negating spontaneous emotional responses.
The environment of Saint Petersburg
Dostoevsky was among the first to recognize the symbolic possibilities of city life and imagery drawn from the city.
The environment of Saint Petersburg

Evnin regards Crime and Punishment as the first great Russian novel "in which the climactic moments of the action are played out in dirty taverns, on the street, in the sordid back rooms of the poor".
Structure
At the same time, this tragedy contains a Christian component, and the logical demands of this element are met only by the resurrection promised in the Epilogue".
Reception
The first part of Crime and Punishment published in the January and February issues of The Russian Messenger met with public success.
Reception
In his memoirs, the conservative belletrist Nikolay Strakhov recalled that Crime and Punishment was the literary sensation of 1866 in Russia.
Reception
Crime and Punishment was regarded as an important work in a number of 20th-century European cultural movements, notably the Bloomsbury Group, psychoanalysis, and existentialism.
Reception
An exception was the work of Mikhail Bakhtin, considered by many commentators to be the most original and insightful analyst of Dostoevsky's work.
Reception

In Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics, Bakhtin argues that attempts to understand Dostoevsky's characters from the vantage point of a pre-existing philosophy, or as individualized "objects" to be psychologically analysed, will always fail to penetrate the unique "artistic architechtonics" of his works.
Film
There have been over 30 film adaptations of Crime and Punishment.
Film

Little Women is a coming-of-age novel written by American novelist Louisa May Alcott, originally published in two volumes, in 1868 and 1869.
lead
The story follows the lives of the four March sisters—Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy—and details their passage from childhood to womanhood.

lead

lead

lead

lead

The Great Gatsby is a 1925 tragedy novel by American writer F.
lead

Set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City, the novel depicts first-person narrator Nick Carraway's interactions with Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire obsessed with reuniting with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan.
lead
The novel was inspired by a youthful romance Fitzgerald had with socialite Ginevra King and the riotous parties he attended on Long Island's North Shore in 1922.
lead

lead

lead

lead

lead
After its publication by Scribner's in April 1925, The Great Gatsby received generally favorable reviews, though some literary critics believed it did not equal Fitzgerald's previous efforts.
Historical and biographical context
Set on the prosperous Long Island of 1922, The Great Gatsby provides a critical social history of Prohibition-era America during the Jazz Age.
Historical and biographical context

Fitzgerald uses many of these 1920s societal developments to tell his story, from simple details like petting in automobiles to broader themes such as bootlegging as the illicit source of Gatsby's fortune.
Historical and biographical context
Fitzgerald conveys the hedonism of Jazz Age society by following a down-to-earth narrator as a spectator of the flashiest and most raucous era in American history.
Historical and biographical context
In 1915, the 18-year-old Fitzgerald met Ginevra King, a 16-year-old socialite with whom he fell deeply in love.
Historical and biographical context

While awaiting deployment to the Western front where he hoped to die in combat, he was stationed at Camp Sheridan in Montgomery, Alabama, where he met Zelda Sayre, a vivacious 17-year-old Southern belle.
Plot summary
In spring 1922, Nick Carraway—a Yale alumnus from the Midwest and a World War I veteran—journeys to New York City to obtain employment as a bond salesman.

Major characters

Writing and production

Alternative titles
Fitzgerald had difficulty choosing a title for his novel and entertained many choices before reluctantly deciding on The Great Gatsby, a title inspired by Alain-Fournier's Le Grand Meaulnes.

Dust jacket art

The artwork for the first edition of The Great Gatsby, known as Celestial Eyes, is among the most celebrated in American literature and represents a unique instance in literary history in which a novel's commissioned artwork directly influenced the composition of the text.
Dust jacket art
In a preliminary sketch, Cugat drew a concept of a dismal gray landscape inspired by Fitzgerald's original title for the novel, Among Ash Heaps and Millionaires.
Dust jacket art

Initial reviews

Partially serialised in the American journal The Little Review from March 1918 to December 1920, the entire work was published in Paris by Sylvia Beach on 2 February 1922, Joyce's fortieth birthday.
lead
It is considered one of the most important works of modernist literature and a classic of the genre, having been called "a demonstration and summation of the entire movement".
lead
Ulysses chronicles the experiences of three Dubliners over the course of a single day, 16 June 1904 (which its fans now celebrate annually as Bloomsday).
lead
Joyce chose this date because it was the day of his first outing with Nora Barnacle, who became his wife.
lead

Ulysses is the Latinised name of Odysseus, the hero of Homer's epic poem the Odyssey, and the novel establishes a series of parallels between Leopold Bloom and Odysseus, Molly Bloom and Penelope, and Stephen Dedalus and Telemachus.
lead
There are also correspondences with William Shakespeare's play Hamlet and with other literary, religious, and mythological figures, including Jesus, Elijah, Moses, Dante Alighieri and Don Juan.
lead
Such themes as antisemitism, human sexuality, British rule in Ireland, Catholicism and Irish nationalism are treated in the context of early-20th-century Dublin.

To Kill a Mockingbird is a 1960 Southern Gothic novel by American author Harper Lee.
lead
It became instantly successful after its release; in the United States, it is widely read in high schools and middle schools.
lead
To Kill a Mockingbird won the Pulitzer Prize a year after its release, and it has become a classic of modern American literature.
lead
The plot and characters are loosely based on Lee's observations of her family, her neighbors and an event that occurred near her hometown of Monroeville, Alabama, in 1936, when she was ten.
lead
Despite dealing with the serious issues of rape and racial inequality, the novel is renowned for its warmth and humor.
lead
Atticus Finch, the narrator's father, has served as a moral hero for many readers and as a model of integrity for lawyers.
lead
Scholars have noted that Lee also addresses issues of class, courage, compassion, and gender roles in the Deep South.

sents: lead
Nineteen Eighty-Four (also published as 1984) is a dystopian and speculative fiction novel by the English writer George Orwell.
lead
It was published on 8 June 1949 by Secker & Warburg as Orwell's ninth and final completed book.
lead
Thematically, it centres on totalitarianism, mass surveillance and repressive regimentation of people and behaviours.
lead
Nineteen Eighty-Four has often been regarded as a classic and has been acknowledged for its impact on 20th-century literature.
lead
The story takes place in a fictional future.
lead
The year is believed to be 1984, but this is uncertain.
lead
Much of the world is in perpetual war.
lead

Great Britain, now known as Airstrip One, has become a province of the totalitarian superstate Oceania, which is led by Big Brother, a dictatorial leader supported by an intense cult of personality manufactured by the Party's Thought Police.
Plot summary
As the narrative opens on "April 4th, 1984", a date whose validity is questioned by the protagonist, the world has been ravaged for decades by global war, civil conflict and revolution.
Plot summary

The Party brutally purges anyone who does not fully conform to their regime, using the Thought Police and constant surveillance through telescreens (two-way televisions), cameras and hidden microphones.
Plot summary
Winston revises past editions of The Times, while the original documents are destroyed after being dropped into ducts known as memory holes, which lead to an immense furnace.
Plot summary
One day, Julia discreetly hands Winston a love note, and the two begin a secret affair.
Plot summary
During the affair, Winston remembers the disappearance of his family during the civil war of the 1950s and his tense relationship with his estranged wife Katharine.
Plot summary
Winston is recalled to the Ministry to assist in making the necessary revisions to the records.
Plot summary
For the final stage of re-education, O'Brien takes Winston to Room 101, which contains each prisoner's worst fear.
Epilogue

The novel includes an epilogue, an appendix of around 1,000 words, titled Principles of Newspeak, and written in the voice of the (or possibly a second) narrator, using counterfactual past-subjunctive tense.
Epilogue
Orwell wrote to his literary agent in 1949, urging that the appendix be retained for the American edition.
Main characters
Winston Smith: the 39-year-old protagonist who is a phlegmatic everyman harbouring thoughts of rebellion and is curious about the Party's power and the past before the Revolution.
Main characters
Big Brother and Emmanuel Goldstein never physically appear, but are important to the plot and have a significant role in the worldbuilding.
Secondary characters
Tom Parsons: Winston's naïve neighbour, and an ideal member of the Outer Party: an uneducated, suggestible man who is utterly loyal to the Party, and fully believes in its perfect image.
Conception
The notebooks have been deemed "unlikely to have been completed later than January 1944", and "there is a strong suspicion that some of the material in them dates back to the early part of the war".
Conception
Orwell had toured Austria in May 1945 and observed manoeuvring he thought would probably lead to separate Soviet and Allied Zones of Occupation.
Conception
In January 1944, the Russian literary historian Gleb Struve introduced Orwell to Yevgeny Zamyatin's 1924 dystopian novel, We.
Conception
In 1946 Orwell wrote about the 1931 dystopian novel Brave New World by Aldous Huxley in his article "Freedom and Happiness" for the Tribune, and noted similarities to We.
Conception
By this time Orwell had scored a critical and commercial hit with his 1945 political satire, Animal Farm, which raised his profile.
Writing

In a June 1944 meeting with Fredric Warburg, co-founder of his British publisher Secker & Warburg, shortly before the release of Animal Farm, Orwell announced that he had written the first 12 pages of his new novel.
Writing
As he could then only earn a living from journalism, he predicted the book would not see a release before 1947.
Writing
Progress was slow; by the end of September 1945 Orwell had written some 50 pages.
Writing
His first stay lasted until October 1946, and during it he made little progress on the few already completed pages, and for a period of three months he did not work on it at all.
Writing
After spending the winter in London, Orwell returned to Jura; in May 1947 he reported to Warburg that despite progress being slow and difficult, he was roughly a third of the way through.
Writing

On 7 November 1947, he completed the first draft in bed, and subsequently travelled to East Kilbride near Glasgow for medical treatment at Hairmyres Hospital, where a specialist confirmed a chronic and infectious case of tuberculosis.
Writing
Orwell was discharged in the summer of 1948, after which he returned to Jura and produced a full second draft of Nineteen Eighty-Four, which he finished in November.
Writing
He asked Warburg to have someone come to Barnhill and retype the manuscript, which was so untidy that the task was only considered possible if Orwell were present, as only he could understand it.
Writing

The previous volunteer had left the country and no other could be found at short notice, so an impatient Orwell retyped it himself at a rate of roughly 4,000 words a day during bouts of fever and bloody coughing fits.
Writing
On 4 December 1948, Orwell sent the finished manuscript to Secker & Warburg and left Barnhill for good in January 1949.
Title
Shortly before completion of the second draft, Orwell vacillated between two titles: The Last Man in Europe, an early title, and Nineteen Eighty-Four.
Title

There has been a theory – doubted by Dorian Lynskey (author of a 2019 book about Nineteen Eighty-Four) – that 1984 was chosen simply as an inversion of the year 1948, the year in which it was being completed.
Title

Lynskey says the idea was "first suggested by Orwell's US publisher", and it was also mentioned by Christopher Hitchens in his introduction to the 2003 edition of Animal Farm and 1984, which also notes that the date was meant to give "an immediacy and urgency to the menace of totalitarian rule".
Title
Scholars have raised other possibilities. [His wife] Eileen wrote a poem for her old school's centenary called 'End of the Century: 1984.' G.

Chesterton's 1904 political satire The Napoleon of Notting Hill, which mocks the art of prophecy, opens in 1984.

First he wrote 1980, then 1982, and only later 1984.

Title

Title

Eileen served as Orwell's typist and her influence on his style is analyzed in the books Eileen: The Making of Georges Orwell (2020) by Sylvia Topp and Wifedom: Mrs Orwell’s Invisible Life (2023) by Anna Funder.

He also refused a proposal from the American Book of the Month Club to release an edition without the appendix and chapter on Goldstein's book, a decision which Warburg claimed cut off about £40,000 in sales.

A first print of 25,575 copies was followed by a further 5,000 copies in March and August 1950.
Publication
It had the most immediate impact in the United States, following its release there on 13 June 1949 by Harcourt Brace, & Co.
Publication
An initial print of 20,000 copies was quickly followed by another 10,000 on 1 July, and again on 7 September.
Publication
By 1970, over 8 million copies had been sold in the US, and in 1984, it topped the country's all-time best seller list.
Publication
In June 1952 Orwell's widow, Sonia Brownell, sold the sole remaining manuscript at a charity auction for £50.
Publication
The draft remains the only surviving literary manuscript from Orwell, and is held at the John Hay Library at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, US.

As "The Book" explains, society is in fact designed to remain on the brink of starvation, as "In the long run, a hierarchical society was only possible on a basis of poverty and ignorance."
Critical reception
When it was first published, Nineteen Eighty-Four received critical acclaim.
Critical reception

Critical reception

Even those who know Orwell only by hearsay are amazed that a writer who never lived in Russia should have so keen a perception into its life." The writer Christopher Hitchens has called this "one of the greatest compliments that one writer has ever bestowed upon another...
Critical reception

Adaptations

A second feature-length adaptation, Nineteen Eighty-Four, followed in 1984, a reasonably faithful adaptation, which starred John Hurt as Winston Smith and also featured Richard Burton in his final role.
Adaptations
The BBC's 2013 Orwell season saw Christopher Eccleston star as Winston in a BBC Radio 4 adaptation.
Adaptations

Adaptations
The 2023 novel Julia, written by Sandra Newman, retold the novel from Julia's perspective.

The novel was banned in the Soviet Union until 1988, when the first publicly available Russian version in the country, translated by Vyacheslav Nedoshivin, was published in Kodry, a literary journal of Soviet Moldavia.
Translations
In 1989, another Russian version, translated by Viktor Golyshev, was also published.
Translations
Outside the Soviet Union, the first Russian version was serialised in the emigre magazine Grani in the mid-1950s, then published as a book in 1957 in Frankfurt.
Translations
Another Russian version, translated by Sergei Tolstoy from a French version, was published in Rome in 1966.
Translations

In the People's Republic of China the first Simplified Chinese version, translated by Dong Leshan, was serialised in the periodical Selected Translations from Foreign Literature in 1979, for senior officials and intellectuals deemed politically reliable enough.
Translations
In 1985, the Chinese version was published by Huacheng Publishing House, as a restricted publication.
Translations
It was first available to the general public in 1988, by the same publisher.
Translations
By 1989, Nineteen Eighty-Four had been translated into 65 languages, more than any other novel in English at that time.
Translations
The amateur translator Tsiu Ing-sing's Taiwanese Hokkien translation, which uses romanisation alongside Chinese characters, was published in 2025.
Cultural impact
Orwell is perpetually associated with 1984; in July 1984 an asteroid was discovered by Antonín Mrkos and named after Orwell.
Cultural impact

So if you win, you suddenly produce what sounds like 1984..."

The Sun Also Rises is the first novel by the American writer Ernest Hemingway, following his experimental novel-in-fragments In Our Time (1925).
lead
It portrays American and British expatriates who travel from Paris to the Festival of San Fermín in Pamplona and watch the running of the bulls and the bullfights.
lead
An early modernist novel, it received mixed reviews upon publication.
lead
Hemingway biographer Jeffrey Meyers writes that it is now "recognized as Hemingway's greatest work", and Hemingway scholar Linda Wagner-Martin calls it his most important novel.
lead
The novel was published in the United States in October 1926, by Charles Scribner's Sons.
lead
A year later, Jonathan Cape published the novel in London under the title Fiesta.
lead

The novel is a roman à clef: the characters are based on people in Hemingway's circle and the action is based on events, particularly Hemingway's life in Paris in the 1920s and a trip to Spain in 1925 for the Pamplona festival and fishing in the Pyrenees.
lead

Hemingway converted to Catholicism as he wrote the novel, and Jeffrey Herlihy-Mera notes that protagonist Jake Barnes, a Catholic, was "a vehicle for Hemingway to rehearse his own conversion, testing the emotions that would accompany one of the most important acts of his life."
Plot summary
Jake is an expatriate American journalist living in Paris, while Brett is a twice-divorced Englishwoman with bobbed hair and numerous love affairs, and embodies the new sexual freedom of the 1920s.
Plot summary

Brett's affair with Jake's Princeton friend Robert Cohn (whom the characters often refer to by his last name) causes Jake to be upset and break off his friendship with Cohn; her seduction of the 19-year-old matador Romero causes Jake to lose his good reputation among the Spaniards in Pamplona.
Plot summary
Jake introduces Brett to the 19-year-old matador Romero at the Hotel Montoya; she is smitten with him and seduces him.
Paris and the Lost Generation
The first book of The Sun Also Rises is set in mid-1920s Paris.
Paris and the Lost Generation
Americans were drawn to Paris in the Roaring Twenties by the favorable exchange rate, with as many as 200,000 English-speaking expatriates living there.
Paris and the Lost Generation
The Paris Tribune reported in 1925 that Paris had an American Hospital, an American Library, and an American Chamber of Commerce.
Paris and the Lost Generation
For example, Hemingway was in Paris during the period when Ulysses, written by his friend James Joyce, was banned and burned in New York.
Paris and the Lost Generation

The first is an allusion to the "Lost Generation", a term coined by Gertrude Stein referring to the post-war generation; the other epigraph is a long quotation from Ecclesiastes: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever.
Women and love
In the 1920s, divorces were common and easy to be had in Paris.
Women and love
James Nagel writes that, in Brett, Hemingway created one of the more fascinating women in 20th-century American literature.
Women and love
Meyers sees Brett as a woman who wants sex without love while Jake can only give her love without sex.
The ''corrida'', the fiesta, and nature
To be accepted as an aficionado was rare for a non-Spaniard; Jake goes through a difficult process to gain acceptance by the "fellowship of afición."

The ''corrida'', the fiesta, and nature

Hemingway named Romero after Pedro Romero, an 18th-century bullfighter who killed thousands of bulls in the most difficult manner: having the bull impale itself on his sword as he stood perfectly still.
Masculinity and gender
Elliot wonders if Jake's wound perhaps signifies latent homosexuality, rather than only a loss of masculinity; the emphasis in the novel, however, is on Jake's interest in women.
Antisemitism
Hemingway has been called antisemitic, most notably because of the characterization of Robert Cohn in the book.
Antisemitism
Cohn is never really part of the group—separated by his difference or his Jewish faith.
Antisemitism

Disillusionment
Hemingway suggests that the only viable response to this existential crisis is a stoic acceptance of life’s inherent tragedy.
Background
In the 1920s, Hemingway lived in Paris as a foreign correspondent for the Toronto Star, and traveled to İzmir to report on the Greco–Turkish War.
Background
With his wife Hadley Richardson, Hemingway first visited the Festival of San Fermín in Pamplona in 1923, where he was following his recent passion for bullfighting.
Background

Background

Background

A few days after the fiesta ended, on his birthday (21 July), he began writing what would eventually become The Sun Also Rises.

In August, alone and depressed in Paris, Hemingway considered suicide and drafted a last will, but he completed the proofs, dedicating the novel to his wife and son.

He believes the expatriate writers of the 1920s appeal for this reason, but that Hemingway was the most successful in capturing the time and the place in The Sun Also Rises.

The Grapes of Wrath is an American realist novel written by John Steinbeck and published in 1939.

Set during the Great Depression, the novel focuses on the Joads, a poor family of tenant farmers driven from their Oklahoma home by drought, economic hardship, agricultural industry changes, and bank foreclosures forcing tenant farmers out of work.
lead

Due to their nearly hopeless situation, and in part because they are trapped in the Dust Bowl, the Joads set out for California on the "mother road", along with thousands of other "Okies" seeking jobs, land, dignity, and a future.
lead
The Grapes of Wrath is often listed as among the greatest novels in the English language and as a contender for the Great American Novel.
lead

Ma realizes there is only one way to save the man.

modf_invisibel_man.title: Invisible Man

name: Invisible Man
caption: Front dust jacket art of the first edition
author: Ralph Ellison

sents: lead
Invisible Man is Ralph Ellison's first novel, and the only one published during his lifetime.
lead

It was published by Random House in 1952, and addresses many of the social and intellectual issues faced by African Americans in the early 20th century, including Black nationalism, the relationship between Black identity and Marxism, and the reformist racial policies of Booker T.
lead
Washington, as well as issues of individuality and personal identity.
lead
National Book Award for Fiction in 1953, making Ellison the first African-American writer to win the award.
lead
In 1998, the Modern Library ranked Invisible Man 19th on its list of the 100 best English-language novels of the 20th century.
Background

Ellison says in his introduction to the 30th Anniversary Edition that he started to write what would eventually become Invisible Man in a barn in Waitsfield, Vermont (actually in the neighboring town of Fayston), in the summer of 1945 while on sick leave from the Merchant Marine.
Background
The book took five years to complete with one year off for what Ellison termed an "ill-conceived short novel." Invisible Man was published as a whole in 1952.
Background

Ellison had published a section of the book in 1947, the famous "Battle Royal" scene, which had been shown to Cyril Connolly, the editor of Horizon magazine by Frank Taylor, one of Ellison's early supporters.
Background

In his speech accepting the 1953 National Book Award, Ellison said that he considered the novel's chief significance to be its "experimental attitude." Before Invisible Man, many (if not most) novels dealing with African Americans were written solely for social protest, notably, Native Son and Uncle Tom's Cabin.
Background
Finally, why is it that so many of those who would tell us the meaning of Negro life never bother to learn how varied it really is?"
Background
In an interview with Richard Kostelanetz, Ellison states that what he had learned from his The Waste Land was imagery and also improvisation techniques he had only before seen in jazz.
Background
Ellison once called Faulkner the South's greatest artist, and in the Spring 1955 Paris Review, Ellison said of Hemingway: "I read him to learn his sentence structure and how to organize a story.
Background
The first line of Invisible Man ("I am an invisible man") for example, is a conscious echo of Notes from Underground ("I am a sick man").
Background

Ellison acknowledged this borrowing in his 1981 introduction to his novel saying the novel's main character can be "associated, ever so distantly, with the narrator of Dostoevsky's Notes From Underground".
Political influences and the Communist Party

In a letter to Wright on August 18, 1945, Ellison poured out his anger toward party leaders for betraying African-American and Marxist class politics during the war years: "If they want to play ball with the bourgeoisie they needn't think they can get away with it...
Plot summary
The narrator, an unnamed black man, begins by describing his living conditions: an underground room wired with hundreds of electric lights, operated by power stolen from the city's electric grid.
Plot summary

The narrator travels to New York and distributes his letters, with no success; the son of one recipient shows him the letter, which reveals Bledsoe's intent never to admit the narrator as a student again.
Plot summary
The rallies go smoothly at first, with the narrator receiving extensive indoctrination on the Brotherhood's ideology and methods.
Reception

Critic Orville Prescott of The New York Times called the novel "the most impressive work of fiction by an American Negro which I have ever read", and felt it marked "the appearance of a richly talented writer".
Reception
Novelist Saul Bellow in his review found it "a book of the very first order, a superb book...it is tragi-comic, poetic, the tone of the very strongest sort of creative intelligence".
Reception

In 2003, a sculpture titled "Invisible Man: A Memorial to Ralph Ellison" by Elizabeth Catlett, was unveiled at Riverside Park at 150th Street in Manhattan, opposite from where Ellison lived and three blocks from the Uptown Manhattan Trinity Church Cemetery and Mausoleum, where he is interred in a crypt.
Reception
The 15-foot-high, 10-foot-wide bronze monolith features a hollow silhouette of a man and two granite panels that are inscribed with Ellison quotations.

Brave New World is a dystopian novel by English author Aldous Huxley, written in 1931, and published in 1932.
lead
Huxley followed this book with a reassessment in essay form, Brave New World Revisited (1958), and with his final novel, Island (1962), the utopian counterpart.
lead
This novel is often used as a companion piece or inversion counterpart to George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).
lead
In 1998 and 1999, the Modern Library ranked Brave New World at number 5 on its list of the 100 Best Novels in English of the 20th century.
lead

In 2003, Robert McCrum, writing for The Observer, included Brave New World chronologically at number 53 in "the top 100 greatest novels of all time", and the novel was listed at number 87 on The Big Read survey by the BBC.
lead
Brave New World has frequently been banned and challenged since its original publication.
lead
It has landed on the American Library Association list of top 100 banned and challenged books of the decade since the association began the list in 1990.
Title

The first Standard Chinese translation, done by novelist Lily Hsueh and Aaron Jen-wang Hsueh in 1974, is entitled "美麗新世界" (Pinyin: Měilì Xīn Shìjiè, literally "Beautiful New World"), quoting the Chinese translation of The Tempest.
History
Huxley wrote Brave New World while living in Sanary-sur-Mer, France, in the four months from May to August 1931.
History
Brave New World was Huxley's fifth novel and first dystopian work.
History
A short passage in Crome Yellow foreshadows Brave New World, showing that Huxley had such a future in mind already in 1921.
History
Huxley said that Brave New World was inspired by the utopian novels of H.
History
Wells, including A Modern Utopia (1905), and as a parody of Men Like Gods (1923).
History
Unlike the most popular optimistic utopian novels of the time, Huxley sought to provide a frightening vision of the future.
History
The Brave New World character Mustapha Mond, Resident World Controller of Western Europe, is named after Sir Alfred Mond.
Plot

The novel opens in the World State city of London in AF (After Ford) 632 (AD 2540 in the Gregorian calendar), where citizens are engineered through artificial wombs and childhood indoctrination programmes into predetermined castes based on intelligence and labour.
Plot
The classes are Alpha (planned leaders), Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Epsilon (menial labourers of limited intelligence).
Plot
In chapter 2, a recording tells Beta children that Alphas work harder because they are "frightfully clever".
Plot

Bernard takes a holiday with Lenina outside the World State to a "Savage Reservation" in New Mexico, in which the two observe natural-born people, disease, the ageing process, other languages, and religious lifestyles for the first time.
Plot
Bernard and Lenina witness a violent public ritual and then encounter Linda, a woman originally from the World State who is living on the reservation with her son John, now a young man.
Plot
Despite spending his whole life in the reservation, John has never been accepted by the villagers, and his and Linda's lives have been hard and unpleasant.
Plot
Linda has taught John to read, although from the only book in her possession—a scientific manual—and another book left behind by a local resident named Popé: the complete works of Shakespeare.
Plot
Ostracised by the villagers, John is able to articulate his feelings only in terms of Shakespearean drama, quoting often from The Tempest, King Lear, Othello, Romeo and Juliet and Hamlet.
Plot
Bernard, as "custodian" of the "savage" John who is now treated as a celebrity, is fawned on by the highest members of society and revels in attention he once scorned.
Plot
Bernard's popularity is fleeting, though, and he becomes envious that John only really bonds with the literary-minded Helmholtz.
Plot
The islands are full of the most interesting people in the world, individuals who did not fit into the social model of the World State.
Plot
That evening, a swarm of helicopters appear on the horizon, with the story of last night's orgy having been in all the newspapers.
Plot
The first onlookers and reporters to arrive find that John is dead, having hanged himself.
Characters

He defends the caste system, behavioural conditioning, and the lack of personal freedom in the World State: these, he says, are a price worth paying for achieving social stability, the highest social virtue because it leads to lasting happiness.
Characters
Fanny Crowne, Lenina Crowne's friend (they have the same last name because only ten thousand last names are in use in a World State comprising two billion people).
Characters

, John's mother, decanted as a Beta-Minus in the World State, originally worked in the DHC's Fertilizing Room, and subsequently lost during a storm while visiting the New Mexico Savage Reservation with the Director many years before the events of the novel.
Characters
John asks if the students read Shakespeare but the Provost says the library contains only reference books because solitary activities, such as reading, are discouraged.
Others
In the book, government policy requires freemartins to form 70% of the female population.
Background figures
William Shakespeare, whose banned works are quoted throughout the novel by John, "the Savage".
Background figures
Thomas Robert Malthus, 19th century British economist, believed the people of the Earth would eventually be threatened by their inability to raise enough food to feed the population.
Background figures
John Henry Newman, 19th century Catholic theologian and educator, believed university education the critical element in advancing post-industrial Western civilization.
Background figures
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first President of Republic of Turkey.
Reception
In an article in the 4 May 1935 issue of the Illustrated London News, G.
Reception
Much of the discourse on man's future before 1914 was based on the thesis that humanity would solve all economic and social issues.
Common misunderstandings

Various authors assume that the book was first and foremost a cautionary tale regarding human genetic enhancement, indeed about—as a report of Bush associate Leon Kass states—"producing improved [...] perfect or post-human" people.
Common misunderstandings
there does not seem to be any genetic testing in Brave New World, and most of the methods described involve hormones and chemicals rather than heritable interventions.
Common misunderstandings
Although Huxley wrote that "[[eugenics]] and dysgenics were practiced systematically", this seems to refer only to selective breeding and not to any kind of direct manipulation on the genetic level.
Common misunderstandings

Despite claims to the contrary then, Huxley remained a committed eugenicist all throughout his life, much like his comparably famous brother Julian, and one just as keen on stressing its humanistic underpinnings.
The World State and Fordism
The World State calendar numbers years in the "AF" era—"After Ford"—with the calendar beginning in AD 1908, the year in which Ford's first Model T rolled off his assembly line.
The World State and Fordism
The novel's Gregorian calendar year is AD 2540, but it is referred to in the book as AF 632.
Comparisons with George Orwell's ''Nineteen Eighty-Four''
Social critic Neil Postman contrasted the worlds of Nineteen Eighty-Four and Brave New World in the foreword of his 1985 book Amusing Ourselves to Death.
''Brave New World Revisited''

Brave New World Revisited (Harper & Brothers, US, 1958; Chatto & Windus, UK, 1959), written by Huxley almost thirty years after Brave New World, is a non-fiction work in which Huxley considered whether the world had moved toward or away from his vision of the future from the 1930s.
''Brave New World Revisited''
In Brave New World Revisited, he concluded that the world was becoming like Brave New World much faster than he originally thought.
''Brave New World Revisited''
The last chapter of the book aims to propose action which could be taken to prevent a democracy from turning into the totalitarian world described in Brave New World.
''Brave New World Revisited''
In Huxley's last novel, Island, he again expounds similar ideas to describe a utopian nation, which is generally viewed as a counterpart to Brave New World.
Censorship
It landed on the list of the top ten most challenged books in 2010 (3) and 2011 (7).
Censorship
The book also secured a spot on the association's list of the top one hundred challenged books for 1990–1999 (54), 2000–2009 (36), and 2010–2019 (26).

In 1932, the book was banned in Ireland for its language, and for supposedly being anti-family and anti-religion.
Censorship
In 1965, a Maryland English teacher alleged that he was fired for assigning Brave New World to students.
Censorship
The teacher sued for violation of First Amendment rights but lost both his case and the appeal, with the appeals court ruling that the assignment of the book was not the reason for his firing.
Censorship
The book was banned in India in 1967, with Huxley accused of being a "pornographer".

In 1980, it was removed from classrooms in Miller, Missouri, among other challenges.

The English writer Rose Macaulay published What Not: A Prophetic Comedy in 1918.

Wells' novel The First Men in the Moon (1901) used concepts that Huxley added to his story.

Influences and allegations of plagiarism
Kurt Vonnegut said that in writing Player Piano (1952), he "cheerfully ripped off the plot of Brave New World, whose plot had been cheerfully ripped off from Yevgeny Zamyatin's We".
Influences and allegations of plagiarism
In 1982, Polish author Antoni Smuszkiewicz, in his analysis of Polish science-fiction Zaczarowana gra ("The Magic Game"), presented accusations of plagiarism against Huxley.

Smuszkiewicz showed similarities between Brave New World and two science fiction novels written earlier by Polish author Mieczysław Smolarski, namely Miasto światłości ("The City of Light", 1924) and Podróż poślubna pana Hamiltona ("Mr Hamilton's Honeymoon Trip", 1928).
Influences and allegations of plagiarism
Lewis's That Hideous Strength (1945) and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).
Legacy
In 1998–1999, the Modern Library ranked Brave New World fifth on its list of the 100 Best Novels in English of the 20th century.
Legacy

In 2003, Robert McCrum writing for The Observer included Brave New World chronologically at number 53 in "the top 100 greatest novels of all time", and the novel was listed at number 87 on the BBC's survey The Big Read.
Legacy
On 5 November 2019, BBC News listed Brave New World on its list of the 100 Most Inspiring Novels.
Legacy
In 2021, Brave New World was one of six classic science fiction novels by British authors selected by Royal Mail to feature on a series of UK postage stamps.
Theatre
Brave New World (opened 4 September 2015) in co-production by Royal & Derngate, Northampton and Touring Consortium Theatre Company which toured the UK.

Brave New World (radio broadcast) CBS Radio Workshop (27 January and 3 February 1956): music composed and conducted by Bernard Herrmann.

The 1993 film Demolition Man, starring Sylvester Stallone and Sandra Bullock, is said to draw heavily from the novel.

In May 2015, The Hollywood Reporter reported that Steven Spielberg's Amblin Television would bring Brave New World to Syfy network as a scripted series, adapted by Les Bohem.
Television
The adaptation was eventually written by David Wiener with Grant Morrison and Brian Taylor, with the series ordered to air on USA Network in February 2019.
Television
The series eventually moved to the Peacock streaming service and premiered on 15 July 2020.

modf_lolitta.title: Lolita
sents: lead
Lolita is a 1955 novel written by the Russian and American novelist Vladimir Nabokov.
lead
The protagonist and unreliable narrator is a French literature professor who moves to New England and writes under the pseudonym Humbert Humbert.
lead
He details his obsession with and victimization of a 12-year-old girl, Dolores Haze, whom he describes as a "nymphet".
lead
Humbert becomes sexually obsessed with Dolores after becoming her stepfather, and romanticizes his obsession.
lead
Privately, he calls her "Lolita", the Spanish diminutive for Dolores.
lead
The novel was written in English, but fear of censorship in the U.S.
lead
(where Nabokov lived) and Britain led to its being first published in Paris, France, in 1955 by Olympia Press.
lead
The book has received critical acclaim in spite of the controversy it caused with the public.
Plot
The memoir, which addresses the audience as his jury, begins with Humbert's birth in Paris in 1910 to an English mother and Swiss father.
Plot
In 1947, he moves to Ramsdale, a small town in New England, where he can calmly continue working on his book.
Plot
The house that he intends to live in is destroyed in a fire.
Plot
Humbert sees in Dolores, whom he calls Lolita, the perfect nymphet and the embodiment of his first love Annabel, and quickly decides to move in.
Plot

But while Dolores is at summer camp, Charlotte discovers Humbert's diary, previously locked in his nightstand and deliberately written esoterically so only he could understand its meaning, albeit unsuccessfully.
Plot
Deeply depressed, Humbert unexpectedly receives a letter from a 17-year-old Dolores, telling him that she is married, pregnant, and in desperate need of money.
Plot
Dolores reveals to Humbert that her abductor was the famous playwright Clare Quilty, who had crossed paths with Humbert and Dolores several times.
Plot
The deaths of Humbert (shortly after his imprisonment) and Dolores (in childbirth on Christmas Day 1952) have already been related in the foreword.
Erotic motifs and controversy
Lolita is frequently described as an "erotic novel", not only by some critics but also in a standard reference work on literature, Facts on File: Companion to the American Short Story.
Erotic motifs and controversy
Books focused on the history of erotic literature such as Michael Perkins' The Secret Record: Modern Erotic Literature also so classify Lolita.
Erotic motifs and controversy

Malcolm Bradbury writes that "at first famous as an erotic novel, Lolita soon won its way as a literary one—a late modernist distillation of the whole crucial mythology." Samuel Schuman says that Nabokov "is a surrealist, linked to Gogol, Dostoevsky, and Kafka.
Style and interpretation
Christine Clegg notes that this is a recurring theme in criticism of the novel in the 1990s.
Style and interpretation
Actor Brian Cox, who played Humbert in a 2009 one-man stage monologue based on the novel, stated that the novel is "not about Lolita as a flesh and blood entity.
Style and interpretation
Clegg sees the novel's non-disclosure of Lolita's feelings as directly linked to the fact that her real name is Dolores and only Humbert refers to her as Lolita.
Style and interpretation
In 2003, Iranian expatriate Azar Nafisi published the memoir Reading Lolita in Tehran about a covert women's reading group.
Style and interpretation

In 1958, Dorothy Parker described the novel as "the engrossing, anguished story of a man, a man of taste and culture, who can love only little girls" and Lolita as "a dreadful little creature, selfish, hard, vulgar, and foul-tempered".
Style and interpretation
In 1959, novelist Robertson Davies wrote that the theme of Lolita is "not the corruption of an innocent child by a cunning adult, but the exploitation of a weak adult by a corrupt child.
Style and interpretation
In Japan, the novel gave rise in the early 1980s to lolicon, a genre of fictional media in which young (or young-looking) girl characters appear in romantic or sexual contexts.
Publication and reception
Nabokov finished Lolita on 6 December 1953, five years after starting it.
Publication and reception
Lolita was published in September 1955, as a pair of green paperbacks "swarming with typographical errors".
Publication and reception
Although the first printing of 5,000 copies sold out, there were no substantial reviews.
Publication and reception
Eventually, at the very end of 1955, Graham Greene, in the London Sunday Times, called it one of the three best books of 1955.
Publication and reception
In December 1956, France followed suit, and the Minister of the Interior banned Lolita; the ban lasted for two years.
Publication and reception
Despite initial trepidation, there was no official response in the U.S., and the first American edition was issued by G.
Publication and reception
The book was into a third printing within days and became the first since Gone with the Wind to sell 100,000 copies in its first three weeks.
Publication and reception
This review failed to influence the book's sales and it is estimated that Lolita had sold 50 million copies by 2005.
Publication and reception
Lolita was later translated into Russian by Nabokov himself and published in New York City in 1967 by Phaedra Publishers.
Publication and reception
The Russian Lolita contains Nabokov’s only known published instance of poetry self-translated from English into Russian.
Present-day views

In 2020, a podcast hosted by Jamie Loftus set out to examine the cultural legacy of the novel, and argued that depictions and adaptations have "twisted" Nabokov's original intention of condemning Humbert in Lolita.
Present-day views
Besides the United Kingdom and France, Lolita had been banned in Argentina, Austria, Australia, Belgium, Myanmar, and parts of the United States.
Present-day views
In October 2023 the Canby School District in Oregon banned Lolita from its schools.
Present-day views

Between 1947 and 1950, while writing what would become The Town and the City (1950), Kerouac engaged in the road adventures that would form On the Road.

name: Catch-22
caption: First edition cover
author: Joseph Heller
genre: Dark comedy, absurdist fiction, satire, war fiction, historical fiction

sents: lead
Catch-22 is a satirical war novel by American author Joseph Heller.
lead
He began writing it in 1953, and the book was first published in 1961.
lead

Often cited as one of the most significant novels of the 20th century, it uses a distinctive non-chronological third-person omniscient narration, describing events from the points of view of different characters.
lead
The separate storylines are out of sequence so the timeline develops along with the plot.
lead
The novel satirizes military bureaucracy and greed.
lead
The novel is set during World War II, from 1942 to 1944.
lead
It mainly follows the life of antihero Captain John Yossarian, a U.S.
lead
Army Air Forces B-25 bombardier of Assyrian heritage.
Synopsis
As the novel progresses, Yossarian's moral character and courage emerge more clearly, in contrast to his seeming selfishness and cowardice when first introduced.
Synopsis
The first (chapters 1–11) broadly follows the story fragmented between characters, but in a single chronological time in 1944.
Synopsis
The second (chapters 12–20) flashes back to focus primarily on the "Great Big Siege of Bologna" before once again jumping to the third part.
Synopsis
The third (chapter 21–25) is the chronological present of 1944.
Synopsis
The fourth (chapters 26–28) flashes back to the origins and growth of Milo's syndicate.
Synopsis
The fifth part (chapters 28–32) returns again to the narrative present and maintains the tone of the previous four.
Synopsis
The sixth and final part (chapter 32 and on) remains in the story's present, but takes a much darker turn and emphasizes the darkness and brutality of war and life in general.
Synopsis
For most of the book, the reader is cushioned from directly experiencing the full horror of war, but it is implied by the extreme trauma and fear that afflicts the airmen.
Synopsis
In Chapter 41 the full details of the death of Snowden are finally revealed.
Style

Many events in the book are repeatedly described from differing points of view, so the reader learns more about each event from each iteration, with the new information often completing a joke, the setup of which was told several chapters previously.
Style
Much of Heller's prose in Catch-22 is circular and repetitive, exemplifying in its form the structure of a Catch-22.
Style
The only thing missing was something to charge him with." This atmosphere of apparently logical irrationality pervades the book.
Style

While a few characters are most prominent, especially Yossarian and the Chaplain, the majority of named characters are described in detail with fleshed out or multidimensional personas to the extent that there are few if any "minor characters".
Style
There are no traditional heroes in the novel, reflecting the underlying commentary that war has no heroes, only victims.
Style
Although its nonchronological structure may at first seem random, Catch-22 is highly structured.
Style
As Heller utilizes an episodic structure for most of the novel, many chapters may appear to be a disjointed series of events with little or no connection with each other.
Style

However, individual chapters often deal with thematically unique ideas, such as Chapter 11 (“Captain Black”) which parodies Red Scare-era McCarthyism, and Chapter 18 (“The Soldier Who Saw Everything Twice”) which explores theological concepts of mortality.
Theodicy
Any jukebox manufacturer worth his salt could have done that.
Characters
The novel has over 50 named characters, many of whom have titular chapters dedicated to expanding on their personalities or motivations.
Influences
His experiences as a bombardier during World War II inspired Catch-22; Heller later said that he "never had a bad officer".
Influences
In a 1977 essay on Catch-22, Heller stated that the "antiwar and antigovernment feelings in the book" were a product of the Korean War and the 1950s rather than World War II itself.
Influences
The influence of the 1950s on Catch-22 is evident through Heller's extensive use of anachronism.
Influences
Though the novel is ostensibly set in World War II, Heller intentionally included anachronisms like loyalty oaths and computers (IBM machines) to situate the novel in the context of the 1950s.
Influences
The question of "Who promoted Major Major?" alludes to Joseph McCarthy's questioning of the promotion of Major Peress, an army dentist who refused to sign loyalty oaths.
Influences
Czech writer Arnošt Lustig recounts in his book 3x18 that Joseph Heller told him that he would never have written Catch-22 had he not first read The Good Soldier Švejk by Jaroslav Hašek.
Influences
In 1998, some critics raised the possibility that Heller's book had questionable similarities to Louis Falstein's 1950 novel, Face of a Hero.
Influences
Falstein never raised the issue between Catch-22 publication and his death in 1995 and Heller claimed never to have been aware of Falstein's novel.
Concept
A "Catch-22" is "a problem for which the only solution is denied by a circumstance inherent in the problem or by a rule".
Concept
But if the thing lost is one's glasses, one cannot see to look for them – a Catch-22.
Concept
The term "Catch-22" is also used more broadly to mean a tricky problem or a no-win or absurd situation.
Concept
In the book, Catch-22 is a military rule typifying bureaucratic operation and reasoning.
Concept
Either for not applying to be excused, or for applying and being (inevitably) refused, one will always be obliged to the war.
Concept
There was only one catch and that was Catch-22, which specified that a concern for one's safety in the face of dangers that were real and immediate was the process of a rational mind.
Concept
Yossarian was moved very deeply by the absolute simplicity of this clause of Catch-22 and let out a respectful whistle.
Concept
Other forms of Catch-22 are invoked throughout the novel to justify various bureaucratic actions.
Concept
Yossarian comes to realize that Catch-22 does not actually exist, but because the powers that be claim it does, and the world believes it does, it nevertheless has potent effects.
Concept
The motif of bureaucratic absurdity is further explored in 1994's Closing Time, Heller's sequel to Catch-22.
Historical context
The idea for Catch-22 was based on Joseph Heller's personal experience in World War II.
Historical context
Heller flew 60 bombing missions from May to October in 1944.
Historical context
Heller was able to make it out of the war, but it took until 1953 before he could start writing about it.
Historical context
After publication in 1961, Catch-22 became very popular among teenagers at the time.
Historical context
Catch-22 seemed to embody the feelings that young people had toward the Vietnam War.
Historical context
A common joke was that every student who went off to college at the time took along a copy of Catch-22.
Historical context
The popularity of the book created a cult following, which led to more than eight million copies being sold in the United States.
Historical context
On October 26, 1986, professor and author John W.

The opening chapter of the novel was first published, in 1955, by New World Writing as Catch-18, but Heller's agent, Candida Donadio, asked him to change the title, to avert its confusion with Leon Uris's recently published Mila 18.
Title
The implications in Judaism of the number 18 – which refers to chai, meaning "alive", in Gematria – were relevant to Heller's somewhat greater emphasis on Jewish themes in early drafts of his novel.
Title
Parallels among a number of character exchanges in the novel suggested the doubled-one title of Catch-11, but the 1960 release of Ocean's Eleven eliminated that.
Title
Catch-17 was rejected so as not to be confused with the World War II film Stalag 17, as was Catch-14, apparently because the publisher did not believe that 14 was a "funny number".
Title
Eventually, the title came to be Catch-22, which, like 11, has a duplicated digit, with the 2 also referring to a number of déjà vu-like events common in the novel.

Publication and movie rights

Reception
One commentator of Catch-22 recognized that "many early audiences liked the book for just the same reasons that caused others to hate it".
Reception
The book eventually gained a cult following, especially among teenagers and college students.
Reception

Heller later remarked that in 1962, after appearing on the Today show he went out drinking with the host at the time, John Chancellor, who handed him stickers that Chancellor had got privately printed reading "YOSSARIAN LIVES".
Reception
Although the novel won no awards upon release, it has remained in print and is seen as one of the most significant American novels of the 20th century.
Reception
Scholar and fellow World War II veteran Hugh Nibley said it was the most accurate book he ever read about the military. over ten million copies have been sold.
Reception
Although he continued writing, including a sequel novel Closing Time, Heller's later works were inevitably overshadowed by the success of Catch-22.
Reception

Their Eyes Were Watching God is a 1937 novel by American writer Zora Neale Hurston.
lead
It is considered a classic of the Harlem Renaissance and is also considered Hurston's best-known work.
lead
The novel explores protagonist Janie Crawford's "ripening from a vibrant, but voiceless, teenage girl into a woman with her finger on the trigger of her own destiny."

Hurston wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God in Haiti in the span of seven weeks.
lead
Hurston was self-described as "under internal pressure" when writing and wished she could "write it again".
lead
However, retrospectively, she later stated that the work captured "all the tenderness of [her] passion".
lead
Set in central and southern Florida in the early 20th century, the novel was initially poorly received by the African-American community.
lead

The Sound and the Fury is a novel by the American author William Faulkner, published in 1929.
lead
Faulkner's fourth novel, it is the second to be set in Yoknapatawpha County and the first featuring the Compson family, both of which would reappear in his later fiction.

The novel's highly experimental style, including its use of stream of consciousness and multiple different unreliable narrators, are hallmarks of modernist literature.

Its bleak and candid portrait of Southern life in the early 20th century is paradigmatic of the Southern Gothic genre.
lead
The Sound and the Fury centers around Quentin, Benjy, Jason, and Caddy Compson as their wealthy Mississippi family descends into chaos and disorder.
lead
Each of the siblings has unique problems that impact the others, such as Benjy's mental disability, Caddy's promiscuity, Quentin's neuroticism, and Jason's impulsiveness.
lead

Mrs Dalloway is a novel by Virginia Woolf published on 14 May 1925.
lead
It details a day in the life of Clarissa Dalloway, a wealthy woman in post-First World War London.
lead
The working title of Mrs Dalloway was The Hours.
lead
The novel originated from two short stories, "Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street" and the unfinished "The Prime Minister".
lead
In autumn 1922, Woolf began to think of the "Mrs Dalloway" short story as the first chapter of her new novel, and she completed the manuscript in late autumn 1924.
lead
The book describes Clarissa's preparations for a party she will host in the evening and the ensuing party.
lead
With an interior perspective, the story travels forwards and backwards in time to construct an image of Clarissa's life and the inter-war social structure.
lead
The novel addresses the nature of time in personal experience through multiple interwoven stories, using a stream of consciousness narration style.
Plot summary

Woolf herself, writing in 1928, denied any deliberate "method" to the book, saying instead that the structure came about "without any conscious direction".
Time and secular living
Woolf's writing style crosses the boundaries of the past, present and future, emphasizing her idea of time as a constant flow, connected only by some force (or divinity) within each person.
Time and secular living
Yet, although these crossings seem random, they only demonstrate the infinite possibilities that the world can offer once it is interconnected by the individual character of each person.
Mental illness
Using the characters of Clarissa and Rezia, she makes the argument that people can only interpret Septimus' shell shock according to their cultural norms.
Mental illness
By never having these characters meet, Woolf is suggesting that mental illness can be contained to the individuals who suffer from it without others, who remain unaffected, ever having to witness it.
Mental illness
Her use of Septimus as the stereotypically traumatised veteran is her way of showing that there were still reminders of the First World War in London in 1923.
Mental illness
Shell shock, or post traumatic stress disorder, is an important addition to the early 20th century canon of post-war British literature.

Most of the plot in Mrs Dalloway consists of realizations that the characters subjectively make.
Feminism

As a commentary on inter-war society, Clarissa's character highlights the role of women as the proverbial "Angel in the House" and embodies sexual and economic repression and the narcissism of bourgeois women who have never known the hunger and insecurity of working women.

Battle of Utoy Creek, August 5–7, 1864, Sherman's failed attempt to break the railroad line at East Point, into Atlanta from the west, heavy Union losses.
Atlanta campaign
Battle of Jonesborough, August 31 – September 1, 1864, Sherman successfully cut the railroad lines from the south into Atlanta.
President Lincoln's murder
Although Abraham Lincoln is mentioned in the novel 14 times, no reference is made to his assassination on April 14, 1865.
Manhood
A "young girl's dream of the Perfect Knight", Ashley is like a young girl himself.
Scallawag
Literary scholars have identified elements of Mitchell's first husband, Berrien "Red" Upshaw, in the character of Rhett.
Survival
I only know that survivors used to call that quality "gumption." So I wrote about people who had gumption and people who didn't.
Reviews

The sales of Margaret Mitchell's novel in the summer of 1936, as the nation was recovering from the Great Depression and at the virtually unprecedented price of three dollars, reached about 1 million by the end of December.
Reviews
The book was popular in Nazi Germany; within two days of its publication there in 1937, it had sold 12 thousand copies; by 1941 it had sold 276 thousand copies.
Reviews
Shirer noted in 1939 that it was one of the most popular novels in Germany; the novel for the most part received positive reviews.
Reviews
The novel continued to have high sales until 1942, when books by American authors were banned.
Scholarship: racial, ethnicity and social issues

As a result of this criticism, the novel has faced challenges a number of times leading to a successful ban in Anaheim, California (1978) and an unsuccessful attempt to remove it from schools in Waukegan, Illinois (1984).
Awards and recognition
As of 2010, over 30 million copies have been printed in the United States and abroad.
Awards and recognition
Time magazine critics Lev Grossman and Richard Lacayo included the novel on their list of the 100 best English-language novels published between 1923 and 2005.
Awards and recognition
In 2003, the book was listed at number 21 on the BBC's The Big Read poll of the UK's "best-loved novel".
Censorship
In 1978, the book was banned from English classrooms in the Anaheim Union High School District in Anaheim, California.
Adaptations
The book was adapted into a musical, Scarlett, which opened in Tokyo in 1970 (in 1966 it was produced as a nine-hour play without music), and in London in 1972, where it was reduced to four hours.
Adaptations
The London production opened in 1973 in Los Angeles and again in Dallas in 1976.
Adaptations
The most recent performance was in January 2014 by the Moon Troupe, with Todoroki Yuu as Rhett Butler and Ryu Masaki as Scarlett O'Hara.
Adaptations
The comic-book adaptation Gone with the wind by Pierre Alary was published in French in 2023–2025.
Books, television and more
In the season 3 episode of I Love Lucy, "Lucy Writes a Novel", which aired on April 5, 1954, "Lucy" (Lucille Ball) reads about a housewife who makes a fortune writing a novel in her spare time.
Books, television and more
In a MADtv comedy sketch (2007), "Slave Girl #8" introduces three alternative endings to the film.
Collectibles
On June 30, 1986, the 50th anniversary of the day Gone with the Wind went on sale, the U.S.
Collectibles
Post Office issued a 32-cent stamp as part of its Celebrate the Century series, recalling various important events in the 20th century.
Collectibles
To commemorate the 75th anniversary (2011) of the publication of Gone with the Wind in 1936, Scribner published a paperback edition featuring the book's original jacket art.
Legacy
In North Korea, readers relate to the novel's theme of survival, finding it to be "the most compelling message of the novel".
Perceptions of the Old South
The plantation legend was burned into the public consciousness.
Differences with the film
Some readers of the novel have seen the film first and read the novel afterward.
Place in American literature

The Library of Congress began a multiyear "Celebration of the Book" in July 2012 with an exhibition on Books That Shaped America and an initial list of 88 books by American authors that have influenced American lives.
Margaret Mitchell Estate

On August 16, 2012, the Archdiocese of Atlanta announced that it had been bequeathed a 50% stake in the trademarks and literary rights to Gone With the Wind from the estate of Margaret Mitchell's deceased nephew, Joseph Mitchell.
Original manuscript
The last four chapters of the novel are held by the Pequot Library of Southport, Connecticut.
Publication and reprintings (1936 – US)
The first printing of 10,000 copies contains the original publication date: "Published May, 1936".
Publication and reprintings (1936 – US)
The second printing of 25,000 copies (and subsequent printings) contains the release date: "Published June, 1936".
Publication and reprintings (1936 – US)
Gone with the Wind was officially released to the American public on June 30, 1936.
Sequels and prequels
Although Mitchell refused to write a sequel to Gone with the Wind, Mitchell's estate authorized Alexandra Ripley to write a sequel, which was titled Scarlett.
Sequels and prequels
Houghton Mifflin) against publication on the basis that the book was a parody and therefore protected by the First Amendment.
Sequels and prequels
The first picks up where Ripley's Scarlett ended; the next is about Scarlett's daughter Cat.
Copyright status
Gone with the Wind has been in the public domain in Australia and Canada since 1999 (50 years after Margaret Mitchell's death).
Copyright status
On January 1, 2020, the book entered the public domain in the European Union (70 years after the author's death).
Copyright status
