modf_one_hundred_years_of_solitood.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
sents: lead

One Hundred Years of Solitude is a 1967 novel by Colombian author Gabriel García Márquez that tells the multi-generational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch, José Arcadio Buendía, founded the fictitious town of Macondo.
lead
The novel is often cited as one of the supreme achievements in world literature.
lead
It was recognized as one of the most important works of the Spanish language during the 4th International Conference of the Spanish Language held in Cartagena de Indias in March 2007.
lead

The magical realist style and thematic substance of the book established it as an important representative novel of the literary Latin American Boom of the 1960s and 1970s, which was stylistically influenced by Modernism (European and North American) and the Cuban Vanguardia (Avant-Garde) literary movement.
lead
Since it was first published in May 1967 in Buenos Aires by Editorial Sudamericana, the book has been translated into 46 languages and sold more than 50 million copies.
lead
The novel, considered García Márquez's magnum opus, remains widely acclaimed and is recognized as one of the most significant works both in the Hispanic literary canon and in world literature.
lead
The novel was adapted into an authorized TV series executive produced by García Márquez's sons, and ran for a total of 16 episodes on Netflix.
Background
Though inspired by Colombian history and his experiences as a journalist, García Márquez was greatly influenced by his maternal grandparents: Nicolás Ricardo Márquez and Tranquilina Iguarán Cotes.
Background
The couple's house in Aracataca where García Márquez spent his childhood inspired him to make Macondo his book's setting.
Background

García Márquez was one of the four Latin American novelists first included in the literary Latin American Boom of the 1960s and 1970s; the other three were the Peruvian Mario Vargas Llosa, the Argentine Julio Cortázar, and the Mexican Carlos Fuentes.
Background
In 1967, the book earned García Márquez international fame as a novelist of the magical realism movement within Latin American literature.
Background
The English translation by Gregory Rabassa was published in 1970; García Márquez famously praised Rabassa's work, stating that he preferred the English translation to his original Spanish text.
Plot

Rebeca unknowingly infects the town with a plague of insomnia, causing the residents to lose their memory and lack of sleep; Melquíades stays with the Buendías after he cures them of the plague, and permanently dies from drowning, becoming the first man to be buried in Macondo; he leaves behind an encrypted booklet.
Plot

Ultimately, José Arcadio Buendía is driven insane by his impulsive curiosity and paranoia, speaking only in Latin, and is tied to a chestnut tree by his family for many years until his death, causing yellow petals to rain over Macondo.
Plot
Eventually, Macondo becomes exposed to the outside world and the government of newly independent Colombia, with Don Apolinar Moscote as Macondo's first mayor.
Plot
José Arcadio Segundo, the only survivor of the massacre, finds no evidence of the massacre, and the surviving townspeople deny or refuse to believe it happened.
Plot

With Fernanda succumbing to her health complications and isolation, her son, José Arcadio, takes over the house as he discovers Úrsula's treasure hidden under her bed; he squanders all of Úrsula's fortune to build a luxurious swimming pool and abuses the four oldest children he invited.
Plot

The sole survivors are Amaranta Úrsula and her nephew Aureliano Babilonia, whose parentage (Meme and Mauricio Babilonia) is hidden by his grandmother Fernanda; he and Amaranta Úrsula unknowingly begin an incestuous relationship as Aureliano gets drunk.
Plot
Amaranta Úrsula dies in childbirth, and the child is devoured by ants, leaving Aureliano as the last member of the family.
Plot
In the last sentence of the book, the narrator describes Aureliano reading this last line just as the entire town of Macondo is scoured from existence.
Úrsula Iguarán
From a strong and active matriarch, Úrsula is reduced to a plaything for Amaranta Úrsula and Aureliano in her last years and shrinks to the size of a newborn baby when she finally dies.
Colonel Aureliano Buendía
José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula's second child and the first person to be born in Macondo.
Colonel Aureliano Buendía
During the wars he fathered 17 sons by unknown women, all named Aureliano.
Remedios Moscote
Remedios was the youngest daughter of the town's Conservative administrator, Don Apolinar Moscote.
Rebeca
At first, she is extremely timid, refuses to speak, and has the habits of eating earth and whitewash from the walls of the house, a condition known as pica.
Pilar Ternera
She dies some time after she turns 145 years old (she had eventually stopped counting), surviving until the last days of Macondo.
Arcadio
Arcadio is José Arcadio's illegitimate son with Pilar Ternera, although he never learns about his origins.
17 Aurelianos
During his 32 civil war campaigns, Colonel Aureliano Buendía has 17 sons by 17 different women, each named after their father.
17 Aurelianos
The only survivor of the massacre is A.
17 Aurelianos
Amador, who escapes into the jungle only to be assassinated at the doorstep of his father's house many years later.
Remedios the Beauty
Remedios the Beauty is Arcadio and Santa Sofía's first child.
Fernanda del Carpio
Fernanda is never accepted by anyone in the Buendía household for they regard her as an outsider, although none of the Buendías rebel against her inflexible conservatism.
José Arcadio
José Arcadio, named after his ancestors in the Buendía tradition, is Aureliano Segundo and Fernanda's oldest child and follows the trend of previous Arcadios.
Renata Remedios (a.k.a. Meme)
Renata Remedios, or Meme, is Aureliano Segundo and Fernanda's second child and first daughter.
Gastón
When he moves with Amaranta Ursula to Macondo he thinks it is only a matter of time before she realizes that her European ways are out of place, causing her to want to move back to Europe.
Gastón
The plane is shipped to Africa by mistake.
Gastón
Gastón takes the news in stride, only asking that they ship him his velocipede.
Melquíades
Melquíades dies a second time from drowning in the river near Macondo and, following a grand ceremony organized by the Buendías, is the first individual buried in Macondo.
Don Apolinar Moscote
Apolinar Moscote is the father of Remedios Moscote and is a corrupt magistrate who is the first mayor of Macondo.
Mr. Herbert and Mr. Brown
After tasting the local bananas for the first time, he arranges for a banana company to set up a plantation in Macondo.
Mr. Herbert and Mr. Brown
José Arcadio is the only one who remembers the slaughter.
Mr. Herbert and Mr. Brown
The event is likely based on the Banana massacre that took place in Ciénaga, Magdalena in 1928.
Visitación
Visitación is a Guajiro Indian and is the Buendía family’s first housekeeper.
Father Nicanor Reyna
Father Nicanor is the first Catholic priest of Macondo.
Gabriel (Márquez)
Gabriel is only a minor character in the novel but he has the distinction of bearing almost the same name as the author.
Symbolism and metaphors

"Ideological transfiguration ensured that Macondo and the Buendías always were ghosts to some extent, alienated and estranged from their own history, not only victims of the harsh reality of dependence and underdevelopment but also of the ideological illusions that haunt and reinforce such social conditions."
Symbolism and metaphors
Yellow and gold are the most frequently used and symbolize imperialism and the Spanish Siglo de Oro.
Subjectivity of reality and magic realism
One Hundred Years of Solitude is an example of magic realism, a term coined by German art critic Franz Roh in 1925.
Incest
The patriarch of the family, Jose Arcadio Buendía, marries his first cousin, Úrsula.
Elitism

The Buendías' family naming is also highly insular: "José Arcadio" appears four times in the family tree, "Aureliano" appears 22 times, "Remedios" appears three times and "Amaranta" and "Ursula" appear twice.
Literary significance and acclaim

The novel topped the list of books that have most shaped world literature over the last 25 years, according to a survey of international writers commissioned by the global literary journal Wasafiri as a part of its 25th-anniversary celebration.
Literary significance and acclaim

Antonio Sacoto describes the novel as one of the five most important novels in Hispanic American literature (together with El Señor Presidente, Pedro Páramo, La Muerte de Artemio Cruz, and La ciudad y los perros).
Literary significance and acclaim
In 2017, Chilean artist Luisa Rivera illustrated a fiftieth anniversary special edition of the book published by Penguin Random House Group Editorial, Spain.
Inclusion of the Roma ("Gypsies")
According to Hazel Marsh, a senior lecturer in Latin American Studies at the University of East Anglia, it is estimated that 8,000 Roma live in Colombia today.
Depiction of the Thousand Days' War
The Thousand Days' War in Colombia was fought between Liberals and Conservatives from 1899 to 1902.
Depiction of the Thousand Days' War

The Conservatives had been "in control more or less constantly since 1867", and the Liberals, mainly coffee plantation owners and workers who had been excluded from representation, sparked a revolution in October 1899.
Depiction of the Thousand Days' War
The fighting continued for a few years, and it is estimated that over 130,000 people died.
Depiction of the Thousand Days' War
In Chapters 5 and 6, the Conservative Army has invaded the town of Macondo, leading Aureliano to eventually lead a rebellion.
Martial law

1, which ordered the dissolution of any meeting of more than three individuals, allowed the military to shoot the strikers if necessary and prohibited the multitude to move after the military bugle sounds.
Martial law
1, with regards to giving the power to the military to shoot to kill.
Martial law
4 read in Macondo, which García Márquez claims to be composed of three articles of eighty words in total.
Martial law
1 contains 75 words, and it is composed of three provisions in total as well.
Martial law
4 which, according to García Márquez, called the strikers a “bunch of hoodlums”, was in reality adopted only the day after the massacre took place, 7 December 1928.
Representation of the "Banana Massacre"
The "Banana Massacre" occurred December 5–6, 1928, in Ciénaga near Santa Marta, Colombia.
Representation of the "Banana Massacre"
Banana plantation workers had been striking against the United Fruit Company to earn better labor conditions when members of the local military fired guns into crowds.
Adaptations

Shūji Terayama's play One Hundred Years of Solitude (Hyakunen no kodoku 百年の孤独; originally performed by the Tenjō Sajiki theater troupe) and his film Farewell to the Ark (Saraba hakobune さらば箱舟) are loose (and unauthorized) adaptations of the novel transplanted into the realm of Japanese culture and history.
Television series
On March 6, 2019, García Márquez's son Rodrigo García Barcha announced that Netflix was adapting the book into a TV series.
Television series
On October 21, 2022, Netflix commemorated the fortieth anniversary of the announcement of García Márquez's Nobel Prize in Literature with an exclusive preview of One Hundred Years of Solitude.
Television series

The book is considered by fans to be García Márquez's masterpiece yet he himself refused to sell the screening rights to his novel because he did not want it to be adapted in any language other than Spanish and felt a film adaptation would not cover the entire plot due to its length.
Television series

The TV series is Netflix's most expensive Latin American-made project to date, with Colombian groups and indigenous communities making and providing props, and a total of 450 locals building three different versions of Macondo for the progression of the series.
Television series
The TV series ran from 2024 to 2026, faithfully adapting the entire novel in 16 episodes.

modf_beloveth.title: Beloved (novel)
sents: lead
Beloved is a 1987 novel by American novelist Toni Morrison.
lead
Set in the period after the American Civil War, the novel tells the story of formerly enslaved people whose Cincinnati home is haunted by a malevolent spirit.
lead
Sethe, a formerly enslaved mother of four, grapples with her traumatic past.
lead
Morrison sought to depict the limitations that enslaved women faced and to present a physical manifestation that was lacking in the world of literature.
lead
Moreover, Beloved explores the interior life of the formerly enslaved.
lead
The novel won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction a year after its publication, and was a finalist for the 1987 National Book Award.
lead
A survey of writers and literary critics compiled by The New York Times ranked it as the best work of American fiction from 1981 to 2006.
lead
It was adapted as a 1998 movie of the same name, starring Oprah Winfrey.
Background
The book's dedication reads "Sixty Million and more", referring to the Africans and their descendants who died as a result of the Atlantic slave trade.
Margaret Garner as inspiration
The narrative of Beloved is loosely derived from the life of Margaret Garner, who was born into slavery in Boone County, Kentucky, and later attempted to run away to Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1856.
Margaret Garner as inspiration
Morrison uncovered the story of Garner in an 1856 newspaper article, "A Visit to the Slave Mother who Killed Her Child," initially published in the American Baptist.
Margaret Garner as inspiration
In January 1856, Garner fled Maplewood Farm in Richwood, Kentucky, alongside her husband, his parents, and their four children in hopes of attaining freedom from slavery in Cincinnati.
Margaret Garner as inspiration
After fleeing, they were subject to capture under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.
Margaret Garner as inspiration
The group first travelled by horse to Covington, Kentucky before continuing on foot to the home of their free relatives, the Kites, in Cincinnati.
Plot summary
Beloved begins in 1873 in Cincinnati, Ohio, with Sethe, a formerly enslaved woman, and her 18-year-old daughter, Denver, who live at 124 Bluestone Road.
Plot summary
The site has been haunted for years by what they believe is the ghost of Sethe's youngest daughter.
Plot summary
Sethe's sons, Howard and Buglar, ran away from home by the age of 13, which she believes was due to the ghost.
Plot summary
He forces out the spirit, receiving Denver's contempt for driving away her only companion, but persuades them to leave the house together for the first time in years for a carnival.
Plot summary
Paul D confronts Sethe, who tells him that after escaping and joining her children at 124, four horsemen came to return her children and her to a life of slavery.
Plot summary
Sethe, terrified of returning to Sweet Home and its vicious manager Schoolteacher, ran to the woodshed with her children to kill them, but only managed to kill her younger infant daughter.
Plot summary
Bodwin, arrives to pick up Denver for her first night-shift as a companion in his house.
Mother-daughter relationships
Sethe only becomes individuated after Beloved's exorcism.
Mother-daughter relationships
Then, she is free to fully accept the first relationship that is completely "for her," her relationship with Paul D.
Mother-daughter relationships
Sethe was traumatized by having had her milk stolen, unable to form the symbolic bond between herself and her daughter by feeding her.
Psychological effects of slavery
Because of the suffering under slavery, most former slaves tried to repress these memories in an attempt to forget the past.
Psychological effects of slavery
Sethe, Paul D., and Denver all suffered a loss of self, which could only be remedied when they were able to reconcile their pasts and memories of earlier identities.
Definition of manhood
Paul D is a victim of racism in that his dreams and goals are so high that he will never be able to achieve them because of racism.
Definition of manhood

In Beloved, Stamp Paid observes Paul D sitting on the base of the church steps "... liquor bottle in hand, stripped of the very maleness that enables him to caress and love the wounded Sethe..." (132).
Family relationships
For example, Sethe, Denver, and Paul D go to the neighborhood carnival, which happens to be Sethe's first social outing since killing her daughter.
Heroism
Yet Sethe herself never doubts her own veracity, justifying, "It ain't my job to know what's worse.
Heroism

From Sethe's point of view, the only method that would have resulted in the complete safety of her children was to kill her children and "keep them away from what [she] know[s] is terrible," because death is far more preferable to life back in the confines of slavery.
Heroism
How she never mentioned or looked at it, so he did not have to feel the shame of being collared like a beast.
Heroism
Only this woman Sethe could have left him his manhood like that.
Heroism
Paul D draws support from Sethe "never mention[ing] or look[ing]" at his scars, but more so, this allows him to retain his own manhood, which to Paul D defines the very basis of his character.
Heroism

When Beloved's influence becomes more and more detrimental to the environment of 124 Bluestone Road and Sethe's outlook on life, Denver does not hesitate to thrust herself into a motherly role and care for her mother.
Heroism

As her experience in slavery came to define her life as a free woman, Sethe wallowed in her past, becoming a hero only when she allowed those she loved to escape their own burdens from the de-humanizing effects of slavery.
Sethe
She lives in the house named 124 (a house on 124 Bluestone Rd., but referred to only as "124") which is believed to be haunted because she killed her infant child there.
Sethe
She was 19 years old when Denver was born, making her birth year to be 1836.
Paul D
Paul D retains his name from enslavement; most of the enslaved men at Sweet Home were named Paul.
Denver
Denver is Sethe's only child who remains at 124.
Denver
In the final chapters, Denver fights not only for her personal independence, but also for her mother's wellbeing, breaking the cycle of isolation at 124.
Baby Suggs
She dies at 70 in the beginning of the book, 8 years before the main events.
Halle
Paul D was the last to see Halle, churning butter at Sweet Home.
Adaptations
In 1998, the novel was made into a film directed by Jonathan Demme, and produced by and starring Oprah Winfrey.
Adaptations
In January 2016, Beloved was broadcast in 10 episodes by BBC Radio 4 as part of its 15 Minute Drama programme.
Legacy

In accepting the award on October 12, 1988, Morrison said that "[t]here is no suitable memorial or plaque or wreath or wall or park or skyscraper lobby" honoring the memory of the human beings forced into slavery and brought to the United States.
Legacy

"And because such a place doesn't exist (that I know of), the book had to." Inspired by her remarks, the Toni Morrison Society began to install benches at significant sites in the history of slavery in America.
Legacy

The New York Times reported that the first 'bench by the road' was dedicated on July 26, 2008, on Sullivan's Island, South Carolina, the place of entry for some 40% of the enslaved Africans brought to the United States.
Legacy
In 2017, the 21st bench was placed at the Library of Congress.
Legacy
It is dedicated to Daniel Alexander Payne Murray (1852–1925), the first African-American assistant librarian of Congress.
Critical reception
The publication of Beloved in 1987 resulted in the greatest acclaim yet for Morrison.
Critical reception

Although nominated for the National Book Award for Fiction, it surprisingly lost to Paco's Story, and 48 African-American writers and critics—including Maya Angelou, Amiri Baraka, Jayne Cortez, Angela Davis, Ernest J.
Critical reception
Williams—signed a letter of protest that was published in The New York Times Book Review on January 24, 1988.
Critical reception
Yet, later in 1988, Beloved did receive the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, as well as the Robert F.
Critical reception

Commentators have described Beloved as an exploration of notions of family, trauma, the repression of memory, the restoration of the historical record and an attempt to give voice to the collective memory of African Americans.
Critical reception

Indeed, critics and Morrison herself have indicated that the controversial epigraph to Beloved, "60 million and more", is drawn from a number of studies on the African slave trade, which estimate that approximately half of each ship's "cargo" perished in transit to America.
Critical reception
Since the late 1970s, the focus on Morrison's representation of African-American experience and history has been strong.
Critical reception

As Jill Matus argues, however, Morrison's representations of trauma are "never simply curative": in raising the ghosts of the past to banish or memorialize them, the texts potentially "provoke readers to the vicarious experience of trauma and act as a means of transmission".
Critical reception
In her 1987 review of Beloved, Snitow argues that Beloved, the ghost at the center of the narrative, is "too light" and "hollow", rendering the entire novel "airless".
Critical reception
On November 5, 2019, the BBC News listed Beloved on its list of the 100 most inspiring novels.
Critical reception
In 2026, a Guardian poll of more than 170 novelists, critics, and academics ranked Beloved'' as the second greatest English-language novel of all time.
Banning and controversy
Beloved has been banned in many U.S. schools, including at least eleven during the 2021–2022 academic year.
Banning and controversy
In 2007, twenty years after its 1987 publication, the novel was abruptly abandoned by an AP English class at Eastern High School in Louisville, Kentucky, at the order of the school's principal.
Banning and controversy
The class had nearly reached the end of the book when a parent complained about language on page 13.
Banning and controversy

Upon being informed that the book was being immediately banned, the English teacher who was teaching the book argued to the school's Site Based Decision Making Council that a college-level English literature course should be taught.
Banning and controversy

Parental concern about Beloveds content inspired the Beloved Bill, legislation that would have required Virginia public schools to notify parents of any "sexually explicit content" and provide an alternative assignment if requested.
Banning and controversy
Student activist group Voters of Tomorrow announced plans in February 2022 to distribute banned books to students in Texas and Virginia, including Beloved.
Banning and controversy

Parents in the Katy Independent School District responded to the book distributions by filing a request to review Beloved, resulting in the book's removal from school libraries and restriction to 11th and 12th Grade students.
Banning and controversy

The ACLU of Texas delivered a letter to school board members and the superintendent in April 2022 claiming that the district's book removal of Beloved and other titles violated the First Amendment, the Texas Constitution, and the district's own policies.
Trilogy
Beloved is the first of three novels about love and African-American history, sometimes called the Beloved Trilogy.
Trilogy
The third novel Paradise, about citizens of an all-Black town, came out in 1997.

name: The Hobbit, or
There and Back Again

sents: lead
The Hobbit, or There and Back Again is a children's fantasy novel by the English author J.
lead
It was published in 1937 to wide critical acclaim, being nominated for the Carnegie Medal and awarded a prize from the New York Herald Tribune for best juvenile fiction.
lead
It is recognized as a classic in children's literature and is one of the best-selling books of all time, with over 100 million copies sold.
lead

The Hobbit is set in Middle-earth and follows home-loving Bilbo Baggins, the titular hobbit who joins the wizard Gandalf and the thirteen dwarves of Thorin's Company on a quest to reclaim the dwarves' home and treasure from the dragon Smaug.
lead
Bilbo's journey takes him from his peaceful rural surroundings into more sinister territory.
lead
The story is told in the form of a picaresque or episodic quest; several chapters introduce a new type of monster or threat as Bilbo progresses through the landscape.
lead
Bilbo gains a new level of maturity, competence, and wisdom by accepting the disreputable, romantic, fey and adventurous sides of his nature and applying his wits and common sense.
lead
The story reaches its climax in the Battle of Five Armies, where many of the characters and creatures from earlier chapters re-emerge to engage in conflict.
Characters
Thorin Oakenshield is the proud, pompous head of the company of dwarves and heir to the destroyed dwarvish kingdom under the Lonely Mountain.
Plot
Gandalf unveils Thror's map showing a secret door into the Mountain and proposes that dumbfounded Bilbo should serve as the expedition's "burglar".
Plot
In Mirkwood, Bilbo first saves the dwarves from giant spiders and then from the dungeons of the Wood-elves.
Plot
The expedition reaches the mountain and finds the secret door.
Plot
When the dwarves take possession of the mountain, Bilbo finds the Arkenstone, the most-treasured heirloom of Thorin's family, and hides it away.
Plot

The dwarves, men and elves band together, but only with the timely arrival of the eagles and Beorn, who fights in his bear form and kills the goblin general, do they win the climactic Battle of Five Armies.
Plot
Bilbo accepts only a small portion of his share of the treasure, having no want or need for more, but still returns home a very wealthy hobbit roughly a year and a month after he first left.
Background
In the early 1930s Tolkien was pursuing an academic career at the University of Oxford as Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon, with a fellowship at Pembroke College.
Background

Several of his poems had been published in magazines and small collections, including Goblin Feet and The Cat and the Fiddle: A Nursery Rhyme Undone and its Scandalous Secret Unlocked, a reworking of Hey Diddle Diddle, an English nursery rhyme.
Background
Auden, Tolkien recollects that he began The Hobbit one day early in the 1930s.
Background

In April 1955 Pan Books issued a paperback version and sold 41,000 copies in the first year.
Publication history
Casino Royale was published on 23 March 1954 in the US, but sales were poor, totalling only 4,000 copies across the entire US during the course of the year.
Critical reception
Hugh I'Anson Fausset, writing in The Manchester Guardian, thought that Casino Royale was "a first-rate thriller... with a breathtaking plot".
Critical reception
John Betjeman, writing in The Daily Telegraph, considered that "Ian Fleming has discovered the secret of the narrative art... which is to work up to a climax unrevealed at the end of each chapter.
Critical reception
He praised the first part, saying that Fleming "manages to make baccarat clear even to one who's never played it and produced as exciting a gambling sequence as I've ever read.
Critical reception
But then he decides to pad out the book to novel length and leads the weary reader through a set of tough clichés to an ending which surprises nobody save Operative 007.
Adaptations
In 1954 CBS paid Ian Fleming $1,000 to adapt Casino Royale into a one-hour television adventure as part of its Climax! series.
Adaptations
The episode aired live on 21 October 1954 and starred Barry Nelson as secret agent "Card Sense" James 'Jimmy' Bond and Peter Lorre as Le Chiffre.
Adaptations
In March 1955 Ian Fleming sold the film rights of Casino Royale to the producer Gregory Ratoff for $6,000.
Adaptations
Feldman decided the best way to profit from the film rights was to make a satirical version, which was produced and released in 1967 by Columbia Pictures.
Adaptations
The 1967 version is described by the British Film Institute as "an incoherent all-star comedy".
Adaptations
Casino Royale was the first James Bond novel to be adapted as a daily comic strip; it was published in The Daily Express and syndicated worldwide.
Adaptations
The strip ran from 7 July 1958 to 13 December 1958, and was written by Anthony Hern and illustrated by John McLusky.
Adaptations
McLusky felt that Fleming's 007 looked too "outdated" and "pre-war" and changed Bond to give him a more masculine look.
Adaptations
A graphic novel adaptation of the book was released by Dynamite Entertainment in April 2018, written by Van Jensen and illustrated by Dennis Calero.
Adaptations

Following the 1967 adaptation, the rights to the film remained with Columbia Pictures until 1989 when the studio, and the rights to their intellectual property portfolio was acquired by the Japanese company Sony.
Adaptations
In 1999, following legal action between Sony Pictures Entertainment and MGM/UA, Sony traded the rights to Casino Royale for MGM's partial-rights to Spider-Man.
Adaptations
Casino Royale is a reboot, showing Bond at the beginning of his career as a 00-agent, and overall stays true to the original novel.

genr_the_maltease_falcon.title: The Maltese Falcon (novel)
sents: lead
The Maltese Falcon is a 1930 detective novel by American writer Dashiell Hammett, originally serialized in the magazine Black Mask beginning with the September 1929 issue.
lead
The story is told entirely in external third-person narrative; there is no description whatsoever of any character's thoughts or feelings, only what they say and do, and how they look.
lead
The novel has been adapted several times for the cinema.
lead
The main character, Sam Spade (who also appeared later in some lesser-known short stories), was a departure from Hammett's nameless detective, The Continental Op.
lead

Spade combined several features of previous detectives, notably his cold detachment, keen eye for detail, unflinching and sometimes ruthless determination to achieve his own form of justice, and a complete lack of sentimentality.
lead
In 1990 the novel ranked 10th in Top 100 Crime Novels of All Time list by the Crime Writers' Association.
lead
Five years later, in a similar list by Mystery Writers of America, the novel was ranked third.
Plot
Archer takes the first stint but is found shot dead that night.
Plot
Gutman presents $10,000 in cash for the falcon, but Spade argues that the police must arrest someone for the murders.
Plot
Spade has Effie fetch the falcon, but Gutman discovers it is a fake (a decoy made by General Kemidov, or possibly the falcon of legend was never real).
Background
The novel was serialized in five parts in Black Mask in 1929 and 1930 before being published in book form in 1930 by Alfred A.
Adaptations
The Maltese Falcon (1931), the first version, a pre-Code production starring Ricardo Cortez as Sam Spade and Bebe Daniels as Brigid O'Shaughnessy.
Adaptations
In 1936, Warner Brothers attempted to re-release the film but was denied approval by the Hays Production Code censors because of its "lewd" content; this led to the production of the 1936 adaptation.
Adaptations
It was not until after 1966 that unedited copies of the 1931 film could be shown in the United States.
Adaptations
Satan Met a Lady (1936), a comedic adaptation starring Bette Davis and Warren William, with Sam Spade becoming "Ted Shane".
Adaptations
The Maltese Falcon (1941), the third and best-known version, considered to be a film noir classic.
Adaptations
The Black Bird (1975), a spoof sequel, featuring George Segal as Sam Spade Jr.
Adaptations
The Maltese Falcon (1984), a full-cast dramatization by BBC Radio 4, featuring Jane Lapotaire and Tom Wilkinson.
Adaptations
Dashiell Hammett's The Maltese Falcon (2008), an audio dramatization by the Hollywood Theater of the Ear.
Adaptations
The Maltese Falcon was produced by The Long Beach Shakespeare Company and premiered on April 29, 2005, when Hammett's book was adapted and directed by Martin Pope.
Adaptations
The Maltese Murder (2008), by playwright Bryan Colley, commissioned by the Johnson County Library in Kansas as part of the National Endowment for the Arts Big Read.

genr_the_shadow_over_inn_s_mouth.title: The Shadow over Innsmouth

Author: H. P. Lovecraft
Text: The Shadow over Innsmouth at Wikisource

sents: lead
The Shadow over Innsmouth is a horror novella by American author H.
lead
Lovecraft, written in November–December 1931.
lead

It forms part of the Cthulhu Mythos, using its motif of a malign undersea civilization, and references several shared elements of the Mythos, including place-names, mythical creatures, and invocations.
lead
The Shadow over Innsmouth is the only Lovecraft story that was published in book form during his lifetime.
lead
The narrator is a student conducting an antiquarian tour of New England.
lead
He travels through the nearby decrepit seaport of Innsmouth which is suggested as a cheaper and potentially interesting next leg of his journey.
lead
There he interacts with strange people and observes disturbing events that ultimately lead to horrifying and personal revelations.
Plot

The narrator explains how he instigated a secret investigation of the decrepit town of Innsmouth, Massachusetts —a former seaport isolated from other nearby towns by vast salt marshes —by the U.S. government after fleeing it on July 16, 1927.
Plot

The narrator proceeds to describe in detail the events surrounding his initial interest in the town, which lies along the route of his tour across New England, taken when he was a 21-year-old student at Oberlin College.
Plot
The town was once a profitable port and shipbuilding center during the colonial and post- revolutionary periods, but began to decline after the War of 1812 interrupted shipping.
Plot
A local merchant named Obed Marsh built a profitable gold refinery, but the town only deteriorated further after riots and a mysterious epidemic eliminated half of its residents in 1845.
Plot
Marsh also founded a pagan cult called the Esoteric Order of Dagon, which became the town's primary religion.
Plot
The only resident who appears normal is a grocery store clerk from neighboring Arkham, who was transferred there by the chain.
Plot
When hard times fell on the town, Marsh's cult performed similar sacrifices to the Deep Ones in exchange for wealth in the form of large fish hauls and unique jewelry.
Plot
The survivors were left with no other choice than to join the cult and continue Marsh's practices.
Plot
Once he leaves, Zadok disappears and is never seen again.
Plot

After returning home to Toledo, the narrator begins researching his family tree and discovers that he is a descendant of Marsh through his second wife Pth’thya-l’yi, and by 1930 begins to gradually transform into a Deep One.
Inspiration
Lovecraft based the town of Innsmouth on his impressions of Newburyport, Massachusetts, which he had visited in 1923 and fall 1931.
Inspiration
Chambers' story concerns the discovery of "the remnants of the last race of amphibious human beings," living in a five-mile deep chasm just off the Atlantic coast.
Inspiration
But the humanity of the face was not the most extraordinary thing about the creature.
Cthulhu Mythos
The creature known as Dagon is first introduced in Lovecraft's 1917 tale of the same name.
Cthulhu Mythos
August Derleth also used the Deep Ones in the short story "Innsmouth Clay", which was inspired by an entry in Lovecraft's Commonplace Book.
Cthulhu Mythos
"The Shuttered Room" is another short story by Derleth, inspired by a note by Lovecraft, which also involves the Deep Ones.
Publication
The story was rejected by Weird Tales editor Farnsworth Wright when Derleth surreptitiously submitted it for publication in 1933.
Publication

The project came to fruition in November 1936 (although the copyright page declares the date of publication as April 1936), but the book had so many typographical errors that Lovecraft insisted on an errata sheet (which was also faulty).
Publication

Lovecraft was displeased with the production; writing to his correspondent Lee McBride White on Nov 30, 1936, he wrote: "My Shadow over Innsmouth is now out - but as a first cloth-bound book it doesn't awake any enthusiasm in me.
Publication
Indeed, it is one of the lousiest jobs I've ever seen - 30 misprints, slovenly format, & loose, slipshod binding.
Publication
It had a bound run of 200 copies — the only book of Lovecraft's fiction distributed during his lifetime.
Publication
Crawford had printed 400 copies but bound only 200; the others were destroyed later.
Publication
Of this edition Robert Weinberg has written: "Only a few hundred copies of the book were printed, and even less than that were sold, even though it was available at the bargain price of $1 per copy.
Publication
The book was the only bound hardcover to appear during Lovecraft's lifetime and became one of the true rarities in the collecting field.
Publication
After Lovecraft's death (and Wright's), the story appeared in an unauthorized abridged version in the January 1942 issue of Weird Tales.
Reception

As L Sprague de Camp noted, the action sections of Innsmouth are a departure for Lovecraft; the story's tense and memorable siege scene within the titular town's hotel reveals a flair in execution on a par with some of the most compelling chapters of R L Stevenson's Kidnapped.
Film and television
The movie City Under the Sea (1965) is loosely based on The Shadow over Innsmouth.
Film and television
Colombian writer Andres Caicedo adapted The Shadow over Innsmouth into a screenplay in 1973.
Film and television
Konaka adapted The Shadow over Innsmouth for Japanese television as Insmus wo Oou Kage in 1992.
Film and television
The Shadow over Innsmouth forms the principal storyline in Stuart Gordon 's 2001 film Dagon.
Film and television
Full Moon Entertainment was going to release Gordon's original adaptation (under the original novella's title) in 1991, using Bernie Wrightson 's character designs, but the project was unrealized.
Film and television
The 2007 film Cthulhu is loosely based on The Shadow over Innsmouth.
Film and television
The 2014 music video for " Escape from Midwich Valley " by Carpenter Brut and the 2015 short film Innsmouth are also based on The Shadow over Innsmouth.
Film and television

A 2005 episode of The Mighty Boosh, " The Legend of Old Gregg ", appears to draw inspiration from the story, including a town with strange residents surrounded by mystery, an elderly fisherman who tells the main characters the history of the town and Old Gregg himself, who is a human-fish hybrid.
Film and television
In 2015, the production and eventual publication of a film titled The Shadow over Innsmouth was announced on the website The Lovecraft Ezine.
Film and television
In 2020, a visual effects studio (Providence VFX) has for the first time reproduced the city of Innsmouth in computer graphics.
Film and television
The 2020 film The Deep Ones, set in modern Southern California.
Video games
Shadow of the Comet, a 1993 adventure game, takes place in a cult-controlled town of Illsmouth, an alteration on Lovecraft's Innsmouth.
Video games
" The Mansion of Innsmouth ") is a 1995 3D first-person shooter video game for the Virtual Boy, released in Japan based on Chiaki J.
Video games
The 2005 video game Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth uses many elements from "The Shadow over Innsmouth" with a great degree of accuracy.
Video games

Dark Corners of the Earth was supposed to be followed by a sequel set in the 2000s, titled Call of Cthulhu: Destiny's End, but due to the closure of its developer Headfirst Productions, the game was cancelled.
Video games
Indie game Chronicle of Innsmouth (production started in 2015) is directly based on the plot of The Shadow over Innsmouth.
Video games

In the fictional universe of the 2013 fighting game Skullgirls, there's a neighborhood in the game's world known as "Little Innsmouth", which is inhabited by fish-like humanoids, and which also serves as the stage for Ms.
Video games
The Far Harbor expansion of the 2015 game Fallout 4 may draw inspiration from the Lovecraft universe, particularly The Shadow over Innsmouth.
Video games

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion has a quest named "A Shadow Over Hackdirt", where the player goes to a mysterious small town and finds out the townspeople are part of a cult who worship beings known as "The Deep Ones".
Video games
The online video game The Secret World features a town called Kingsmouth in which many supernatural events occur.
Video games
The Secret World borrows heavily from the Lovecraftian mythos as well as many other continuities.
Video games

The game The Sinking City, a 2019 horror game, takes inspiration from the novella with the inclusion of Innsmouth, the Esoteric Order of Dagon, and residents with fish-like physical appearance called the "Innsmouthers."
Video games
The game Call of the Sea, a 2020 adventure game, takes inspiration from the book: The Shadow over Innsmouth.
Comics

Several plot elements from "Shadow over Innsmouth" appear in two comics of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles franchise, namely in the Mirage comic "Men of Shadow" (TMNT Vol.1 #29) and the Archie comic "In the Dark" (TMNT Adventures #27).
Comics
Steven Philip Jones and Trey Baldwin adapted The Shadow over Innsmouth into a graphic novel published by Caliber Comics in 2020.
Other

In January 2012, the Cape Cod based Provincetown Theater announced a reading of a full-length play of the story, entitled HP Lovecraft's The Shadow over Innsmouth, adapted for the stage by Bragan Thomas.
Other
A reading of the story performed by Richard Coyle was produced and first broadcast by BBC Radio 4 Extra in 2011.
Other
WildClaw Theatre of Chicago presented a world premiere stage production of The Shadow Over Innsmouth in 2013, adapted to the stage by Scott Barsotti and directed by Scott Cummins.
Other
BBC Radio 4 released the third installment of The Lovecraft Investigations, a radio play in the style of a mystery podcast-like serial, based on and titled "The Shadow Over Innsmouth".
Other
Technically a sequel to the original story, the setting is changed to 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, with Obed Marsh established as an alias of the Count of St.
Other

Germain, Innsmouth's settlement being by those fleeing the Witchfinder Matthew Hopkins during the English Civil War, the Deep Ones also being responsible for the disappearances of the Roanoke Colony and the urban legend of Hoer Verde in Brazil, and the Somerton Man as a Deep One.
Shadows over Innsmouth
The Shadow over Innsmouth was republished in a 1994 anthology entitled Shadows over Innsmouth, containing stories by other authors based on Innsmouth and the Old Ones.

genr_doon.title: Dune (novel)

sents: lead
Dune is a 1965 epic science fiction novel by American author Frank Herbert, originally published as two separate serials (1963–64 novel Dune World and 1965 novel Prophet of Dune) in Analog magazine.
lead
It tied with Roger Zelazny 's This Immortal for the Hugo Award for Best Novel and won the inaugural Nebula Award for Best Novel in 1966.
lead
It is the first installment of the Dune Chronicles.
lead
It is one of the world's best-selling science fiction novels.
lead
Dune is set in the distant future in a feudal interstellar society, descended from terrestrial humans, in which various noble houses control planetary fiefs.
lead
It tells the story of young Paul Atreides, whose family accepts the stewardship of the planet Arrakis.
lead
While the planet is an inhospitable and sparsely populated desert wasteland, it is the only source of melange, or "spice", a drug that extends life and enhances mental abilities.
lead
Melange is also necessary for space navigation, which requires a kind of multidimensional awareness and foresight that only the drug provides.
Origins
After his novel The Dragon in the Sea was published in 1957, Herbert traveled to Florence, Oregon, at the north end of the Oregon Dunes.
Origins
" White men are eating the earth," Hansen told Herbert in 1958, after sharing a piece on the effect of logging on the Quileute reservation.
Origins
After an interval of a year, he published the much slower-paced five-part The Prophet of Dune in the January–May 1965 issues.
Origins
The first serial became "Book One: Dune" in the final published Dune novel, and the second serial was divided into "Book Two: Muad'dib" and "Book Three: The Prophet".
Origins
The novel, Dune, was finally accepted and published in August 1965 by Chilton Books, a printing house better known for publishing auto repair manuals.
Origins
However, the first printing, priced at $5.95 (equivalent to $57.53 in 2023), did not sell well and was poorly received by critics as being atypical of science fiction at the time.
Origins
Chilton considered the publication of Dune a write-off and Lanier was fired.
Origins
At first Herbert considered using Mars as setting for his novel, but eventually decided to use a fictional planet instead.
Plot

Although Arrakis is a harsh and inhospitable desert planet, it is of enormous importance because it is the only planetary source of melange, or the "spice", a unique and incredibly valuable substance that extends human youth, vitality and lifespan.
Plot
Paul reveals that Jessica is the daughter of the Baron, a secret kept from her by the Bene Gesserit.
Plot
Paul's powerful prescience manifests, which confirms for the Fremen that he is their prophesied "Lisan al-Gaib" messiah, a legend planted by the Bene Gesserit's Missionaria Protectiva.
Themes and influences
I consider it an epic adventure in the classic storytelling tradition, a story of myth and legend not unlike the Morte d'Arthur or any messiah story.
Themes and influences
In the 1960s, there were just these two colossal superpowers duking it out.
Themes and influences

Herbert said Paul's messiah figure was inspired by the Arthurian legend, and that the scarcity of water on Arrakis was a metaphor for oil, as well as air and water itself, and for the shortages of resources caused by overpopulation.
Themes and influences
Frank Herbert drew parallels, used spectacular metaphors, and extrapolated present conditions into world systems that seem entirely alien at first blush.
Middle-Eastern and Islamic references
In particular, words related to the messianic religion of the Fremen, first implanted by the Bene Gesserit, are taken from Arabic, including Muad'Dib (from Arabic: مؤدب, romanized: muʾaddib, lit.
Middle-Eastern and Islamic references
The environment of the desert planet Arrakis was primarily inspired by the environments of the Middle East.
Environmentalism and ecology
Dune has been called the "first planetary ecology novel on a grand scale".
Environmentalism and ecology
After the publication of Silent Spring by Rachel Carson in 1962, science fiction writers began treating the subject of ecological change and its consequences.
Environmentalism and ecology
Dune responded in 1965 with its complex descriptions of Arrakis life, from giant sandworms (for whom water is deadly) to smaller, mouse-like life-forms adapted to live with limited water.
Environmentalism and ecology
Dune was followed in its creation of complex and unique ecologies by other science fiction books such as A Door into Ocean (1986) and Red Mars (1992).
Environmentalism and ecology
While the genre of climate fiction was popularized in the 2010s in response to real global climate change, Dune as well as other early science fiction works from authors like J.
Gender dynamics
By setting up certain women with leaders of certain Houses in the Imperium, the Bene Gesserit can control bloodlines across generations through their secret breeding program.
Heroism
As such, Dune is representative of a general trend beginning in 1960s American science fiction in that it features a character who attains godlike status through scientific means.
Heroism
Author Frank Herbert said in 1979, "The bottom line of the Dune trilogy is: beware of heroes.
Critical reception
Dune tied with Roger Zelazny 's This Immortal for the Hugo Award in 1966 and won the inaugural Nebula Award for Best Novel.
Critical reception
The novel has been translated into dozens of languages, and has sold almost 20 million copies.
Critical reception
Dune has been regularly cited as one of the world's best-selling science fiction novels.
Critical reception
Clarke described Dune as "unique" and wrote, "I know nothing comparable to it except The Lord of the Rings." Robert A.
Critical reception
Heinlein described the novel as "powerful, convincing, and most ingenious." It was described as "one of the monuments of modern science fiction" by the Chicago Tribune, and P.
Critical reception
On November 5, 2019, the BBC News listed Dune on its list of the 100 most influential novels.
Critical reception
Tolkien refused to review Dune, on the grounds that he disliked it "with some intensity" and thus felt it would be unfair to Herbert, another working author, if he gave an honest review of the book.
First edition prints and manuscripts
The first edition of Dune is one of the most valuable in science fiction book collecting.
First edition prints and manuscripts
Copies have been sold for more than $20,000 at auction.
Sequels and prequels

The series included Dune Messiah (1969), Children of Dune (1976), God Emperor of Dune (1981), Heretics of Dune (1984), and Chapterhouse: Dune (1985), each sequentially continuing on the narrative from Dune.
Sequels and prequels
Brian Herbert's and Anderson's Dune prequels first started publication in 1999, and have led to additional stories that take place between those of Frank Herbert's books.
Sequels and prequels

The notes for what would have been Dune 7 also enabled them to publish Hunters of Dune (2006) and Sandworms of Dune (2007), sequels to Frank Herbert's final novel Chapterhouse: Dune, which complete the chronological progression of his original series, and wrap up storylines that began in Heretics of Dune.
Early stalled attempts
In 1971, the production company Apjac International (APJ) (headed by Arthur P.
Early stalled attempts
Jacobs' first choice for director was David Lean, but he turned down the offer.
Early stalled attempts

Initially, the first treatment had been handled by Robert Greenhut, the producer who had lobbied Jacobs to make the movie in the first place, but subsequently Rospo Pallenberg was approached to write the script, with shooting scheduled to begin in 1974.
Early stalled attempts
In December 1974, a French consortium led by Jean-Paul Gibon purchased the film rights from APJ, with Alejandro Jodorowsky set to direct.
Early stalled attempts

Dalí later demanded to be paid $100,000 per hour; Jodorowsky agreed, but tailored Dalí's part to be filmed in one hour, drafting plans for other scenes of the emperor to use a mechanical mannequin as substitute for Dalí.
Early stalled attempts

Frank Herbert traveled to Europe in 1976 to find that $2 million of the $9.5 million budget had already been spent in pre-production, and that Jodorowsky's script would result in a 14-hour movie ("It was the size of a phone book", Herbert later recalled).
Early stalled attempts
O'Bannon entered a psychiatric hospital after the production failed, then worked on 13 scripts, the last of which became Alien.
Early stalled attempts
A 2013 documentary, Jodorowsky's Dune, was made about Jodorowsky's failed attempt at an adaptation.
Early stalled attempts
In 1976, Dino De Laurentiis acquired the rights from Gibon's consortium.
Early stalled attempts
De Laurentiis commissioned Herbert to write a new screenplay in 1978; the script Herbert turned in was 175 pages long, the equivalent of nearly three hours of screen time.
Early stalled attempts
De Laurentiis then hired director Ridley Scott in 1979, with Rudy Wurlitzer writing the screenplay and H.
Early stalled attempts
But after seven months I dropped out of Dune, by then Rudy Wurlitzer had come up with a first-draft script which I felt was a decent distillation of Frank Herbert's.
Early stalled attempts
But I also realised Dune was going to take a lot more work—at least two and a half years' worth.
1984 film by David Lynch
This first film of Dune, directed by Lynch, was released in 1984, nearly 20 years after the book's publication.
2000 miniseries by John Harrison
In 2000, John Harrison adapted the novel into Frank Herbert's Dune, a miniseries that premiered on the Sci-Fi Channel.
2000 miniseries by John Harrison
As of 2004, the miniseries was one of the three highest-rated programs broadcast on the Sci-Fi Channel.
Further film attempts
In 2008, Paramount Pictures announced that they would produce a new film based on the book, with Peter Berg attached to direct.
Further film attempts
Anderson and Frank Herbert's son Brian Herbert, who had together written multiple Dune sequels and prequels since 1999, were attached to the project as technical advisors.
Further film attempts
In October 2009, Berg dropped out of the project, later saying that it "for a variety of reasons wasn't the right thing" for him.
Further film attempts
Subsequently, with a script draft by Joshua Zetumer, Paramount reportedly sought a new director who could do the film for under $175 million.
Further film attempts
In 2010, Pierre Morel was signed on to direct, with screenwriter Chase Palmer incorporating Morel's vision of the project into Zetumer's original draft.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
In November 2016, Legendary Entertainment acquired the film and TV rights for Dune.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
Variety reported in December 2016 that Denis Villeneuve was in negotiations to direct the project, which was confirmed in February 2017.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
In April 2017, Legendary announced that Eric Roth would write the screenplay.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
Villeneuve explained in March 2018 that his adaptation will be split into two films, with the first installment scheduled to begin production in 2019.
Films by Denis Villeneuve

Pictures distributed the film, which had its initial premiere on September 3, 2021, at the Venice Film Festival, and wide release in both theaters and streaming on HBO Max on October 21, 2021, as part of Warner Bros.'s approach to handling the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the film industry.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
It has gone on to win multiple awards and was named by the National Board of Review as one of the 10 best films of 2021, as well as the American Film Institute in their annual top 10 list.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
The film went on to be nominated for ten Academy Awards, winning six, the most wins of the night for any film in contention.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
A sequel, Dune: Part Two, was scheduled for release on November 3, 2023, but was released on March 1, 2024, due to the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
It had its world premiere at the Odeon Luxe Leicester Square, London, on February 15, 2024, and opened in the United States on March 1.
Films by Denis Villeneuve
It received critical acclaim especially for its visual effects and has grossed over $711 million worldwide, making it the second-highest grossing film of 2024.
Audiobooks
In 1993, Recorded Books Inc. released a 20-disc audiobook narrated by George Guidall.
Audiobooks
In 2007, Audio Renaissance released an audio book narrated by Simon Vance with some parts performed by Scott Brick, Orlagh Cassidy, Euan Morton, and other performers.
Cultural influence
Dune was cited as a source of inspiration for Hayao Miyazaki 's anime film Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984) for its post-apocalyptic world.
Cultural influence
Dune was parodied in 1984's National Lampoon's Doon by Ellis Weiner, which William F.
Cultural influence

Touponce called "something of a tribute to Herbert's success on college campuses", noting that "the only other book to have been so honored is Tolkien 's The Lord of the Rings," which was parodied by The Harvard Lampoon in 1969.
Music
In 1977, David Matthews became one of the first artists to dedicate an entire composition to Dune, publishing an album of the same name on CTI Records.
Music
In 1978, French electronic musician Richard Pinhas released the nine-track Dune -inspired album Chronolyse, which includes the seven-part Variations sur le thème des Bene Gesserit.
Music
In 1979, German electronic music pioneer Klaus Schulze released an LP titled Dune featuring motifs and lyrics inspired by the novel.
Music
A similar musical project, Visions of Dune, was released also in 1979 by Zed (a pseudonym of French electronic musician Bernard Sjazner).
Music
1981 French zeuhl band Dün released their album Eros which was inspired by the Dune novel, also their band name Dün was a short form from their temporary name Dune.
Music
Dune inspired the German happy hardcore band Dune, who have released several albums with space travel-themed songs.
Music
"Traveller in Time", from the 1991 Blind Guardian album Tales from the Twilight World, is based mostly on Paul Atreides' visions of future and past.
Music
The title of the 1993 Fear Factory album Fear is The Mindkiller is a quote from the " litany against fear ".
Music
Dune also inspired the 1999 album The 2nd Moon by the German death metal band Golem, which is a concept album about the series.
Music
The song "The Eyes of Ibad" from Panchiko 's 2000 EP D>E>A>T>H>M>E>T>A>L, takes its name from Dune, referencing the blue-in-blue eyes of the Fremen.
Music
In 2015, the Baltimore-based band Tendrills released a psych rock album called 10,191.
Music
The album's title, sound, emotionality, and some of its lyrics were inspired by the Dune novels.
Music
The song was released on 2017, and it was created using the voice synthesizer Hatsune Miku for her 10th anniversary.
Music
"Rare to Wake", from Shannon Lay 's album Geist (2019), is inspired by Dune.
Games
The most important game adaptation is Dune II (1992), which established the conventions of modern real-time strategy games and is considered to be among the most influential video games of all time.
Games
Rick Priestley cites Dune as a major influence on his 1987 wargame, Warhammer 40,000.
Space exploration
The Apollo 15 astronauts named a small crater on Earth's Moon after the novel during the 1971 mission, and the name was formally adopted by the International Astronomical Union in 1973.

The Hound of the Baskervilles is the third of the four crime novels by British writer Arthur Conan Doyle featuring the detective Sherlock Holmes.
lead

Originally serialised in The Strand Magazine from August 1901 to April 1902, it is set largely in Dartmoor, Devon, in England's West Country and follows Holmes and Watson investigating the legend of a fearsome, diabolical hound of supernatural origin.
lead
This was the first appearance of Holmes since his apparent death in " The Final Problem ", and the success of The Hound of the Baskervilles led to the character's eventual revival.
lead
One of the most famous stories ever written, in 2003, the book was listed as number 128 of 200 on the BBC's The Big Read poll of the UK's "best-loved novel".
lead
In 1999, a poll of "Sherlockians" ranked it as the best of the four Holmes novels.
Plot

James Mortimer asks for the aid of Sherlock Holmes, beginning by reading him a legend that has run in the Baskerville family since the time of the English Civil War, when Sir Hugo Baskerville kidnapped a farmer's daughter.
Plot
Mortimer explains that his friend, the philanthropic baronet Sir Charles Baskerville, took the legend very seriously.
Plot
Sir Charles, who had a weak heart, had retired to Baskerville Hall in 1887, after amassing a fortune in South Africa.
Plot
The rather immoral third brother, Rodger, died of yellow fever in South America in 1876.
Plot
Though Holmes dismisses the legend as a fairy-tale, he meets with Sir Henry when the new baronet arrives in London.
Plot

Mortimer reveals that Sir Henry's inheritance is about £ 740,000 (equivalent to £ 103,000,000 in 2023); in view of these high stakes, Holmes asks Watson to act as Sir Henry's bodyguard, and to investigate things in Dartmoor.
Plot
Frankland, is a perpetual busybody and troublemaker, including threatening to bring a lawsuit against Dr.
Plot
After a failed attempt to interrogate Laura, Watson investigates the man on the tor and learns that it is Holmes, who has been investigating in secret to hide his direct involvement.

Barrymore had given Selden Sir Henry's discarded clothes, and Stapleton's hound, having been set on the trail with Sir Henry's stolen boot, had confused the scent.
Plot
Holmes remarks that he considers Stapleton one of his most cunning adversaries.
Plot
After they leave, Holmes explains to Watson that Jack Stapleton was really Rodger Baskerville II, the secret son of Sir Charles' youngest brother.
Origins and background

He was assisted with the legend of the hound and local colour by a Daily Express journalist named Bertram Fletcher Robinson (1870–1907), with whom he explored Dartmoor in June, 1901; Robinson received a 1 ⁄ 3 royalty payment that amounted to over 500 pounds by the end of 1901.
Origins and background
Doyle may also have been inspired by his own earlier story (written and published in 1898) of a terrifying giant wolf, " The King of the Foxes ".
Inspiration
There was also a rumour that he had murdered his wife, Elizabeth Fowell, a daughter of Sir Edmund Fowell, 1st Baronet (1593–1674), of Fowelscombe.
Inspiration
On 5 July 1677, he died and was buried in the sepulchre.
Inspiration
The house was formerly named Clyro Court and was renamed Baskerville Hall towards the end of the 19th century.
Inspiration
Arthur Conan Doyle was apparently a family friend who often stayed there and may have been aware of a local legend of the hound of the Baskervilles.
Inspiration
Still other tales claim that Conan Doyle was inspired by a holiday in North Norfolk, where the tale of Black Shuck is well known.
Technique

The novel incorporates five plots: the ostensible 'curse' story, the two red-herring subplots concerning Selden and the other stranger living on the moor, the actual events occurring to Baskerville as narrated by Watson, and the hidden plot to be discovered by Holmes.
Technique
Doyle wrote that the novel was originally conceived as a straight 'Victorian creeper' in the style of Le Fanu, with the idea of introducing Holmes as the deus ex machina arising only later.
Publication
The Hound of the Baskervilles was first serialised in The Strand Magazine in 1901.
Original manuscript

In 1902, Doyle's original manuscript of the book was broken up into individual leaves as part of a promotional campaign by Doyle's American publisher – they were used in window displays by individual booksellers.
Original manuscript
Out of an estimated 185–190 leaves, only 37 are known still to exist, including all the leaves from Chapter 11, held by the New York Public Library.

Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
lead
(retrospectively titled Blade Runner: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? in some later printings) is a 1968 dystopian science fiction novel by American writer Philip K.
lead
It is set in a post-apocalyptic San Francisco, where Earth's life has been greatly damaged by a nuclear global war, leaving most animal species endangered or extinct.
lead

The main plot follows Rick Deckard, a bounty hunter who has to "retire" (i.e. kill) six escaped Nexus-6 model androids, while a secondary plot follows John Isidore, a man of sub-par IQ who aids the fugitive androids.
lead

The book served as the basis for the 1982 film Blade Runner and, even though some aspects of the novel were changed, many elements and themes from it were used in the film's 2017 sequel Blade Runner 2049.
Background and setting

On Earth, owning real animals has become a fashionable status symbol, both because mass extinctions have made living animals rare and expensive and because of an accompanying cultural push for greater empathy.
Background and setting
Poor people can only afford realistic electric robotic imitations of live animals, often going to great lengths to conceal from their neighbors the animal's false nature.
Background and setting

Most of the world observes a new technology-based religion called Mercerism, which uses "empathy boxes" to link users simultaneously to a virtual reality of collective suffering, centered on a martyr -like character, Wilbur Mercer, who eternally climbs up a hill while being pelted with stones.
Background and setting
Acquiring high-status animal pets and linking in to empathy boxes appear to be the only two ways characters in the story strive for existential fulfillment.
Plot summary

Rick Deckard, a bounty hunter for the San Francisco Police Department, is assigned to "retire" (kill) six androids of the new Nexus-6 model which have recently escaped from Mars and traveled to Earth.
Plot summary
As it is unknown whether the Voigt-Kampff test is effective on the Nexus-6 model androids, Deckard visits the Rosen Association's headquarters in Seattle to confirm the accuracy of the test.
Plot summary

The Rosen Association attempts to use this information to blackmail Deckard and get him to drop the case, but Deckard re-tests Rachael and determines that Rachael is, indeed, a Nexus-6 android, which she ultimately admits.
Plot summary
Deckard meets a Soviet police contact who turns out to be one of the Nexus-6 renegades in disguise.
Plot summary
Failing to recognize Deckard as a bounty hunter, the cops arrest and detain him at a police station he has never heard of, filled with officers whom he is surprised to have never met.
Plot summary
The building's only other inhabitant, John R.
Plot summary
When the androids attack him first, Deckard is legally justified to kill all three without testing them beforehand.
Plot summary
Isidore is devastated and Deckard is rewarded for a record number of Nexus-6 kills in a day.
Film
Hampton Fancher and David Peoples wrote a loose cinematic adaptation that became the film Blade Runner, released in 1982, featuring several of the novel's characters.
Film
This movie led to a sequel in 2017 entitled Blade Runner 2049 which retains many themes of the novel.

Comic books

Critical reception
Critical reception of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? has been overshadowed by the popularity of its 1982 film adaptation, Blade Runner.
Critical reception

Critical reception

Summarizing the essential point of Dick's speech, Galvan argues, "nly by recognizing how has encroached upon our understanding of 'life' can we come to full terms with the technologies we have produced" (414).

In a departure from the tendency among most critics to examine the novel in relation to Dick's other texts, Klaus Benesch examined Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? primarily in connection with Jacques Lacan 's essay on the mirror stage.

The Trillian instant messaging app (2000–) was named after a character of the series.
Legacy
Towel Day is celebrated every year on 25 May as a tribute to Douglas Adams by his fans.
Legacy
The commemoration was first held 25 May 2001, two weeks after Adams' death on 11 May.
Legacy
In 2022, the novel was included on the " Big Jubilee Read " list of 70 books by Commonwealth authors, selected to celebrate the Platinum Jubilee of Elizabeth II.
Legacy

The novel's popularity (or the entire Hitchhikers franchise) has contributed to many homages and references involving the number 42, ranging from numerous mentions in pop culture to frequent mentions of the novel whenever the number 42 is addressed in Western media.
Awards
Waterstone's Books/Channel Four's list of the 'One Hundred Greatest Books of the Century', at number 24.

genr_the_shyning.title: The Shining (novel)
sents: lead
The Shining is a 1977 horror novel by American author Stephen King.
lead
It is King's third published novel and first hardcover bestseller; its success firmly established King as a preeminent author in the horror genre.
lead
The setting and characters are influenced by King's personal experiences, including both his visit to The Stanley Hotel in 1974 and his struggle with alcoholism.
lead
The novel was adapted into a 1980 film and a 1997 miniseries.
lead
The book was followed by a sequel, Doctor Sleep, published in 2013, which in turn was adapted into a film of the same name in 2019.
lead
The Shining centers on Jack Torrance, a struggling writer and recovering alcoholic who accepts a position as the off-season caretaker of the historic Overlook Hotel in the Colorado Rockies.
lead
His family accompanies him on this job, including his young son Danny, who possesses "the shining", an array of psychic abilities that allow the child to glimpse the hotel's horrific true nature.
lead
Soon, after a winter storm leaves the family snowbound, the supernatural forces inhabiting the hotel influence Jack's sanity, leaving his wife and son in grave danger.
Plot
Jack starts to develop cabin fever and becomes increasingly unstable, destroying a two-way radio and sabotaging a snowmobile, the family's only means of escape.
Plot
Fighting off a last attempt by the hotel to possess him, Hallorann guides Danny and Wendy to safety.
Background
On October 30, 1974, King and his wife Tabitha checked into The Stanley Hotel in nearby Estes Park, Colorado.
Background

They were the only two guests in the hotel that night: "When we arrived, they were just getting ready to close for the season, and we found ourselves the only guests in the place — with all those long, empty corridors".
Background
Ten years earlier, King had read Ray Bradbury 's 1950 short story " The Veldt " and was inspired to write a story about a person whose dreams would become real.
Background
In 1972, King started a novel entitled Darkshine, which was to be about a psychic boy in a psychic amusement park, but the idea never came to fruition and he abandoned the book.
Background
Taped orchestral music played in the room and theirs was the only table set for dining: "Except for our table all the chairs were up on the tables.
Background

The Shining was also heavily influenced by Shirley Jackson 's 1959 novel The Haunting of Hill House, Edgar Allan Poe 's short stories " The Fall of the House of Usher " (1839) and " The Masque of the Red Death " (1842), and Robert Marasco 's 1973 novel Burnt Offerings.
Background
The first draft of The Shining took less than four months to complete and he was able to publish it before the others.
Background
The title was inspired by the 1970 John Lennon song " Instant Karma!
Deleted prologue and epilogue
The Shining originally included a prologue titled "Before the Play" that chronicled earlier events in the Overlook's history, as well as an epilogue titled "After the Play".
Deleted prologue and epilogue

The prologue was later published in Whispers magazine in August 1982, and an abridged version appeared in the April 26–May 2, 1997 issue of TV Guide to promote the then-upcoming miniseries of The Shining.
Deleted prologue and epilogue
The epilogue was thought to have been lost but was re-discovered in 2016 as part of an early manuscript version of the novel.
Sequel
In November 2009, during a reading at the Canon Theatre in Toronto, King described to the audience an idea for a sequel to The Shining.
Sequel
Voting ended on December 31, and it was revealed that Doctor Sleep received 5,861 votes, while The Wind Through the Keyhole received 5,812.
Sequel
In Doctor Sleep, published in September 2013, the plot includes a traveling group of psychic vampires called The True Knot.
Adaptations
The novel was adapted into a 1980 feature film of the same name directed by Stanley Kubrick and co-written with Diane Johnson.
Adaptations
King's disdain of the film has not lessened in recent years, with his 2018 novel The Outsider even including a jab about how poorly done Kubrick's interpretation of the film is.
Adaptations
The novel was also later adapted into a television miniseries, which premiered in 1997 on ABC.
Adaptations
The novel was adapted into an opera of the same name in 2016.
